Q2162
External Disease & Cornea
What slit-lamp illumination technique is the most sensitive for detecting early guttae?
Correct answer: C. specular reflection
Rationale
Endothelial imaging can be performed using various techniques. Specular reflection at the slit-lamp is the most sensitive slit-lamp technique for demonstrating early guttae. Other options include specular microscopy and confocal microscopy.
Direct illumination is useful for enhancing the visibility of raised lesions of the ocular surface and iris. Broad-beam illumination is optimal for visualizing eyelid lesions as well as the corneal opacities seen in dystrophies or scarring.
Sclerotic scatter is a form of indirect illumination and total internal reflection in the cornea; decentering the isocentric light beam so that an intense beam shines on the limbus and scatters off the sclera causes a very faint glow of the cornea. Reflective opacities stand out against the dark field, whereas areas of reduced light transmission in the cornea are seen as shades of gray. This technique is effective in demonstrating epithelial edema, mild stromal infiltration, nebulae, and cornea verticillata.
Retroillumination from the iris is performed by displacing the beam tangentially while examining the cornea. Through observing the zone between the light and dark backgrounds, the examiner can detect subtle corneal abnormalities. Retroillumination from the fundus is performed by aligning the light beam nearly parallel with the examiner’s visual axis and rotating the light so that it shines through the edge of the pupil. Opacities in the cornea, phakic or pseudophakic lens, or posterior capsule are highlighted against the red reflex, and iris defects can be transilluminated.

Q2163
External Disease & Cornea
A patient with keratoconus presents for evaluation of progressive visual loss. Glasses and contact lenses no longer fully correct his vision. He is interested in improving his vision but does not want to have a corneal transplant. What refractive procedure would be most appropriate for his condition?
Correct answer: D. intrastromal corneal ring segment implantation
Rationale
In corneal ectasias such as keratoconus, the cornea becomes thinner and weaker. PRK and LASIK are not preferred procedures by themselves, because the ablation of tissue increases the risk for ectasia progression and attendant poor refractive and structural outcomes. Corneal relaxing incisions also are not preferred to improve refractive demands, because they weaken the cornea, and the astigmatic error, which is often irregular in keratoconus, may not be amenable to correction with relaxing incisions. Intrastromal corneal ring segments such as Intacs can be implanted in the stroma to reduce refractive demands in patients with keratoconus, acting to flatten the cone and improve contact lens fitting.

Q2164
External Disease & Cornea
A 26-year-old man with a history of herpes simplex dendritic keratitis presents with ocular redness, photophobia, and blurred vision. Examination reveals corneal stromal edema, keratic precipitates, and an anterior chamber reaction. The corneal epithelium is intact. What is the most appropriate treatment?
Correct answer: C. Administer prednisolone acetate drops and oral acyclovir.
Rationale
Recommendations of the Herpetic Eye Disease Study (HEDS) included treating stromal herpetic disease with topical corticosteroids together with a prophylactic antiviral medication to reduce persistence or progression of stromal inflammation and shorten the duration of herpes simplex virus (HSV) stromal disease. Because of the absence of ocular side effects, prophylactic oral acyclovir is preferred by many to trifluridine drops. Topically applied antivirals are not absorbed by the cornea through intact corneal epithelium. HEDS showed no additional benefit when oral acyclovir was added to trifluridine and prednisolone in the treatment for herpetic stromal keratitis. Although bacterial superinfections are rare, in nonresponsive cases subsequent stromal cultures for Acanthamoeba may be warranted.

Q2165
External Disease & Cornea
A 41-year-old patient with no significant ocular history presents with unilateral photophobia and blurred vision for 1 week. Examination reveals intact epithelium with a focal area of corneal edema with large underlying keratic precipitates. A 2+ cellular anterior chamber reaction is present. What is the most likely etiology?
Correct answer: B. herpes simplex virus
Rationale
The presentation described is consistent with disciform keratitis, the most common cause of which is herpes simplex virus.
Adenovirus can present as severe unilateral or bilateral conjunctivitis, typically with conjunctival membranes. Subepithelial infiltrates develop after the acute phase resolves.
EBV presents with multifocal subepithelial or deep infiltrates, similar to post epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC). Diagnosis is based on recent history of EBV or high titers.
CMV typically causes retinitis; however, some anterior findings, such as anterior uveitis and endotheliitis, can be found.

Q2166
External Disease & Cornea
A patient has peripheral ulcerative keratitis (PUK) with threatened perforation due to rheumatoid arthritis. What is the next step?
Correct answer: A. cyanoacrylate glue and bandage contact lens
Rationale
Definitive management of PUK often cannot be achieved by local measures alone. It may require institution or escalation of systemic treatment, including immunosuppression with oral prednisone, cytotoxic agents such as cyclophosphamide, or immunomodulatory agents such as methotrexate or cyclosporine. Biologic agents such as infliximab have reportedly been used with some success. Threatened perforation should be treated with temporizing measures such as cyanoacrylate glue and bandage contact lens placement until systemic therapy has been initiated.
Conjunctival flaps are best avoided in immune-mediated disease, because bringing the conjunctival vasculature closer to the area of corneal disease could accelerate melting. Interferon therapy is sometimes helpful in hepatitis C-associated cases of Mooren ulcer-type PUK. Scraping of the cornea is not indicated in this case of threatened perforation, because it may turn into a full perforation.

Q2167
External Disease & Cornea
Two days ago, a 27-year-old man's left eye was struck by an opponent's thumb during a basketball game. Now, he has light sensitivity, blurred vision, and conjunctival injection. His slit-lamp examination reveals 1+ cells in the anterior chamber. What treatment is recommended?
Correct answer: A. topical cycloplegics
Rationale
This man has a traumatic iritis from his athletic efforts. Photophobia, tearing, and ocular pain may occur within 24 hours after injury. The inflammation of traumatic iritis is often associated with diminished vision and perilimbal conjunctival injection. The anterior chamber reaction can be surprisingly minimal but is usually present if carefully sought. Treatment should consist of, at the very least, a topical cycloplegic agent to relieve patient discomfort. Topical corticosteroids can be used if significant inflammation is present. Once the iritis has diminished, cycloplegia can be discontinued, and topical corticosteroids should be tapered slowly to prevent rebound iritis.
Treatment with oral steroids is not usually necessary for mild traumatic uveitis. Hypertonic saline may be indicated for patients with recurrent corneal erosion, but it is not likely to be helpful or comforting for patients with traumatic iritis. Antibiotic drops are not therapeutic for iritis.

Q2168
External Disease & Cornea
A 72-year-old man presents with the lesion shown below. The clinician suspects an ocular surface squamous neoplasia. What is the most appropriate treatment?
Correct answer: D. topical mitomycin C
Rationale
Topical mitomycin C 0.02% or 0.04% can be used 4 times a day to treat ocular surface squamous neoplasia. Treatment generally consists of cycling 1 week on and 1 week off, with a maximum of 3-4 cycles. Patients should be instructed to use punctal occlusion to prevent risk of punctal stenosis. Punctal plugs can also be utilized to reduce the likelihood of systemic absorption and help prevent punctal stenosis.
The BCSC specifies that excision for ocular surface squamous neoplasia should be performed with wide (2 mm-4 mm) margins utilizing a "no-touch" technique to prevent tumor seeding. Topical chemotherapeutic agents can be used as an adjunct after or before excision.
The BCSC states that all ocular surface squamous lesions should be treated as possible carcinomas with metastatic potential, making observation less appropriate. Cisplatin is a systemic chemotherapeutic agent that crosslinks DNA and would not be appropriate therapy in this patient.

Q2169
External Disease & Cornea
A 70-year-old woman presents for a routine examination. Her slit-lamp examination is abnormal, as shown. What is the most likely cause of her corneal finding?
Correct answer: C. indomethacin
Rationale
The patient demonstrates corneal verticillata. The most common causes of verticillata include amiodarone, chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine, indomethacin, phenothiazines, and Fabry disease. Topical epinephrine can cause adrenochrome deposits in the conjunctivae.

Q2170
External Disease & Cornea
What range of myopia can intracorneal ring segments (ICRSs) treat?
Correct answer: B. -1.00 to -3.00 D
Rationale
The correct answer is mild levels of myopia. Corneal ring segments are approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to treat mild levels of myopia (-1.00 to -3.00 D). They are not indicated for the treatment of astigmatism. While not commonly used for the treatment of myopia anymore, they are most commonly used for patients with keratoconus (KCN). They are contraindicated in patients with autoimmune disease, immunodeficiency, or collagen vascular disease; in pregnant or nursing women; or in the presence of significant corneal pathology. The rings are inserted after the creation of an intrastromal channel by either mechanical means or femtosecond laser ablation.
Patients must be older than 21 years of age, experience a decline in visual acuity that limits functional abilities, have clear central corneas, and have a corneal thickness greater than 450 microns at the channel site. Complications can include bothersome white deposits around the ring segments, sterile or microbial keratitis, implant extrusion or penetration into the eye, corneal thinning, induced astigmatism, iritis, monocular diplopia, and poor night vision.

Q2171
External Disease & Cornea
A 32-year-old man visits the clinic for a routine examination. He has a history of uncontrolled hypertension and thyroid cancer. His anterior segment examination is shown in Figure 1. What additional finding is most likely present in this patient?
Correct answer: C. marfanoid body habitus
Rationale
Enlarged corneal nerves are associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B (MEN 2B), a condition that is also characterized by pheochromocytoma, medullary carcinoma of the thyroid, mucosal neuromas, and a marfanoid body habitus. Additional conditions that are associated with enlarged and prominent corneal nerves include Refsum syndrome, Hansen disease, Riley-Day syndrome, neurofibromatosis, and Acanthamoeba perineuritis.
Preauricular skin tags can be seen in Goldenhar-Gorlin or oculoauriculovertebral syndrome. Additional manifestations include strabismus, limbal dermoids, upper eyelid colobomas, and hearing difficulties.
Microspherophakia is seen in Weill-Marchesani syndrome, a condition also associated with short stature, ectopia lentis, and brachydactyly.
Angioid streaks can be seen in a number of conditions, including pseudoxanthoma elasticum, Paget disease of bone, sickle cell disease, and rarely Ehler-Danlos syndrome; it can also be idiopathic.

Q2172
External Disease & Cornea
What is the most common presentation for herpes simplex conjunctivitis in an immunocompetent patient?
Correct answer: B. unilateral follicular conjunctivitis
Rationale
Herpes simplex conjunctivitis causes a follicular conjunctivitis that is almost always unilateral (except in immunocompromised hosts or patients with atopic disease). Also of note, when it is the first event of ocular infection, ocular herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection typically manifests as blepharoconjunctivitis. Epithelial keratitis may also occur during a primary ocular HSV infection; however, stromal keratitis or uveitis would be atypical.
Bilateral follicular conjunctivitis is more typically seen in adenoviral conjunctivitis. Papillary conjunctivitis is typically caused by allergic, bacterial, or mechanical factors.

Q2173
External Disease & Cornea
A 57-year-old woman has confluent guttae in both eyes. She complains of intermittent, transient blurred vision in the OS on waking. Her best-corrected acuity is 20/25 OD and 20/30 OS at 8 AM. What would an appropriate course of management be?
Correct answer: C. hypertonic sodium chloride ointment OS at night
Rationale
The description is typical of early Fuchs endothelial dystrophy. The most commonly used treatments for early Fuchs are hyperosmotic agents (5% sodium chloride); drops during the day and ointment at night may reduce edema upon awakening. Another option is a hair dryer set on cool.
Bandage soft contact lenses can be used to treat painful erosions and ruptured bullae, but they are not routinely used to treat early morning edema. Surgical options are considered in more advanced disease, with the first-line therapy being endothelial replacement surgery in those without significant stromal scarring.

Q2174
External Disease & Cornea
What corneal deposit would be expected from the corneal dystrophy pictured?
Correct answer: A. glycosaminoglycan
Rationale
The photograph is most consistent with macular dystrophy, an autosomal recessive condition associated with different mutations in the carbohydrate sulfotransferase gene located on chromosome 16q22. Patients develop whitish opacities with intervening haze, usually between the ages of 3 and 9. On histology, these deposits are glycosaminoglycans that stain with colloidal iron and alcian blue.
Amyloid is deposited in lattice corneal dystrophy. Phospholipid and cholesterol are deposited in Snyder corneal dystrophy. Hyaline is deposited in granular corneal dystrophy.

Q2175
External Disease & Cornea
A patient is diagnosed with acute viral follicular conjunctivitis. The patient starts using preservative-free tears and returns in 1 week with bilateral loss of vision, worse in the right than the left eye. His best-corrected visual acuity is 20/40 OD and 20/30 OS. What is the most likely finding on his slit-lamp examination?
Correct answer: A. subepithelial infiltrates
Rationale
Although most cases of adenoviral conjunctivitis are self-limited, epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC) is distinguished by significant corneal involvement. Within 7 to 14 days after onset of symptoms, multifocal subepithelial corneal infiltrates can appear, associated with decreased vision and photophobia. Other complications of EKC include geographic corneal erosions, pseudomembranes and membranes with eventual conjunctival scarring, symblepharon, and chronic dry eye. Anterior chamber cell would be more common in other conditions, including HSV keratoconjunctivitis. Geographic ulceration is also more characteristic of HSV keratitis. Corneal stromal melts can be associated with numerous conditions (neurotrophic cornea, collagen vascular disease, infectious keratopathy) but is not characteristic of EKC.

Q2176
External Disease & Cornea
A 56-year-old patient with herpes simplex dendritic keratitis was treated with topical trifluridine, 9 times per day for 3 weeks. The dendrite resolved, but the patient developed marked punctate epithelial keratopathy and epithelial irregularity. The corneal stroma is clear. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
Correct answer: A. Discontinue topical trifluridine and add lubricants.
Rationale
Topical trifluridine is toxic to the corneal epithelium and discontinuation after 10 to 14 days is generally recommended. If epithelial irregularities persist due to prolonged exposure, the treatment is to discontinue trifluridine and begin using topical lubricants. Adding oral prednisone will have no effect on epithelial integrity. Similarly, vidarabine and tobramycin are not useful in the scenario presented.

Q2177
External Disease & Cornea
Primary Sjögren syndrome can be differentiated from secondary Sjögren syndrome using what method?
Correct answer: A. systemic rheumatologic evaluation
Rationale
Primary Sjögren syndrome is defined by the absence of a predisposing autoimmune condition (eg, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus). Secondary Sjögren syndrome occurs in patients with a well-defined, generalized, connective tissue disease. Both primary and secondary subsets of patients can present with abnormal (decreased) Schirmer tear testing, dry mouth, and positive lip biopsy results. For this reason, a systemic rheumatologic evaluation is necessary to differentiate primary from secondary Sjögren syndrome.

Q2178
External Disease & Cornea
What is an appropriate therapy for gonococcal conjunctivitis without corneal ulceration in an adult?
Correct answer: B. intramuscular ceftriaxone or oral ciprofloxacin on an outpatient basis with close follow-up
Rationale
Hyperacute conjunctivitis is usually due to Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Management of gonococcal conjunctivitis requires systemic treatment, with topical antibiotics used as adjunctive therapy only. Options for adjunctive topical treatment include erythromycin ointment, bacitracin ointment, gentamicin ointment, and ciprofloxacin solution. Aggressive cases required copious irrigation of the conjunctival sac every 30 to 60 minutes. Current treatment recommendations incorporate concern for the increasing prevalence of penicillin-resistant N gonorrhoeae (PRNG). Adults can be managed on an outpatient regimen of intramuscular ceftriaxone or oral ciprofloxacin. Up to one-third of patients with gonococcal conjunctivitis are reported to also have Chlamydia trachomatis and can require additional antibiotic coverage. Corneal ulceration and perforation can occur quickly, so very close follow-up is required.

Q2179
External Disease & Cornea
What technique should be avoided in pterygium excision surgery?
Correct answer: B. excision with bare sclera
Rationale
Several options are available to repair the defect left in the conjunctiva after pterygium removal. These include free conjunctival autograft, sliding conjunctival pedicle flap, and/or amniotic membrane graft. Leaving the area bare is not advised, as this increases the risk of pterygium recurrence. The rate of recurrence with bare sclera is 32% to 88%.

Q2180
External Disease & Cornea
What condition is typified by stromal opacification with corneal thinning but with an intact corneal epithelium?
Correct answer: C. Terrien marginal degeneration
Rationale
Terrien marginal corneal degeneration and senile furrow degeneration present as nonulcerative opacities (eg, stromal opacification with corneal thinning but intact corneal epithelium).
Phlyctenulosis, rosacea keratitis, and vernal and atopic keratoconjunctivitis present as nonulcerative keratitis (eg, stromal inflammation without an epithelial defect). Traumatic corneal abrasion, toxic keratopathy, and neurotrophic keratopathy are all examples of conditions where there is a corneal epithelial defect without stromal inflammation. Mooren ulcer is an example of a nonsuppurative ulcerative keratitis and, when active, presents with an epithelial defect.

Q2181
External Disease & Cornea
A patient presents with a pigmented conjunctival lesion, which he notes has enlarged over the past 3 months. What is the most appropriate management option?
Correct answer: C. excisional biopsy
Rationale
Periodic observation with sequential photographs is a reasonable option for stable melanocytic lesions. For pigmented lesions with documented growth, however, excisional biopsy (and not incisional biopsy) is the preferred approach. Diagnostic results can determine the need for further treatment, including surgery, cryotherapy, radiotherapy, or chemotherapy.

Q2182
External Disease & Cornea
Sectoral iris atrophy frequently accompanies what inflammatory condition?
Correct answer: B. varicella-zoster keratitis and uveitis
Rationale
Sectoral atrophy of the iris is commonly seen during varicella-zoster infection.
Although herpes simplex infections may also be accompanied by iris atrophy, the pattern of atrophy is patchy.
Iris atrophy may be seen following chronic treatment of Acanthamoeba keratitis, but the condition is secondary to the toxicity of the therapies and is not a primary effect of the infection. Iris atrophy is not seen in rosacea keratitis.

Q2183
External Disease & Cornea
What is the current recommendation with regard to using corneal tissue from a donor with suspected Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease?
Correct answer: C. The tissue is disqualified from all transplantation uses.
Rationale
Prion diseases can be transmitted through any type of transplanted human tissue, so patients in whom prion diseases are suspected (even without biopsy confirmation) are automatically disqualified from organ transplantation status. At least 1 confirmed case of Creutzfeldt-Jakob case transmitted by corneal tissue has been reported.

Q2184
External Disease & Cornea
What portion of the average cornea is the steepest?
Correct answer: A. The central cornea is steeper than the peripheral cornea.
Rationale
The central corneal thickness is approximately 540-550 microns, which is significantly thinner than the peripheral corneal thickness of approximately 650-1000 microns. This is mostly due to the fact that the posterior surface of the cornea has a smaller radius of curvature than the anterior surface. The central cornea is steeper than the peripheral cornea. It is worth noting that there is a lot of variability in the literature regarding the thickness of the peripheral cornea, and the Basic and Clinical Science Course (BCSC) notes a peripheral thickness of 650-1000 microns.

Q2185
External Disease & Cornea
Why is tissue from donors younger than 2 years generally not used in corneal transplantation?
Correct answer: C. The tissue is steeply curved and flaccid.
Rationale
Most eye banks accept corneal tissue from donors 2 to 75 years of age. Tissue from donors younger than 2 years is typically not used because it is extremely steeply curved and flaccid. This makes the tissue difficult to handle and poses challenges for the surgeon in creating a watertight closure and achieving a predictable outcome.

Q2186
External Disease & Cornea
What is the pathology of Meesmann corneal dystrophy?
Correct answer: B. intraepithelial cysts consisting of degenerated epithelial products
Rationale
Intraepithelial cysts consisting of degenerated epithelial products occur in Meesmann corneal dystrophy. Diffuse cytoplasmic vacuolization of affected cells occurs in Lisch epithelial corneal dystrophy. Subepithelial and stromal amyloid deposits occur in gelatinous droplike corneal dystrophy. Disruption of the Bowman layer and replacement by a sheetlike connective tissue layer occurs in Reis-Bücklers corneal dystrophy.

Q2187
External Disease & Cornea
What organism is the most likely cause of this ocular finding?
Correct answer: A. Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Rationale
Neisseria gonorrhoeae

The ocular finding depicted is hyperacute conjunctivitis, which is characterized by onset within 24 hours. It features rapidly progressive purulent conjunctivitis, with chemosis and ulcerative keratitis that may lead to perforation if untreated. Neisseria species, most commonly Neisseria gonorrhoeae, but also Neisseria meningitidis, are the typical organisms responsible for hyperacute conjunctivitis.
Gonococcal conjunctivitis is also unique in being associated with preauricular lymphadenopathy and the formation of conjunctival membranes, which are most classically associated with viral conjunctivitis. Gonococcal conjunctivitis requires treatment with a systemic antibiotic, typically ceftriaxone, in addition to topical antibiotics and frequent lavage of the conjunctival sac, to prevent complications. Due to high concordance with chlamydial venereal infection, systemic oral antibiotic treatment for chlamydia is also recommended.
Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae are not typically associated with hyperacute conjunctivitis and present later upon exposure, with less rapid progression.

Q2188
External Disease & Cornea
What feature characterizes pellucid marginal degeneration?
Correct answer: A. inferior peripheral corneal thinning
Rationale
Pellucid marginal degeneration is characterized by protrusion above a band of inferior peripheral thinning in the absence of inflammation. In keratoconus, corneal protrusion occurs at the area of maximal thinning. Peripheral neovascularization and corneal lipid deposition are not characteristic of pellucid marginal degeneration.

External Disease & Cornea
What material are intrastromal corneal ring segments made from?
Correct answer: D. polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA)
Rationale
Intrastromal corneal ring segments are made of polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA).

Q2190
External Disease & Cornea
In a patient with a worsening posttraumatic corneal ulcer and negative scrapings, what is the best next step in managing the condition?
Correct answer: B. Perform a corneal biopsy.
Rationale
Posttraumatic corneal ulcers can be polymicrobial and/or be associated with inoculation by unusual bacteria, fungi, or other microorganisms. When faced with a worsening clinical picture, corneal biopsy is indicated. The use of empiric steroids when the organism(s) may not be known is generally not advised. The likelihood of a viral superinfection in a post-traumatic setting is low and would miss more immediate infectious dangers.

Q2191
External Disease & Cornea
What risk is lower in deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty (DALK) than in penetrating keratoplasty (PK)?
Correct answer: D. cystoid macular edema
Rationale
The primary advantage of deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty (DALK) over penetrating keratoplasty (PK) is the preservation of the host endothelium and avoidance of the "open sky" condition during surgery. The "big-bubble" technique relies on pneumatic dissection of the host Descemet membrane.
As there is no penetration into the anterior chamber, lamellar keratoplasty has lower risks of cystoid macular edema (CME), glaucoma, cataract, expulsive hemorrhage, retinal detachment (RD), and endophthalmitis.
Lamellar keratoplasty can be associated with irregular astigmatism, stromal rejection (but not endothelial rejection), and interface opacification and vascularization (which is not a risk in PK as there is no interface).

Q2192
External Disease & Cornea
What is the most common ocular neoplasm in patients affected by xeroderma pigmentosum?
Correct answer: B. squamous cell carcinoma
Rationale
Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common ocular neoplasm in patients with xeroderma pigmentosum.
Xeroderma pigmentosum is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by the inability to repair ultraviolet (UV) light-damaged DNA. It has skin manifestations of hyperpigmentation, actinic keratosis, and telangiectasias, which can appear prior to skin neoplasms. Similarly, ocular manifestations in addition to dry eyes can include pingueculae and pterygia. Also, 11% of xeroderma patients are affected by ocular neoplasms, with squamous cell carcinoma being the most common. These patients need UV protection and careful monitoring for skin and ocular neoplasms.

Q2193
External Disease & Cornea
A patient with a history of penetrating keratoplasty 3 years prior presents with decreased vision and increased photophobia. Slit-lamp examination reveals an area of corneal edema on the graft with an underlying, linear collection of inflammatory precipitates. The graft epithelium is intact. What is the most appropriate treatment?
Correct answer: B. topical steroid
Rationale
The slit-lamp finding of graft edema with an underlying, linear collection of inflammatory precipitates is classic for a Khodadoust line. The most likely diagnosis in this case is graft rejection and should be treated promptly with frequent topical steroids. Graft edema with intact epithelium is less likely to be due to active keratitis and treatment with acyclovir (herpes simplex virus [HSV]), chlorhexidine (acanthamoeba), or moxifloxacin (bacteria) will not be effective.

Q2194
External Disease & Cornea
A 36-year-old phakic patient with a history of rheumatoid arthritis presents with deep, boring ocular pain, posterior scleral thickening on computed tomography (CT), and the fundus findings depicted in the photograph. The anterior chamber is uniformly shallow, the intraocular pressure measures 58 mm Hg and the angle is closed on gonioscopy. In addition to aqueous suppression, what is the most appropriate treatment of the acute glaucoma in this situation?
Correct answer: D. cycloplegia
Rationale
The image shows a fundus with prominent choroidal folds, elevation, and optic nerve edema. The differential diagnosis for choroidal folds is extensive, but in this patient, the most likely cause is posterior scleritis. Posterior scleritis may also present with reduced visual acuity, proptosis, restricted motility, and secondary angle closure from choroidal thickening. Posterior scleritis, along with other varieties of scleritis, is associated with autoimmune disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis, and is considered by some to be a variant of nonspecific orbital inflammation (NSOI), also known as orbital pseudotumor or idiopathic orbital inflammation.
The mechanism of secondary angle-closure in posterior scleritis is posterior pushing from associated choroidal thickening, which causes anterior rotation of the ciliary body and anterior displacement of the lens-iris diaphragm. As a result, cycloplegia is indicated, in addition to aqueous suppression and use of steroids to treat the underlying inflammatory syndrome. Laser iridotomy is not indicated, because pupillary block is not the underlying mechanism of angle closure in this instance. Aqueous paracentesis is risky in a phakic patient with a uniformly shallow chamber and again does not address the underlying mechanism of angle closure. Glaucoma drainage implant surgery would not be immediately indicated in this case as the angle closure is likely reversible. 
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2195
External Disease & Cornea
For 1 week, an 8-year-old boy has had irritated and red eyes as shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. vernal keratoconjunctivitis
Rationale
The figures demonstrate giant papillae on the upper tarsus and limbal follicles (Horner-Trantas dots). These findings are classic for vernal keratoconjunctivitis, a condition most commonly found in males under the age of 10. Findings consistent with blepharokeratoconjunctivitis would include inflamed lid margins with inspissated meibomian glands and inferior corneal changes. Atopic keratoconjunctivitis is a condition more commonly found in adults and often presents with concomitant systemic findings including eczema, atopic dermatitis, and rhinitis. Phlyctenular keratoconjunctivitis presents with a corneal nodule that is connected to the adjacent conjunctivae and limbus by a vascular pannus.

Q2196
External Disease & Cornea
A 62-year-old white woman presents for a routine eye examination. The ophthalmologist inspects the conjunctiva and notes an elevated area along the limbus seen in Figure 1. The patient recalls having an eye lesion removed. The ophthalmologist finds a photo from 6 years ago, shown in figure 2. What is the most likely diagnosis of the patient's current lesion?
Correct answer: C. conjunctival melanoma
Rationale
This question highlights several points:
  1. Think of conjunctival melanoma if there is a pigmented nodule in the palpebral conjunctiva, caruncle, or fornix, as shown in figure 2. Conjunctival melanomas are most commonly found in the bulbar conjunctiva or at the limbus; however, they can be located in the palpebral conjunctiva, caruncle, or fornix, and these locations are actually poor prognostic indicators.
  2. Now that the ophthalmologist suspects that this patient had a melanoma excision previously, it is important to know that conjunctival melanoma has a high rate of recurrence (> 50%). These patients should have close ophthalmic follow-up throughout their lives and contact their physician right away if they notice any changes in the involved eye.
  3. Recurrent melanomas are often amelanotic. It doesn't matter if the primary tumor was pigmented or not.
The correct answer in this case is recurrent melanoma, given the patient's ethnicity (white), ocular history, the elevation of the lesion as shown by the curve in the slit beam, and the heavy vascularization. See below for a review of conjunctival melanoma epidemiology, pathogenesis, and poor indicators.
The other answers are unlikely. A pterygium (think pterodactyl), is a wing-shaped growth of the conjunctiva with fibrovascular tissue onto the superficial cornea as shown in Figure A, and is usually located nasally and/or temporally.
Sebaceous gland carcinoma is a glandular tumor. As shown in Figure B, these carcinomas involve the eyelid and may be misdiagnosed as chalazia or blepharoconjunctivitis. Figure B shows a more obvious case with unilateral blepharoconjunctivitis with diffuse injection, corneal pannus, thickened eyelid margins and madarosis (eyelash loss). The patient in the question stem does not appear to have any eyelid involvement in the figure shown and has a very focal area of vascularization.
A conjunctival nevus near the limbus is usually almost flat, as shown in Figure C. They can be amelanotic as well, like the one in Figure C, resembling the patient's lesion; however, the patient's lesion was already quite elevated, making a nevus less likely. Nevi can enlarge rapidly at the time of puberty (not in a 62-year-old person), and simulate the clinical signs of a conjunctival melanoma.
Conjunctival Melanoma Facts
  • Prevalence: 1 per 2 million in population with European ancestry, rare in black and Asian populations
  • Metastasis rate: 26%
  • Pathogenesis: Arise from primary acquired melanosis (PAM) 70%, nevi 5% or de novo 25% of the time*
  • Location: Most common bulbar conjunctiva and limbus
  • Pigmentation: Variable (25% conjunctival melanomas amelanotic)
  • Vascularization: Heavy, may bleed easily
  • Poor prognostic factors:
       
    1. Found in non-limbal areas* - palpebral conjunctiva, caruncle or fornix
    2. Invasion into deeper tissues
    3. Thickness more than 1.8 mm
    4. Eyelid margin involvement
    5. Pagetoid or full-thickness intraepithelial spread
    6. Lymphatic invasion
    7. Mixed cell type
     
  • Metastasis: regional lymph nodes, brain, lungs, liver, bone (one study detected mets in 26% of patients)
  • Recurrence: >50%, may be amelanotic even if primary was pigmented
  • Death: 13% (10 years after surgical excision)
*Especially poor prognosis, and residual involvement at surgical margins

Q2197
External Disease & Cornea
A 70-year-old patient with bilateral tearing presents with the findings shown in the figure. What is the most useful test to perform?
Correct answer: D. direct immunofluorescent testing of conjunctival biopsy
Rationale
The case described is consistent with ocular findings in mucous membrane pemphigoid, formerly called ocular cicatricial pemphigoid (OCP). Pathologic support for a diagnosis of pemphigoid can be obtained from direct immunofluorescence or immunoperoxidase staining of conjunctival biopsy specimens. Immunohistochemical staining techniques can demonstrate complement 3, IgG, IgM, and/or IgA localized in the epithelial basement membrane zone (BMZ) of the conjunctiva in pemphigoid. Circulating anti-basement membrane antibody has been identified in some patients with pemphigoid. Routine histopathology and electron microscopy would not be as helpful in this situation. Serum antinuclear antibody (ANA) testing would not be helpful.

Q2198
External Disease & Cornea
What is the best culture media for Acanthamoeba?
Correct answer: B. nonnutrient agar with bacterial overlay
Rationale
Acanthamoeba is best cultured on nonnutrient agar with an overlay of killed Enterobacter aerogenes or Escherichia coli. Alternatively, Acanthamoeba can sometimes be recognized by trails left by trophozoites on blood agar. Löwenstein-Jensen agar is best used for isolating mycobacteria. Sabouraud agar is best used for isolating fungi. Thioglycollate broth is best used to isolating aerobic and anaerobic bacteria.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2199
External Disease & Cornea
What is the treatment for the condition seen in this photo?
Correct answer: B. oral and/or topical cysteamine
Rationale
The photo demonstrates cystinosis, a disorder of amino acid metabolism. Corneal findings include refractile polychromatic crystals that cluster most densely in the peripheral cornea but also exist in the anterior stroma and the central cornea. These crystals can also accumulate in the trabecular meshwork, conjunctiva, retina, and optic nerve. Treatment involves the use of oral and/or topical cysteamine.
High-dose ascorbic acid may reduce arthropathy in patients with alkaptonuria. Restriction of tyrosine and phenylalanine intake is used to manage tyrosinemia. Oral penicillamine is used to treat Wilson disease.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2200
External Disease & Cornea
If Acanthamoeba keratitis is suspected, but cultures have not been positive, what is another diagnostic step that can help visualize the organism, especially the cyst forms?
Correct answer: C. confocal microscopy (in vivo)
Rationale
Diagnosis of Acanthamoeba can be made with positive cultures from corneal scrapings grown on nonnutrient agar with E coli or Enterobacter aerogenes overlay, or buffered charcoal-yeast extract agar. Characteristic trails form since the trophozoites are motile and travel across the surface of the culture plate. However, culture yield only ranges from 35% to 50% in larger studies. Thus, many cases are treated based on clinical suspicion (see below for review of clinical features). If available, another option for diagnosis is the use of in vivo confocal microscopy, which is a noninvasive imaging tool to visualize the organism in the cornea, in particular the cyst forms (see figure), though trophozoites can also be seen. In vivo means no corneal sample needs to be taken; the imaging is completed on the patient through his or her cornea.
When scrapings are done, smears are also made with stains to visualize the amebae. If diagnosis is still not definitive with all the above, a lamellar corneal biopsy may be required to obtain more tissue. Acid-fast stain is not used for Acanthamoeba. The amebae are visualized with Giemsa or with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS), calcofluor white, or acridine orange stain. Acid-fast stains should be used in suspected mycobacteria and/or Nocardia cases.
Anterior segment OCT does not yet have sufficient resolution to demonstrate acanthamoeba cysts. An anterior chamber tap is not warranted, and in fact should be avoided, because it may inadvertently seed organisms into the eye.
CLINICAL FEATURES
  • history of contact lens use, exposure to possibly contaminated freshwater or soil
  • severe eye pain (disproportional to signs)
  • photophobia
  • protracted, progressive course
  • bilateral in 7-11%
  • no response to many topical antimicrobial agents
  • Early signs:
    1. If localized to corneal epithelium, diffuse punctate epitheliopathy or dendritic epithelial lesion (misdiagnosed as herpetic keratitis*)
    2. If stromal infection: usually central cornea, gray-white superficial, nonsuppurative infiltrate
  • Later sign:
    1. central, partial or complete, ring infiltrate
  • Inflamed corneal nerves (called radial perineuritis or radial keratoneuritis): nearly pathognomonic
  • Limbitis
  • Scleritis (focal, nodular or diffuse)
  • Dacryoadenitis
  • Intraocular extension may occur
*More likely Acanthamoeba if noncontiguous or multifocal pattern of granular epitheliopathy and subepithelial opacities (HSV contiguous, dendritic pattern), disproportionately severe ocular pain (HSV disproportionately mild pain secondary to trigeminal nerve involvement), risk factors present including contact lens or possible contaminated freshwater, and failure to respond to initial antiviral therapy.

Q2201
External Disease & Cornea
This distribution pattern is consistent with what corneal dystrophy?
Correct answer: B. Schnyder
Rationale
Schnyder corneal dystrophy is characterized by the accumulation of cholesterol and phospholipids in a characteristic pattern. Individuals younger than 20 years old usually have a central corneal opacification. In the third decade of life, a dense corneal arcus develops. Later in life, the midperipheral cornea opacifies. The photo shown is of a central opacity and cornea arcus pattern.
Granular corneal dystrophy opacities spare the limbus and become more confluent with age. Macular corneal dystrophy opacities start centrally and extend peripherally. Reis-Bücklers corneal dystrophy lesion opacities start centrally but can extend to the limbus with time.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2202
External Disease & Cornea
What is the primary mechanism of vision loss in patients with the condition demonstrated in the figure?
Correct answer: A. astigmatism
Rationale
Patients with Terrien marginal degeneration typically present in the fourth or fifth decade of life with decreased vision due to high against-the-rule, oblique, or irregular astigmatism. Hard contact lens fitting can be challenging because of severe inferior peripheral ectasia in these patients. Amblyopia is rarely present, because the degeneration occurs later in life. Corneal opacification secondary to lipid keratopathy typically develops superiorly and can progress circumferentially, but rarely causes vision loss due to opacification of the visual axis. Although progressive peripheral corneal thinning can occur (leading to increased risk of traumatic rupture), spontaneous corneal perforation is rare.

Q2203
External Disease & Cornea
A 25-year-old woman with a recent history of the flu was treated by her primary care physician for "pink eye" with gentamicin eye drops 4 times a day. Five days later the patient presents with increased eye redness, eyelid itching, and epiphora. Slit-lamp examination reveals peripheral infiltrates in the epithelium and anterior stroma with a clear zone between the lesions and the limbus. What is the appropriate management?
Correct answer: D. discontinue gentamicin
Rationale
This presentation is highly suggestive of a toxic reaction to topical gentamicin. The initial symptoms (conjunctivitis following a flu-like illness) were likely viral and the worsening symptoms (particularly eyelid irritation or eczema) after starting topical gentamicin favor an allergic etiology for the clinical deterioration. Toxic reaction to aminoglycosides can even present as peripheral infiltrates in the epithelium and anterior stroma, with a clear zone between the lesions and the limbus. The most appropriate response is to discontinue the offending agent and prescribe preservative-free artificial tears. Increasing the gentamicin would be counterproductive. Topical trifluridine would only be indicated for herpetic corneal disease. Moxifloxacin is a typical antibiotic used for bacterial infections.

Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2204
External Disease & Cornea
A patient reports a foreign body sensation after hammering sheet metal. No foreign body is identified. What should be the next step of the examination?
Correct answer: C. Evert the upper eyelids.
Rationale
When assessing a patient with a potential foreign body, it is important to always evert the upper lids. Gonioscopy and anterior segment OCT may be indicated for other reasons, but not in visualizing a foreign body on the ocular surface. MRI is contraindicated if a metallic foreign body is suspected. Evaluation of a patient with traumatic ocular injury should include a complete general and ophthalmic examination.

Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2205
External Disease & Cornea
For primary pterygium excision, what surgical technique has been shown to provide the lowest recurrence rate?
Correct answer: C. excision with free conjunctival autograft
Rationale
Pterygium excision with a free conjunctival autograft is associated with the lowest recurrence rate following pterygium surgery (0%-4%). Both rotational and primary conjunctival closure methods have performed less favorably, with recurrence rates as high as 39%. Excision with bare sclera is associated with the highest risk of recurrence (up to 88%) and is not a preferred method of treatment. Alternative methods that have been used include amniotic membrane grafting (which may be comparable to conjunctival autografting, although the current literature still tends to favor free conjunctival autografting), or excision with bare sclera and application of mitomycin C (which may increase the odds of other postoperative complications, including delayed wound healing and scleral melting or infectious scleritis).

Q2206
External Disease & Cornea
A 25-year-old diabetic patient presents with a 1-week history of eye pain, redness, and decreased vision. She states that she scratched her eye with her fingernail 1 week ago. Examination reveals a purulent discharge, with a bulbar conjunctival epithelial defect and underlying scleral necrosis. The cornea is clear. What is the most appropriate therapy?
Correct answer: B. broad-spectrum topical antibiotics
Rationale
The description is consistent with a microbial scleritis, likely arising from the previous fingernail injury. The patient's history of diabetes raises the concern for immunocompromise. Therapy should consist of topical broad-spectrum antibiotics, ideally after obtaining cultures for bacterial and fungal pathogens. Cyclophosphamide and corticosteroids are appropriate therapies for immunologically driven forms of scleritis, but in this case a bacterial etiology should be suspected prior to initiating immunosuppressive therapy. Oral NSAIDs can be beneficial for episcleritis or mild anterior scleritis.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2207
External Disease & Cornea
What fungus is most likely to cause fungal keratitis in immunosuppressed patients?
Correct answer: B. Candida
Rationale
Candida

Fungal keratitis in patients with a compromised immune status (eg, diabetes mellitus, chronic illness) is typically caused by a yeast such as Candida. Candida albicans is the most common yeast at these sites. Tissue penetration of the cornea is facilitated by pseudohyphae, which express proteases and phospholipases. Aspergillus and Fusarium are septate filamentous fungi that most commonly infect the eye as a result of trauma with soil or vegetable matter, or with contact lens usage. Streptomyces is a genus of gram-positive bacteria that resembles filamentous fungi, and may produce an indolent keratitis that resembles mycotic keratitis.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2208
External Disease & Cornea
A patient has watery discharge and itching preceding development of conjunctival papillae. What kind of conjunctivitis is she most likely to have?
Correct answer: A. allergic
Rationale
Intense itching is a hallmark symptom and a classic complaint most commonly associated with allergic conjunctivitis. Symptoms develop rapidly after allergen exposure and consist of itching, eyelid swelling, conjunctival hyperemia, chemosis, and mucoid discharge. Attacks are usually short lived and episodic.
Viral, bacterial, and toxic conjunctivitis are typically associated with burning or irritating sensations.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2209
External Disease & Cornea
After surgical removal of a pterygium, what is the best approach to minimize the risk of recurrence and avoid any late-term complications?
Correct answer: C. conjunctival autograft
Rationale
Several studies have demonstrated that the risk of recurrence after pterygium excision is lower if a conjunctival autograft, rather than an amniotic membrane transplant, is used. However, if the defect created following dissection of the pterygium is considerably larger than what can be covered with an autologous conjunctival graft, an amniotic membrane graft or simple limbal epithelial transplantation (SLET) are viable options to cover the entire area of resection. Covering the entire defect decreases postoperative inflammation and speeds re-epithelialization of the ocular surface.
Although there is evidence that the use of MMC with conjunctival autografting reduces the pterygium recurrence rate after surgical excision, further studies are necessary to determine the optimal route of administration and dose for MMC as well as the duration of treatment with MMC and its long-term effects. Any use of topical MMC can be toxic and might cause visually significant complications, such as aseptic scleral necrosis and infectious sclerokeratitis. These complications might occur months, or even years, after use of the drug. The use of bevacizumab in primary pterygium excision apparently has no effect on the recurrence rate of this condition.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2210
External Disease & Cornea
What suture is recommended for surgical repair of the limbus portion of a corneoscleral laceration?
Correct answer: D. 10-0 nylon
Rationale
The preferred type of suture for repair of the limbal portion of corneoscleral lacerations is 9-0 or 10-0 nylon. Nylon suture is monofilament and nonabsorbable, which provides prolonged wound support with minimal induction of inflammation.
Polyglactin (commonly referred to by the brand name Vicryl) suture is absorbable and braided, which can lead to premature loss of wound support and increased inflammation. For scleral wound closure, 8-0 silk or 9-0 nylon suture can be used.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2211
External Disease & Cornea
A 45-year-old patient presents for routine examination. He is asymptomatic and has been wearing rigid gas permeable lenses for many years for his "corneal condition." The slit-lamp photograph shown is representative of both eyes. What is the expected pattern seen on corneal topography?
Correct answer: C. against-the-rule astigmatism
Rationale
Terrien marginal degeneration is a noninflammatory condition in which the peripheral cornea undergoes progressive thinning. The thinning typically begins superiorly and spreads circumferentially. Clinically, a fine vascular pannus extends across the area of thinning and there is often a line of lipid that deposits at the leading edge of the vascular pannus. Patients typically demonstrate high against-the-rule or oblique astigmatism, and often require rigid gas permeable contact lenses to obtain their best visual acuity. Central flattening can be seen following myopic corneal refractive surgery. Inferior steepening is typically seen in keratoconus.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2212
External Disease & Cornea
A 61-year-old woman, referred with dry eyes, has 20/60 visual acuity in both eyes with diffuse punctate staining and whorled epithelium. The Schirmer test is normal and tear breakup time is greater than 10 seconds. She has been using generic artificial tears 4 times daily in addition to latanoprost and timolol in both eyes. What would be appropriate initial management?
Correct answer: C. providing preservative-free alternatives for all drops
Rationale
This patient has bilateral punctate staining with whorled epithelium in the absence of aqueous tear deficiency and evaporative dry eye. These clinical findings, along with her use of multiple eyedrops, are suggestive of toxic keratitis; benzalkonium chloride, the preservative found in most eyedrops, is a common offender. Switching to preservative-free alternatives is likely to improve the ocular surface. Adding topical steroids, increasing the frequency of generic artificial tears (which generally contain preservatives), or performing punctal occlusion would all increase exposure to preservatives and could worsen the condition.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2213
External Disease & Cornea
What is the preferred medium for culturing mycobacteria?
Correct answer: D. Löwenstein-Jensen agar
Rationale
Aerobic bacteria grow best on blood agar, chocolate agar, and in thioglycollate broth. Anaerobic bacteria grow best on anaerobic blood agar, phenylethyl alcohol agar in an anaerobic chamber, and thioglycollate or chopped meat broth. Mycobacteria grow on blood agar and Löwenstein-Jensen agar. (Middlebrook agar is also used, however this is not listed in the BCSC). Fungi grow on blood agar (25ºC), Sabouraud dextrose agar with antibacterial agent (25ºC), and brain-heart infusion agar (25ºC). Acanthamoeba organisms grow on nonnutrient agar with bacterial overlay, blood agar, and buffered charcoal-yeast extract agar.
When it is necessary to send cultures for mycobacteria (species divided into 2 groups by growth rate, both grow on Löwenstein-Jensen medium and blood agar):
Scleritis (microbial scleritis is very rare)
  • mycobacterium tuberculosis (slow growers) and atypical mycobacteria (fast growers)
  • tuberculous scleritis - consider in chronic, steroid-dependent scleritis or in surgically induced necrotizing scleritis (SINS)
Keratitis
  • atypical mycobacteria (fast growers): M fortuitum and M cheloneae (found in soil and water)
  • immunocompromised ocular surface
  • infections following laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) - delayed onset of ulcerative keratitis after refractive surgery, refractory to treatment, nonsuppurative infiltrates, treat with oral and topical clarithromycin, amikacin, linezolid, and fluoroquinolones with antimycobacterial activity (moxifloxacin, besifloxacin, and gatifloxacin).
*Of note, atypical mycobacteria have been supplanted by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) as the most common cause of keratitis after refractive surgery, however they are still an important cause of post-refractive surgery keratitis.
Uveitis
  • M tuberculosis
  • isolated granulomatous anterior uveitis (exceedingly uncommon if no posterior segment disease)
  • usually granulomatous with mutton-fat keratic precipitates, iris nodules, posterior synechiae, secondary glaucoma, nongranulomatous can happen, too
  • vitreous opacities and cystoid macular edema
  • disseminated choroiditis is the most common presentation
  • retina involved usually as extension of choroidal disease, can have a retinal vasculitis/Eales disease (peripheral retinal perivasculitis)
  • histologically proven intraocular TB found in pulmonary and extrapulmonary infections, and in symptomatic and asymptomatic patients (the clinician must ask the patient in the review of systems for fever, night sweats, weight loss)
  • high-risk groups: health care professionals, recent immigrants from endemic areas, the indigent, immunocompromised patients (chronic disease, HIV/AIDS, or on immunomodulatory therapy), and older adults

Q2214
External Disease & Cornea
What is the pattern of inheritance for the corneal dystrophy shown in the image?
Correct answer: D. autosomal dominant
Rationale
The image depicts superficial fibrosis consistent with a diagnosis of a corneal dystrophy of the Bowman layer (Reis-Bücklers dystrophy). This condition is due to a mutation in the TGFBI gene and is transmitted in an autosomal dominant fashion.
Of the other common corneal dystrophies, Thiel-Behnke corneal dystrophy, Meesmann epithelial corneal dystrophy, classic lattice dystrophy, granular corneal dystrophy, Schnyder corneal dystrophy, Fleck corneal dystrophy, posterior amorphous dystrophy, posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy, and some cases of Fuchs endothelial dystrophy have autosomal dominant inheritance. Macular corneal dystrophy, gelatinous droplike corneal dystrophy, and congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy are autosomal recessive. Lisch epithelial corneal dystrophy is an X-linked dominant disorder.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2215
External Disease & Cornea
A 34-year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis has pain in the eye shown. After cultures have been taken, what medication is indicated?
Correct answer: B. oral corticosteroids
Rationale
This is a typical presentation for autoimmune peripheral ulcerative keratitis. It is most often associated with a history of rheumatoid arthritis, but it can be the first presenting sign of underlying systemic illness. It is a vision-threatening condition that requires prompt recognition and treatment with high-dose systemic steroids.
Topical corticosteroids may be used as adjunctive therapy in some cases, but systemic immunosuppression is standard of care. Oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may provide an adjunctive role in some cases, but are not sufficient as monotherapy. Topical NSAIDs would typically be contraindicated in the setting of a corneal melt, based on their potential to inhibit corneal wound healing.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2216
External Disease & Cornea
What is the most effective topical therapy for keratitis caused by Acanthamoeba species?
Correct answer: C. polyhexamethylene biguanide
Rationale
Acanthamoeba is a protozoal infection that can present in many ways. However, severe ocular pain, a ring infiltrate, and radial perineuritis are some of the more distinct features.
Topical biguanides (polyhexamethylene biguanide [polyhexanide] or chlorhexidine) are the most effective treatment against Acanthamoeba keratitis.
Aminoglycosides (including amikacin) and triazoles may have some limited efficacy as adjunctive therapy but are less effective than biguanides. Fluoroquinolones have no role in the treatment of Acanthamoeba.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2217
External Disease & Cornea
For the past week, a 69-year-old woman has had tingling over her right eyelid and forehead, followed by lid edema and a vesicular rash, which respects the vertical midline and involves the tip of her nose. What is her most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. herpes zoster dermatitis
Rationale
The symptoms of paresthesias and a vesicular rash in the first division of the trigeminal nerve, respecting the midline in an elderly patient, likely represents herpes zoster dermatitis, with a previous history of childhood varicella zoster. Herpes simplex does not present with dermatomal distribution. Mycosis fungoides, a cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, presents with a diffuse rash that is not vesicular or acute. Basal cell carcinoma also presents in an indolent fashion and in a discrete way.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2218
External Disease & Cornea
A 4-year-old child is brought to the clinic with the examination finding shown (Figure 1). What additional findings should be looked for in patients with this lesion?
Correct answer: A. upper eyelid coloboma
Rationale
Limbal dermoids can be associated with Goldenhar-Gorlin or oculoauriculovertebral syndrome. This syndrome is also associated with upper eyelid colobomas (upper more often than lower), preauricular skin tags, hemifacial microsomia, and vertebral abnormalities.
Ectropion uveae is the presence of iris pigment epithelium on the anterior portion of the iris and can be associated with iris neovascularization or neurofibromatosis.
Prominent posterior embryotoxon can be seen in multiple conditions, such as Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome, an autosomal dominant condition characterized by anterior segment dysgenesis.
Elongated ciliary processes are associated with persistent fetal vasculature (persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous). This condition is typically associated with retrolenticular membranes and microphthalmia.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2219
External Disease & Cornea
What is the purpose of rose bengal staining?
Correct answer: B. visualize devitalized conjunctival epithelial cells
Rationale
Rose bengal is a vital dye that stains damaged or devitalized epithelial cells. The technique is the same as for fluorescein, but it is important to caution the patient that rose bengal dye may burn. Rose bengal is particularly useful for assessing damage and wound healing in dry eye, exposure, medication toxicity, superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis, herpes simplex virus, and varicella zoster virus. Fluorescein is preferred for detecting wound leaks, measuring tear breakup times, and evaluating for corneal epithelial defects.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2220
External Disease & Cornea
On slit-lamp examination, a patient is found to have easy upper eyelid eversion. In addition to evaluating the patient for keratoconus, what study should be ordered?
Correct answer: D. sleep study
Rationale
Floppy eyelid syndrome consists of easily everted upper eyelids with chronic papillary conjunctivitis. It has been associated with keratoconus, eyelid rubbing, obesity, and sleep apnea. Because of the association with sleep apnea and the health risk with apneic episodes, it is important to refer these patients for a sleep study so they can be treated, as needed (eg, with continuous positive airway pressure [CPAP] therapy). Ocular treatment options include aggressive lubrication, taping or shielding eyelids during sleep, and horizontal eyelid tightening. Patients should be encouraged to lose weight.
Carotid Doppler studies are helpful for patients who develop ocular ischemic syndrome. Patients with this syndrome will present with gradual or sudden visual loss or amaurosis fugax. The ocular findings may include rubeosis, corneal edema, anterior chamber cell and flare, vitreous cells, neovascularization, optic disc pallor, optic nerve swelling, cherry red spot, and retinal hemorrhages in the midperiphery. If a patient is found to have ocular ischemic syndrome, treatment options include lowering intraocular pressure, carotid endarterectomy (if patient has severe stenosis), or panretinal photocoagulation (PRP).
Patients with floppy eyelid syndrome may have a higher rate of atherosclerosis secondary to their obesity, but a carotid Doppler test would not be indicated unless the patient had other symptoms. A single-fiber EMG is a useful diagnostic tool for neuromuscular disorders, especially myasthenia gravis (MG). MG is a weakness of voluntary muscles due to antibodies blocking Ach receptors. MG patients will have intermittent, asymmetric ptosis but is not associated with easy upper eyelid eversion. Other diagnostic tests for MG include the tensilon test, Ach receptor antibody test, ice test, or rest test. MG is treated with mestinon (AChE inhibitor), steroids, plasmapheresis, intravenous gamma globulin, or thymectomy.
A single-fiber EMG test result in a floppy eyelid syndrome patient would be normal. A CT or MRI of the orbits would not help diagnose floppy eyelid syndrome.

Q2221

What immunoglobulin class predominantly mediates the pathophysiology of seasonal allergic conjunctivitis?
Correct answer: A. IgE
Rationale
Seasonal allergic conjunctivitis is predominantly driven by an IgE-mediated hypersensitivity response. Allergens activate mast cells via IgE antibodies. Activation of these antibodies triggers the release of histamine and other inflammatory mediators, producing the characteristic response of edema, vasodilation, and itching.

Q2222
External Disease & Cornea
A 34-year-old individual who does not wear contact lenses presents with bilateral photophobia and decreased vision. Based upon the clinical photos shown, what medical history is the ophthalmologist most likely to elicit?
Correct answer: D. recent viral illness
Rationale
The slit-lamp photo demonstrates diffuse subepithelial infiltrates (SEIs). In the setting of bilateral disease, the most likely etiology is a recent viral infection (including that caused by adenovirus). If epidemic keratoconjunctivitis is suspected, the ophthalmologist should, in addition to examining for subepithelial corneal infiltrates, look for pseudomembranes or true membranes and preauricular lymphadenopathy. Topical steroids may help in resolution of the subepithelial infiltrates, but it will prolong the course of disease and may be difficult to discontinue.
Dry mouth symptoms are suggestive of possible Sjögren disease, which is not associated with SEIs. Ocular trauma does not cause SEIs. Chronic immunosuppression can result in increased risk for a number of infections, but the clinical history is most suggestive of a post-viral keratitis.

Q2223
External Disease & Cornea
What is the predominant mechanism of injury following an alkali chemical burn?
Correct answer: B. saponification of fatty acids
Rationale
Alkali injuries raise the pH of tissues, causing saponification of fatty acids in cell membranes, as well as cellular disruption. Acid injuries, on the other hand, lower the pH of tissues and cause denaturing and precipitation of proteins in tissues.  Complement and immunoglobulin deposition is seen in immunobullous diseases, such as mucous membrane pemphigoid. Mast cell degranulation underlies allergic conditions.

Q2224
External Disease & Cornea
A patient presents with a history of chemical injury to the eye, followed by recurrent ulcerations of the cornea and decreased vision. On slit-lamp examination, there is corneal neovascularization from the 6 o'clock to the 10 o'clock position and a whorl-like surface irregularity emanating from the limbus with fluorescein staining. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. limbal stem cell deficiency
Rationale
The answer is limbal stem cell deficiency (LSCD), which can be primary (aniridia, congenital erythrokeratodermia, multiple endocrine deficiency, neurotrophic, or chronic limbitis) or secondary (chemical or thermal injuries, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, ocular cicatricial pemphigoid, chronic contact lens wear, extensive microbial infection, or multiple surgeries or cryotherapies). It consists of a reduced number or an absence of limbal stem cells, leading to conjunctivalization, corneal vascularization, poor epithelial integrity, and chronic inflammation of the ocular surface.
It can be diagnosed clinically or with impression cytology (presence of goblet cells on the cornea). Treatment can be challenging and may include amniotic membrane graft or limbal stem cell transplant (autograft [from the other eye if unilateral] or allograft [from HLA-matched living related donor or from cadaveric eyes]).
Superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis is associated with a superior papillary reaction, injection and thickening of the superior bulbar conjunctiva, hypertrophy of the superior limbus and superior filamentary keratitis. The inferior cornea is not the primary focus of the disease. Peters anomaly is a congenital central or paracentral opacity that is typically avascular and associated with iridocorneal adhesions. Terrien marginal degeneration typically presents in the superonasal quadrant, with progressive circumferential thinning of the peripheral cornea. The corneal epithelium remains intact. Fine pannus transverses the thinned area with a line of lipid deposits at the leading edge of the pannus.

Rationale
TGFBI) gene

Mutations in the TGFBI gene may lead to a number of corneal dystrophies, including Reis-Bücklers dystrophy, which is a dystrophy of Bowman layer type 1. Mutations in the gelsolin gene are found in lattice dystrophy type II, while mutations in the UBIAD1 gene are responsible for Schnyder dystrophy. Meesmann dystrophy is caused by mutations in the keratin 3 or keratin 12 gene.

Q2226

What organism is most commonly a component of normal ocular flora?
Correct answer: B. Staphylococcus epidermidis
Rationale
Staphylococcus epidermidis

Staphylococcus epidermidis is a gram-positive bacterium that is a common component of normal ocular flora of the conjunctiva, lid margin, skin, and mucosal surfaces.
Although bacillus cereus, a gram-positive, spore-forming rod, can sometimes be found in normal conjunctiva, it is much less commonly found than staphylococcal species.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a gram-negative bacterium often implicated in contact-lens–related bacterial keratitis.
Clostridium perfringens is a gram-positive, spore-forming anaerobe that can cause food poisoning and gas gangrene.

Corneal epithelial microtrauma resulting from the insertion and removal of soft contact lenses seems to play a role in the etiology of what disorder?
Correct answer: A. infectious keratitis
Rationale
Corneal microabrasions from contact lens wear are one risk factor for infectious keratitis, as most bacteria cannot penetrate through intact epithelium. Staining at 3- and 9'oclock suggests a poor contact lens fit. Peripheral corneal neovascularization is thought to be driven by hypoxia.

What cardiac finding is associated with this patient's eye condition?
Correct answer: A. mitral valve prolapse
Rationale
The corneal pentacam demonstrates inferior corneal steepening with a posterior float, consistent with keratoconus. Clinically, keratoconus can demonstrate many findings in addition to corneal steepening and thinning:
  • Rizzutti sign, or cone of light at the nasal limbus when a penlight is shone from the temporal side
  • Munson sign, dramatic steepening of the lower eyelid contour in downgaze
  • Fleischer ring, an iron line at the base of the cone
  • Vogt striae, vertical striae in endothelium that resolve with external pressure
Keratoconus can have multiple systemic associations including mitral valve prolapse, atopic disease, sleep apnea, Down syndrome, and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, to name a few.

Q2229
External Disease & Cornea
A 55-year-old woman with a history of multiple episodes of severe eye pain upon awakening presents to a clinic for evaluation. Both eyes have been affected, although not always simultaneously, by her history. What corneal findings are most likely to be present on slit-lamp examination?
Correct answer: C. basement membrane fingerprint lines
Rationale
Recurrent corneal erosions typically occur in eyes that have suffered prior ocular surface trauma, usually an abrading injury with shearing force. Affected individuals often report sudden onset eye pain during the night or upon first awakening, accompanied by redness, photophobia, and tearing. The corneal epithelium may be heaped up and edematous in the setting of an abrasion, or intact at the time of examination. The contralateral eye must be examined to aid in determining the underlying etiology of the recurrent corneal erosion. Unilaterality is suggestive of posttraumatic etiology or pathology related to herpetic keratitis, while bilaterality is more consistent with dystrophic etiology.
In the case example, the bilaterality of the patient's recurrent corneal erosions is most commonly associated with underlying corneal epithelial basement membrane dystrophy (EBMD), which is a bilateral asymmetric condition. Approximately 50% of patients with recurrent corneal erosion are believed to have underlying EBMD, although only 10% of patients with EBMD will develop recurrent corneal erosion. Patterns of corneal epithelial findings evident on slit-lamp examination in EBMD include fingerprint lines, maps, dots, and a bleb pattern (Bron).
Subepithelial infiltrates are most typical of epidemic keratoconjunctivitis. Punctate epithelial erosions are perhaps the most common corneal finding of all, and they are associated with corneal surface dryness from any and all dry eye disease syndromes and tear insufficiency syndromes, but they are not a hallmark of recurrent corneal erosion. Filamentary keratitis is also more characteristically associated with dry eye disease syndromes than with recurrent corneal erosion.

Q2230

A 19-year-old man with chronic symptoms of bilateral irritation and redness has the eyelid finding demonstrated in the figure. What is the diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. distichiasis
Rationale
Distichiasis is a condition in which an extra row of eyelashes emerges from the ducts of the meibomian glands. It can be congenital (often autosomal dominant) or acquired. Trichiasis is an acquired condition in which eyelashes emerge from their normal origin and curve inward toward the cornea. Eyelash ptosis occurs when the eyelashes of the upper eyelid are displaced downward toward the visual axis. Madarosis is a term that refers to loss of eyebrows or eyelashes.

Q2231
External Disease & Cornea
In immunocompetent individuals, what is the most common ocular presentation of chronic microsporidial infection?
Correct answer: C. stromal keratitis
Rationale
Microsporidia is a rare cause of chronic ocular infection in immunocompetent hosts, but when present, it typically manifests as a chronic stromal keratitis, which may be mistaken for herpetic disease. Conjunctivitis and epithelial keratitis are typically seen when microsporidia infects an immunocompromised host, or rarely as a self-limited (but not chronic) infection in immunocompetent hosts. Endotheliitis is not typically seen in chronic microsporidial infection.  Treatments include restoration of immune function and topical fumagillin; in cases of severe stromal thinning, penetrating keratoplasty may be necessary.

Q2232
External Disease & Cornea
For 2 days, a 30-year-old contact lens wearer has had pain and redness in her right eye, as shown. What type of culturing media will be needed to evaluate her most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: C. nonnutrient agar with bacterial overlay
Rationale
The figures demonstrate prominent radial perineuritis and punctate epithelial erosions characteristic of Acanthamoeba keratitis. Acanthamoeba is relatively fastidious (consumes live cells such as keratocytes and bacteria) and does not grow on traditional nutrient media, including blood and chocolate agar. It is therefore important to plate the corneal scraping on a non-nutrient agar plate with bacterial overlay (typically E coli) to confirm the diagnosis. Other diagnostic testing options include calcofluor white staining, corneal biopsy with pathologic (microscopic) evaluation, and in vivo confocal microscopy, which might identify the cysts. Lowenstein-Jensen media is preferred to grow acid-fast bacteria such as Nocardia and Mycobacteria species. Sabouraud dextrose agar is preferred to grow fungi such as Candida and Fusarium species.

Q2233
External Disease & Cornea
What condition is characterized by bilateral dysfunctional corneal endothelial cells with epithelial-like behavior?
Correct answer: A. posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy
Rationale
Posterior polymorphous corneal dystrophy (PPCD) is characterized by bilateral (can be asymmetric) vesicular or scalloped areas of abnormal endothelium with epithelial characteristics. The abnormal epithelium typically produces progressive or episodic corneal edema and can lead to iridocorneal adhesions, causing corectopia or peripheral anterior synechiae.
Iridocorneal endothelial (ICE) syndrome can mimic all of these features but is characteristically a unilateral condition. Fuchs endothelial dystrophy and congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy are bilateral causes of endothelial dysfunction, but the endothelium does not have the epithelial properties seen in PPMD.

Q2234
External Disease & Cornea
Corneal crosslinking has a primary objective of what endpoint?
Correct answer: C. stabilizing progression of ectatic condition
Rationale
Corneal crosslinking (CXL) is the first-line treatment to stabilize the cornea. Often, functional visual acuity can be restored with rigid gas-permeable or hybrid contact lenses. The implantation of symmetric or asymmetric intrastromal ring segments to reduce the irregular astigmatism can help in selected cases. Crosslinking has been combined with simultaneous or sequential excimer laser treatment to reduce astigmatism. In extreme cases, corneal transplantation may be required.

CXL is performed to arrest or slow the progression of corneal ectasia in its earlier stages to preserve visual function. The patients will still require glasses or contact lenses; thus, surgeons need to counsel the patients and set realistic expectations regarding the surgical outcomes. CXL is the first-line treatment for mild to moderate corneal ectasia.

Q2235
External Disease & Cornea
In the condition depicted in the photograph, what material is deposited in the cornea?
Correct answer: B. calcium
Rationale
The photograph is showing band keratopathy. The grey-white interpalpebral deposits are made of calcium. The keratopathy begins as basophilic deposits in the Bowman layer. The band typically starts peripherally and then coalesces inward. Band keratopathy can result from multiple causes, including chronic inflammatory ocular disease, hypercalcemia from systemic disorders, elevated serum phosphorus, chronic exposure to mercury preservatives or vapors, silicone oil in the anterior chamber, and other rare causes.
Amyloid deposition in the cornea is seen in lattice dystrophy. Hyaline deposition in the cornea is seen in spheroidal degeneration and granular dystrophy. Iron deposition in the cornea occurs in the presence of ocular surface irregularities that result in tear pooling.
