Q2236
External Disease & Cornea
What is the most likely causative agent of the skin condition seen in the figure?
Correct answer: C. topical medication
Rationale
Topical medications, such as dorzolamide, are most likely to cause contact dermatoblepharitis. Medications, cosmetics, and chemicals can trigger a local allergic reaction. Type I (immediate hypersensitivity) reactions, which are immunoglobulin E mediated, typically occur within minutes after exposure to an allergen. A type IV (delayed) hypersensitivity reaction, which is T-cell mediated, usually begins 24–72 hours following instillation of a topical agent. Environmental allergens such as pollen and mold are associated with various ophthalmic manifestations (vernal conjunctivitis, seasonal allergic conjunctivitis), but do not typically cause a contact dermatoblepharitis. Staphylococcus hypersensitivity can also have a variety of ocular manifestations, such as marginal keratitis, but its presentation is not typically similar to that of dermatoblepharitis. Demodex has been implicated in cases of chronic blepharitis, but has not been associated with contact dermatoblepharitis.

Q2237

A woman presents to the emergency department with a 1-day onset of a vesicular rash that respects the right V1 dermatome. If the patient develops ocular involvement, what is the probability that she will have subsequent diminished corneal sensation?
Correct answer: D. 50%
Rationale
Ocular involvement occurs in more that 70% of patients with zoster of CN V1, but it may also occur with zoster of CN V2. Corneal manifestations of herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO) include pseudodendrites, which may occur for weeks to months after resolution of skin lesions. Diminished corneal sensation occurs in up to 50% of patients. Neurotrophic keratopathy due to HZO can be very difficult to manage.

What conjunctival reaction is most commonly seen with a herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection?
Correct answer: D. follicular response
Rationale
Features of HSV blepharoconjunctivitis include:
  • vesicles on skin or eyelid margin
  • raised clear vesicles that progress to blistered, crusted lesions
  • follicular conjunctivitis
  • bulbar conjunctival ulceration
Papillary responses can occur in a variety of conditions, including allergic disease. Pseudomembrane formation can be seen with adenoviral conjunctivitis. Pyogenic granuloma formation can occur after surgery.

Q2239
External Disease & Cornea
A patient is referred to an ophthalmologist for treatment of herpes simplex keratoconjunctivitis OS. She has been treated by the referring doctor with 4 weeks of trifluorothymidine, 1 drop to the affected eye 4 times a day (qid), as well as oral acyclovir. She reports little change in her previous symptoms of blurred vision, ocular redness, and irritation. On examination she has mild conjunctival hyperemia and diffuse punctate corneal erosions OS. What is the next appropriate step in this patient's management?
Correct answer: C. discontinuation of trifluorothymidine
Rationale
Toxic medication injury of the cornea should be in the differential diagnosis of any patient with diffuse punctate epithelial erosions and a history of prolonged topical medication use (common offending agents include anesthetics, aminoglycosides, antivirals, mitomycin, and drops preserved with benzalkonium chloride). Offending medications may also cause erosive corneal epithelial defects, punctate staining of the conjunctiva, conjunctival injection with a papillary or follicular reaction, and occasionally, mucopurulent discharge that may mimic a bacterial conjunctivitis. Before any additional management is undertaken, first-line therapy includes discontinuation of the offending agent.

An 85-year-old man who is a frequent international traveler has chronic conjunctivitis with eye redness and irritation, as shown. What is his most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: A. conjunctival concretions
Rationale
The photograph indicates conjunctival concretions, which appear to be epithelial inclusion cysts filled with epithelial and keratin debris, as well as mucopolysaccharide and mucin. Arlt line is a linear conjunctival scar typically associated with trachoma. Herbert pits are located at the corneoscleral limbus, not the eyelid. A chalazion is a chronic lipogranulomatous nodule involving either the meibomian glands or the glands of Zeis.

Q2241
External Disease & Cornea
Several weeks after being successfully treated for herpes zoster ophthalmicus with oral valacyclovir, an elderly patient presents for evaluation of persistent ocular pain on the affected side. On slit-lamp examination, the patient is noted to have an inferior epithelial defect with rolled margins. What diagnostic technique would elucidate the most likely diagnosis in this scenario?
Correct answer: D. esthesiometry
Rationale
The presentation of an inferior epithelial defect with rolled edges in the setting of herpes zoster keratitis is most consistent with a diagnosis of neurotrophic keratopathy, which is due to damaged trigeminal sensation of the cornea. Neurotrophic keratopathy is diagnosed using esthesiometry, a measure of corneal sensation, and is most commonly clinically tested using a cotton-tipped applicator (prior to instillation of topical anesthetic). More quantitative measurements can be obtained using a handheld esthesiometer (eg, Cochet-Bonnet), which is a device containing a retractable nylon monofilament. The length of the filament, correlated to its flex when touching the cornea, is adjusted to the degree of hypoesthesia encountered.
Clinical features of neurotrophic keratopathy include decreased corneal sensation, punctate epithelial erosions (not punctate epithelial keratitis, which would be seen in conditions such as Thygeson superficial punctate keratitis), sterile ulceration (without an infiltrate), and the presence of thickened, rolled, gray, oval-shaped defect borders. Persistent epithelial defects associated with neurotrophic keratopathy tend to be central or paracentral and are often inferior due to the protective effect of the Bell phenomenon on the superior cornea.

Q2242
External Disease & Cornea
One week following scleral buckling surgery, a patient presents with a corneal dellen adjacent to the conjunctival wound closure. What is the most appropriate initial management?
Correct answer: A. aggressive topical lubrication
Rationale
A corneal dellen is characterized by focal stromal desiccation and thinning, characteristically in the absence of a frank epithelial defect. A dellen most frequently occurs adjacent to an elevated limbal or conjunctival lesion (as may be seen following conjunctival closure or in the setting of a prominent pterygium). The most appropriate first-line management is aggressive lubrication with artificial tears or ointment, with or without pressure patching.
If a positive response is not seen within 1 to 2 days, surgical revision or resection of the offending tissue should be considered. Tarsorrhaphy and amniotic membrane grafting play a role in the treatment of non-healing epithelial defects and corneal ulcers, but typically are not first-line treatment for a corneal dellen.

Q2243

A young child with a new diagnosis of xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is referred for ocular examination. After counseling the child's parents on sun protection and symptoms of dry eye, the ophthalmologist explains the need for frequent follow-up to monitor for the development of what condition?
Correct answer: B. ocular surface or eyelid neoplasm
Rationale
XP is an autosomal recessive disease characterized by the inability to repair DNA damaged by ultraviolet light. Commonly associated ocular conditions are keratoconjunctivitis sicca, exposure keratitis, pinguecula, and pterygia. Ocular neoplasms occur in 11% of patients and require frequent monitoring. These include squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, and melanoma both on the ocular surface and the eyelids. XP is not associated with solar retinopathy, and there is no strong association between early cataract formation and XP.

Marginal keratitis is typically caused by an antigenic immune response to what target?

Staphylococcus

It is important to recognize that marginal keratitis is not associated with an infection but is, rather, an immune-mediated corneal reaction to soluble staphylococcal antigens in the tears. Adenoviral antigens do not cause marginal keratitis. Herpes virus can present with a marginal keratitis similar to Staphylococcus aureus. S. aureus is a much more common cause, however. A host reaction to basement membrane would be mucous membrane pemphigoid (formerly ocular cicatricial pemphigoid).

What primary intraocular malignancy would be considered acceptable in a potential donor cornea?

The Eye Bank Association of America and the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) have developed extensive criteria for screening donor corneas prior to distribution to avoid transmissible infections and other conditions. Intraocular neoplasms contraindicating donor cornea use include retinoblastoma, disseminated lymphoma, adenocarcinoma, and any anterior segment malignancy. Eyes with localized posterior choroidal melanoma are considered acceptable, although some medical eye bank directors decline their use.

Mooren ulcer is a chronic, progressive painful idiopathic ulceration of the peripheral cornea. The epithelium is affected, and there can be severe peripheral corneal thinning and perforation. Staphylococcal marginal keratitis has a more indolent course, and may be characterized by intact epithelium, mild to moderate pain, and little to no corneal stromal thinning. Terrien marginal degeneration and senile furrow degeneration are nonpainful, slowly progressive degenerations of the cornea.

Q2247

What condition is most commonly associated with the finding demonstrated in the picture?

Posterior embryotoxon is a thickened and anteriorly displaced Schwalbe line that can be seen by external examination. Although it is a known characteristic of Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome, most cases of posterior embryotoxon are seen in normal eyes. Peters anomaly is a congenital condition characterized by a paracentral corneal opacity with absence of underlying Descemet membrane and corneal endothelium. Congenital aniridia is incomplete formation of the iris and is associated with corneal pannus, glaucoma, cataracts, and foveal and optic nerve hypoplasia. Posterior embryotoxon is not associated with Peters anomaly or congenital aniridia.

Q2248

A 73-year-old woman was referred for evaluation of a corneal abnormality. The patient underwent trabeculectomy 1 week prior. On examination, there is an elevated bleb superiorly. There is the appearance of thinning and pooling of fluorescein in the corneal periphery adjacent to the bleb. What is the best treatment plan for this patient?
Correct answer: D. patching followed by frequent lubrication
Rationale
Dellen are saucerlike depressions in the corneal surface due to focal stromal dehydration. They often occur at or near the limbus, adjacent to conjunctival surface elevations. There is pooling of fluorescein with minimal staining. Since they are not infectious in nature, topical antibiotics such as fluoroquinolones, vancomycin, or tobramycin will not be effective. A dellen would not be an indication for bleb revision. Patching and frequent lubrication will be most effective in rehydrating the corneal stroma and resolving the dellen.

What is the most appropriate management of the nodular, pigmented conjunctival lesion shown in the figure?

Rationale
The concern is for conjunctival melanoma. In this scenario, as with most suspicious conjunctival lesions, local excision with a 2-mm margin is recommended using the "no touch" technique. Adjunctive cryotherapy is also recommended to improve the prognosis, and curettage of the corneal epithelium with absolute alcohol is recommended to manage corneal epithelial involvement. Topical chemotherapeutic agents such as interferon alpha-2b and mitomycin C are an alternative option for management of ocular surface tumors, but they are generally not considered to be first line. Enucleation and plaque brachytherapy would be inappropriate in this case.

Q2250
External Disease & Cornea
For a 36-year-old woman with a 20-year history of soft contact lens wear and 270 degrees of bilateral, diffuse whorled corneal epithelium, and 3 mm of peripheral neovascularization, what is the most appropriate initial management?
Correct answer: A. Discontinue all contact lens wear.
Rationale
The presentation is consistent with severe limbal stem cell deficiency (LSCD) in a young patient with extensive history of contact lens wear. Women, especially long-term soft contact lens wearers, are the most susceptible to developing LSCD. The most important initial intervention is to remove any ongoing toxic insult to the limbal stem cells; for the patient in this scenario, complete cessation of contact lens wear is necessary.
Bandage soft contact lenses may artificially relieve some of the patient's discomfort, but they are not indicated in this case, because they can worsen the LSCD. Topical steroids may be useful adjunctive measures to long-term management of LSCD, but they are not as important as stopping contact lens wear. Limbal transplantation can sometimes be necessary in severe cases, but it is not appropriate initial treatment.

Q2251
External Disease & Cornea
What test is important to perform in a patient with a persistent corneal epithelial defect?
Correct answer: D. corneal sensation
Rationale
A common cause of persistent epithelial defects is neurotrophic keratopathy, which can be seen in the setting of herpes simplex virus, herpes zoster virus, and diabetes. As such, it is important to check corneal sensation, or corneal esthesiometry, in these patients. While a wisp of cotton from a cotton applicator is most commonly used for this purpose, handheld esthesiometers can better quantify cornea sensation.
Other reasons for a persistent epithelial defect include limbal stem cell deficiency, exposure keratopathy, toxic causes, and neuroparalytic disease. As such, it is important to assess limbal health in these patients, look for anatomic abnormalities (proptosis, ectropion), obtain a complete medication history, and evaluate the cranial nerves for defects.
While rose bengal staining, intraocular pressure, and specular microscopy are important in characterizing different types of corneal pathology, they are less important than corneal sensation when there is concern for a neurotrophic defect.

Q2252
External Disease & Cornea
What anatomic distribution of acquired noncystic, flat, patchy or diffuse brown pigmentation of the conjunctiva is most associated with possible progression to conjunctival melanoma?
Correct answer: B. unilateral, affecting palpebral conjunctiva
Rationale
How worried should you be when you see such acquired pigmentation? The description of the pigmentation points to either complexion-associated melanosis (CAM) or primary acquired melanosis (PAM). It could be a nevus; however, think "cystic" (50%), "may be flat or elevated" when it comes to a nevus (and arising when under 20 years old). Now that you've thought about what it is, where is the lesion? If you see it fairly symmetrically in the other eye, you can rest a little easier. Your diagnosis will likely be complexion-associated melanosis (CAM) which is usually bilateral and symmetric and carries very little risk of progression to melanoma. CAM usually is in the setting of a darker skin; however it can develop in all races (5% of whites). If you don't see another similar pattern of pigmentation in the other eye, then you're likely dealing with primary acquired melanosis (PAM), which is a unilateral or highly asymmetric (if bilateral) premalignant or preinvasive pigmented lesion of the conjunctiva most often seen in light-skinned individuals.
When PAM is clinically suspected (the examiner sees an acquired noncystic, flat, patchy or diffuse, tan to brown pigmentation of the conjunctival epithelium in a middle-aged patient), then the examiner should be aware that this may progress to melanoma. While it is difficult to predict which PAM lesions will progress, the examiner should be most suspicious of lesions involving the palpebral conjunctiva (also the fornix or caruncle). Larger size (3 clock-hours or more) also may predict progression to melanoma. Thus, involvement of more than 2 clock-hours of conjunctiva is a reason to excise the lesion to send to pathology for diagnosis.
Of note, other worrisome findings include enlargement, a nodular appearance, feeder vessels, and thickening.
Most malignant melanoma of the conjunctiva arise from PAM (70%). 5% arise from nevi and 25% arise de novo. Any pigmented lesion on the palpebral conjunctiva, cornea or in the fornix should be biopsied.
Bilateral pigmentation is more commonly associated with CAM, which is very unlikely to progress to melanoma, and bulbar conjunctival involvement is less associated with progression to melanoma than palpebral conjunctival involvement.
Again, bilateral pigmentation is more commonly associated with CAM, which, even with palpebral conjunctival involvement, is still very unlikely to progress to melanoma.
Again, bulbar conjunctival involvement is less associated with progression to melanoma than palpebral conjunctival involvement.

Q2253
External Disease & Cornea
What is the source for the generation of singlet oxygen and superoxide anion-free oxygen radicals in collagen crosslinking procedures?
Correct answer: A. riboflavin and UVA light
Rationale
Collagen crosslinking utilizes vitamin B2 (riboflavin) and ultraviolet A light (UVA) to strengthen the cornea and to stabilize the corneal curvature. This procedure is utilized for the treatment of keratoconus (KCN) and corneal ectasia. The treatment leads to new physical crosslinks of the corneal collagen fibers. It is not useful in the treatment of corneal dystrophies. The procedure involves placing frequent topical riboflavin drops on the cornea either after removal of the epithelium or without epithelial removal (transepithelial) and exposing the cornea to UVA light for a period of time (traditionally 30 minutes). The full effects takes up to 6 months to achieve. Complications can include corneal haze, decreased corneal sensitivity, sterile or microbial keratitis, corneal scarring, persistent corneal edema, and decreased vision.
Glutathione is a naturally occurring protein that acts as an antioxidant. EDTA is used for chelation in band keratopathy treatment to remove calcium. Selenium compounds protect against oxidative stress and have been investigated in the treatment of dry eye.

Q2254
External Disease & Cornea
In a patient with herpes zoster ophthalmicus, what clinical finding may warrant performing a tarsorrhaphy?
Correct answer: A. neurotrophic corneal ulcer
Rationale
There are a number of causes of neurotrophic keratopathy, one being damage to the trigeminal nerve, which results in corneal hypoesthesia or anesthesia. The most common cause of neurotrophic keratopathy is herpetic keratitis, which can produce persistent corneal epithelial defects in the absence of replicating virus or active inflammation. Management of neurotrophic keratopathy can involve frequent lubrication with nonpreserved ointments. Patching; low-water content, high oxygen-permeable therapeutic contact lenses; or scleral-bearing contact lenses with a fluid-filled reservoir can facilitate reepithelialization or improve keratopathy. Lateral and/or medial tarsorrhaphy may be required to prevent surface desiccation. Tarsorrhaphy decreases tear-film evaporation and tear-film osmolarity, presumably by reducing the surface area of corneal exposure.

Q2255
External Disease & Cornea
What are typical skin findings seen in rosacea?
Correct answer: D. pustules, papules, and telangiectasia
Rationale
Rosacea is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction that is more common in fair-skinned individuals aged 30-60 years. Patients have cutaneous sebaceous gland dysfunction that causes erythema, pustules, papules, and telangiectasia of the facial skin. Patients can develop a malar rash. Rhinophyma (large, bulb-shaped, red-colored nose) occurs later in the disease course. More than 50% of patients will have ocular involvement, which can include blepharitis, chalazion, keratoconjunctivitis sicca, and keratitis. The condition may be exacerbated by ultraviolet light, alcohol, and caffeine. Treatment options include oral tetracycline/doxycycline, oral flaxseed oil and omega-3 fatty acids, and topical metronidazole to facial skin. Ocular involvement may be treated with eyelid hygiene, topical antibiotic ointments/gels, and artificial tears.
Erythematous scaling lesions occur with contact dermatitis. Other manifestations may include erythema, edema, and itchy periorbital skin. This condition may occur around the eyes secondary to makeup, soaps, or eye drops.
"Shiny, white-yellow papule with a central umbilication" is a classic description for molluscum contagiosum lesions. The lesions are caused by the poxvirus and can spread with direct contact. The virus can also cause a follicular conjunctivitis and punctate keratitis. Occasionally, basal cell carcinoma on the lid may have a central ulceration that may mimic a molluscum lesion.
Vesicles with ulceration, weeping, and scarring describe a dermatitis from varicella zoster virus. The zoster virus resides in the trigeminal ganglion and can become active in times of stress. If the reactivation occurs in V1 (nasociliary nerve), patients are most likely to have ocular manifestation of the virus. The ocular symptoms include dendrites without terminal bulbs, dendritiform epithelial plaques, stromal keratitis, endotheliitis, uveitis, acute retinal necrosis, ischemic optic neuropathy, CN palsy (3, 4, or 6), Ramsay Hunt syndrome (CN5 and 7 involvement with facial paralysis), zoster sine herpete (zoster-type dermatomal pain without rash).

Q2256
External Disease & Cornea
Where can Hassall-Henle bodies be found?
Correct answer: D. Descemet membrane
Rationale
Hassall-Henle bodies are small, wart-like, transparent peripheral excrescences found in Descemet membrane. Commonly observed in the elderly, they are composed of collagen and result from the thickening of the membrane with age. They represent overactive hyaline production by endothelial cells.

Q2257
External Disease & Cornea
What refractive procedure may be appropriate for the correction of refractive error in a patient with keratoconus?
Correct answer: D. intrastromal corneal ring segments (ICRSs)
Rationale
Patients with keratoconus or other ectatic disorders are not considered for refractive ablation procedures (LASIK, PRK) or incisional ablation procedures (AK), because the thin cornea has an unpredictable refractive response, and further reducing its thickness can lead to progression of ectasia. LASIK and PRK are contraindicated in patients with manifest or forme fruste keratoconus. The safety and efficacy of surface ablation, combined with or performed after collagen cross-linking, is under investigation and may be a viable alternative therapeutic modality for these patients.
Although some early case reports have suggested that combining CCL treatments with PRK may offer some benefit to keratoconus patients, the clinical experience remains preliminary.
ICRSs can be indicated in certain patients with keratoconus. In 2004, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted a humanitarian device exemption for Intacs (Oasis Medical) as a treatment to reduce or eliminate myopia and astigmatism in patients with keratoconus who are no longer able to achieve adequate vision with contact lenses or spectacles, and thus defer the need for keratoplasty.

Q2258
External Disease & Cornea
A 68-year-old man was treated for cutaneous varicella zoster involving the superior division of the 5th cranial nerve. Initially he had no ophthalmic manifestations. Two years later he developed a new epithelial defect in his right eye. What is the most likely etiology of this new finding?
Correct answer: D. neurotrophic ulcer
Rationale
Dysfunction of the superior division of the 5th cranial nerve following herpes zoster ophthalmicus can lead to neurotrophic keratopathy. This manifests as an irregular corneal surface, corneal epithelial defects, or progressive sterile ulceration. In contrast, recurrent varicella zoster ophthalmicus represents live, replicating virus and is characterized by vesicular lesions within the superior division of the trigeminal dermatome. Corneal manifestations of recurrent varicella zoster include punctate and dendritic epithelial keratitis. Bacterial ulcers are generally more rapid in onset and progression of pain and have an associated stromal infiltrate. Toxic conjunctivitis presents with conjunctival injection, papillary reaction, mucopurulent discharge, and punctate keratopathy. Recurrent corneal erosion is seen in the setting of underlying abnormalities in the epithelial basement membrane complex.

Q2259
External Disease & Cornea
What is a risk factor for epithelial basement membrane dystrophy (EBMD)?
Correct answer: B. age greater than 50
Rationale
EBMD (also known as anterior basement membrane dystrophy, map-dot-fingerprint, or Cogan microcystic epithelial dystrophy) is the most common anterior corneal dystrophy. It is usually bilateral and is usually sporadic, but rare cases have been category 1 (gene is mapped, identified, and specific mutations have been described). EBMD is more common in women, and occurs more frequently after the age of 50. It is not associated with use of multiple eye drops or hyperlipidemia. Abnormal serum lipid levels are associated with Schnyder corneal dystrophy, which is a stromal corneal dystrophy.

Q2260
External Disease & Cornea
What is a preferred medium for culturing fungal organisms?
Correct answer: B. Sabouraud agar
Rationale
Sabouraud agar is supportive of fungal cultures. The other media are suitable for culture of aerobic bacteria (chocolate agar), mycobacteria (Lowenstein-Jensen agar), or Acanthamoeba (nonnutrient agar with bacterial overlay).

Q2261
External Disease & Cornea
High-dose oral administration of what vitamin may be beneficial in the treatment of an acute alkali corneal burn?
Correct answer: A. vitamin C
Rationale
When treating a corneal alkali burn, oral administration of high-dose vitamin C (2 g per day) may reduce the risk of corneal perforation by acting as a cofactor in collagen synthesis. Renal function should be monitored when this therapy is initiated.
Chronic vitamin A deficiency (rare in the developed world) can lead to chronic ocular surface disease and corneal ulceration, but it would not play a role in an acute alkali injury.
Vitamins B12 and E do not play a role in treating corneal disease.

Q2262
External Disease & Cornea
What treatment is indicated for active herpes zoster stromal keratitis?
Correct answer: B. topical corticosteroids
Rationale
Herpes zoster stromal keratitis represents an immunologically driven delayed response to previous herpes zoster ophthalmicus infection. It typically manifests as a multifocal nummular anterior stromal keratitis that responds well to topical steroid therapy. These lesions may progress to scar tissue, and steroid treatment is preferred over observation. For stromal keratitis, topical antiviral coverage is not recommended.

Q2263
External Disease & Cornea
For a patient with chronic symptomatic staphylococcal marginal keratitis, what treatment, in addition to daily lid hygiene and use of warm compresses, would be recommended?
Correct answer: D. topical erythromycin ointment at bedtime
Rationale
For chronic staphylococcal marginal keratitis not responsive to eyelid hygiene and warm compresses, addition of a nightly antibiotic ointment can be a useful adjunctive therapy.
To exclude malignancy, eyelid biopsy should be considered for atypical recurrent chalazia, but it is not an appropriate treatment for marginal keratitis. Placement of punctal plugs may actually worsen marginal keratitis if the underlying lid margin disease is not adequately controlled. Topical 5% sodium chloride ointment (Muro-128) is recommended for relief of recurrent erosions or corneal edema, but has no role in the treatment of marginal keratitis.

Q2264
External Disease & Cornea
What is the most common cause of secondary corneal graft failure?
Correct answer: B. allograft rejection
Rationale
The most common cause of secondary graft failure is immune-mediated allograft rejection. Although glaucoma, trauma, or infection can lead to graft failure, the incidence of these causes is significantly lower than allograft rejection.
Primary graft failure describes a graft that is edematous from the first postoperative day and fails to clear in the absence of inflammatory signs. A deficiency of donor endothelium should be suspected in these cases.

Q2265
External Disease & Cornea
While on an ophthalmology mission trip, the clinician examines a 12-year-old boy who reports chronic vision loss in the right eye. He was hit in the right eye with a rock 2 years ago and developed a central corneal scar overlying his pupillary axis. The clinic is in a resource-limited area, and donor corneal tissue and ophthalmic medications are not available. What surgical treatment option can be offered to this patient?
Correct answer: C. rotational corneal autograft
Rationale
A rotational corneal autograft can be used to move a nonprogressive corneal scar out of the visual axis in an otherwise healthy cornea. This is accomplished by making an eccentric trephination with rotation of the scar away from the pupil, followed by resuturing the button. This is especially useful to eliminate the risk of allograft rejection and the hazards of long-term steroid use. Additionally, it may be useful in children where prognosis for PKP is poorer or in areas of tissue scarcity.
Penetrating keratoplasty and deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty require the use of donor tissue and long-term use of steroids. A keratoprosthesis is reserved for patients with severe ocular surface disease or history of multiple graft failures and would necessitate multiple follow-up visits and long-term administration of antibiotics. Such requirements would preclude its use in a resource-limited environment.

Q2266
External Disease & Cornea
What is an appropriate medical treatment for chlamydial conjunctivitis?
Correct answer: B. oral azithromycin 1 g once
Rationale
Adult inclusion conjunctivitis is usually obtained by direct contact with infected secretions. Clinically, a chronic follicular reaction is seen. Medical therapy options for chlamydial conjunctivitis include:
  1. azithromycin 1 g as a single dose (the dosage might have to be repeated in 1 week)
  2. tetracycline 250 mg qid for 1 week
  3. doxycycline 100 mg bid for 1 week
  4. erythromycin 500 mg qid for 1 week
If you answered any of these in challenge mode, give yourself the point.
Topical treatment alone is not adequate, as this is a systemic disease often with concurrent urethritis or cervicitis. In addition, it is important to treat the patient's sexual contacts.

Q2267
External Disease & Cornea
What diagnostic technique provides the most direct assessment of the corneal endothelium?
Correct answer: A. specular microscopy
Rationale
Specular microscopy is a diagnostic technique that provides direct, objective assessment of corneal endothelial health. Density, coefficient of variation (standard deviation of mean cell area divided by mean cell area), and percentage of hexagonal cells are all objective measures of endothelial cell health provided by specular microscopy. Endothelial cell density < 1000 cells/mm2, high polymegethism (variability of individual cell areas) as indicated by coefficient of variation > 0.40, and high pleomorphism (variability of individual cell shape) as indicated by percentage of nonhexagonal cells > 50% are all factors associated with corneal decompensation following cataract surgery. Ultrasound pachymetry indirectly assesses endothelial function by measuring central corneal thickness, which is a function of corneal hydration, and thus a proxy of endothelial pump function. A central corneal thickness measurement of 640 µm also suggests higher risk of corneal decompensation following cataract surgery. Ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) and anterior segment optical coherence tomography both provide high resolution images of the anterior segment, but do not generate indicators of endothelial health.

Q2268
External Disease & Cornea
What test, used in the workup for possible decreased tear production, does not require topical anesthetic and measures both basic and reflex tearing?
Correct answer: B. Schirmer I test
Rationale
In a Schirmer I test, filter strips are placed along the lateral, lower eyelid margin and left in place for a predetermined time (many clinicians use 5 minutes). Because no topical anesthetic is used, both basal and reflex secretion are measured.
If topical anesthetic is used, the test measures only basal secretion and the term "basal secretion test" is applied. Although the Schirmer II test also uses topical anesthetic, this test also involves irritation of the nasal mucosa with a cotton-tipped applicator to measure reflex tear secretion. The dye disappearance test evaluates tear drainage, not secretion.

Q2269
External Disease & Cornea
Nonnutrient agar with an Escherichia coli overlay is useful for culturing what organism?
Correct answer: C. Acanthamoeba
Rationale
Acanthamoeba

This question is most relevant for corneal ulcers. It is important to determine the etiology of a corneal ulcer with a corneal culture when:
  • it is large or sight-threatening
  • an atypical organism is suspected
  • therapy is not working
If you suspect a bacterial or microbial keratitis, the recommended culture plates are (1) blood agar (for most bacteria), (2) chocolate agar (for most bacteria, especially Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Haemophilus species), (3) thioglycollate broth (for aerobic and anaerobic bacteria), and (4) Sabouraud dextrose agar for fungi. Special culture media include (1) Lowenstein-Jensen agar (for Mycobacteria, Nocardia species) and (2) nonnutrient agar with bacterial (killed Escherichia coli or Enterobacter aerogenes) overlay (for Acanthamoeba). Of note, Acanthamoeba can be isolated on blood agar and buffered charcoal-yeast extract agar as well. The trophozoites leave trails on all 3 culture plates. Chlamydia may need to be tested in the setting of conjunctivitis. When collecting a specimen for Chlamydia testing, one should use Chlamydial transport medium, and it is recommended that a Dacron swab is used to collect the specimen. Then a tissue-culture cell line is used for inoculation and observed for cytopathic effects and cellular inclusions. Cellular inclusions are seen on light microscopy when reticulate bodies (the replicating form of Chlamydiae) divide to produce 1 or more elementary bodies (the infectious form) within a cytoplasmic vacuole.  On a different note, Chlamydia trachomatis urethritis may lead to reactive arthritis, which leads to the triad of ocular (conjunctivitis/episcleritis, iridocyclitis or keratitis), urethral, and joint inflammation. In this case, a conjunctival culture will be negative.
Corneal infections can be caused by slow-growing, fastidious bacteria such as anaerobes or other microbes including mycobacteria. Anaerobic bacteria are best grown in thioglycollate broth, anaerobic blood agar, or phenylethyl alcohol agar in an anaerobic chamber. Mycobacteria can be cultured on Lowenstein-Jensen agar and blood agar.

Q2270
External Disease & Cornea
What is the most appropriate long-term treatment of atopic dermatitis and associated atopic keratoconjunctivitis uncontrolled by topical therapies?
Correct answer: A. oral cyclosporine
Rationale
Atopic dermatitis is a chronic condition in genetically susceptible individuals that usually begins in infancy or childhood and might or might not involve the external eye. It involves a type IV hypersensitivity reaction, increased immunoglobulin E hypersensitivity, increased histamine released from mast cells and basophils, and impaired cell-mediated immunity. Treatment includes identifying and minimizing allergens in the environment and in foods. Moisturizing lotions and petrolatum gels can be useful for skin hydration. Acute lesions can be controlled with a topical corticosteroid cream or ointment (eg, clobetasone butyrate 0.05%), but to avoid skin thinning and ocular complications of steroids, long-term use of such medications is strongly discouraged.
Cyclosporine is the only drug approved by the US Food and Drug Administration to treat atopic dermatitis; it remains first line and is the most appropriate treatment. Topical and oral T-cell inhibitors (eg, tacrolimus) have been found effective and have fewer adverse effects than corticosteroids, so they are used in patients with chronic and severe disease. Oral antipruritic agents such as antihistamines and mast-cell stabilizers can alleviate itching, but can exacerbate dry eye with their anticholinergic activity. Oral doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine are not used in the treatment of atopic dermatitis or atopic keratoconjunctivitis.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2271
External Disease & Cornea
What is the most beneficial therapeutic intervention for the acute phase of Stevens-Johnson syndrome?
Correct answer: A. amniotic membrane grafting
Rationale
Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrosis (TEN) are immune-related diseases characterized by acute inflammatory vesiculobullous reactions of the skin and mucous membranes. They have significant ocular morbidity rates as well as mortality rates.
The mainstay of the acute phase treatment is frequent preservative-free lubrication with artificial tears and ointments, along with close observation for ocular involvement. Recently, the benefit of early amniotic membrane grafting to cover the eyelid margins and ocular surface has been shown to have a significant benefit. As a result, amniotic membrane grafts are often performed early in the disease course.
Topical steroids may have a role in the acute treatment of SJS/TEN, but their benefits are controversial. Conjunctival lysis of symblepharon may actually exacerbate inflammation and worsen long-term results. A permanent tarsorrhaphy is not routinely used in the treatment of SJS/TEN. Of the above choices, amniotic membrane grafting has shown the greatest long-term benefit.

Q2272
External Disease & Cornea
Where does the herpes simplex virus (HSV) remain latent?
Correct answer: D. ganglia
Rationale
Almost all persons in the US over 60 years of age have some sort of latency with HSV. Initial HSV infection typically occurs during childhood, through contact with oral secretions or infectious fluid from lesions containing the virus. This initial infection is followed by centripetal migration to the sensory ganglia (usually trigeminal ganglia), resulting in a latency state.

Q2273
External Disease & Cornea
For patients with a history of herpetic stromal keratitis, how does oral acyclovir prophylaxis affect the risk of recurrence?
Correct answer: B. It decreases the risk of recurrence by 50% compared to placebo.
Rationale
According to the Herpetic Eye Disease Study, patients with a history of herpetic stromal keratitis who received a 12-month course of acyclovir 400 mg BID had an approximately 50% less chance of recurrence compared to placebo (28% vs 14%).  Similar benefits were seen in the epithelial keratitis group.

Q2274
External Disease & Cornea
Subtle abnormalities in posterior corneal curvature are best evaluated by what diagnostic tool?
Correct answer: A. Scheimpflug tomography
Rationale
The posterior curvature is best evaluated using a rotating scanning slit-beam device: Scheimpflug imaging. Common devices employing this technology include the Pentacam (Oculus, Arlington, WA) and Galilei (Ziemer USA, Inc, Alton, IL). This technology is particular useful for evaluating subtle changes in the posterior corneal curvature that can indicate a higher risk for keratoconus or corneal ectasia in patients undergoing refractive corneal surgery.
Placido-disk imaging employed in corneal topography only provides information about the anterior corneal surface. The slit-lamp microscope examination is not sensitive enough to identify subtle corneal curvature changes. Anterior segment OCT provides detailed cross-sectional imaging of the cornea and anterior chamber, but it does not provide a good evaluation of the overall shape and curvature of the posterior cornea.

Q2275
External Disease & Cornea
A 35-year-old woman wearing toric soft contact lenses desires laser refractive surgery. Her topography reveals irregular astigmatism and peripheral corneal thinning inferiorly 1-2 mm from the limbus. Her central corneal thickness is normal. Her history is remarkable for long-standing atopic disease. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. pellucid marginal degeneration
Rationale
Pellucid marginal degeneration, keratoconus, and keratoglobus are all bilateral corneal ectatic disorders with corneal thinning.
In pellucid marginal degeneration, the stromal thinning is peripheral, typically seen inferiorly 1 to 2 mm from the limbus. In contrast to keratoconus, maximal corneal protrusion occurs superior to, rather than within, the area of thinning. Corneal topography maps show a typical "crab-claw" appearance corresponding to inferior steepening.
The protrusion of the cornea in keratoconus is central and the apex of the cone is usually centered just below the visual axis. The area of maximal protrusion occurs in the area of maximal thinning.
Patients with keratoglobus have a globular protrusion of the cornea from generalized thinning, most marked in the periphery. The cornea has a normal or slightly increased diameter.
Patients with corneal ectatic disorders are poor candidates for refractive surgery because of the risk of postoperative progressive ectasia.
Corneal warpage refers to irregular astigmatism induced by contact lens wear. There is no corneal thinning present. It occurs most commonly with rigid gas permeable lenses, but it can be seen with soft contact lenses. Corneal warpage resolves when contact lens wear is discontinued and can be followed until refraction and topography stabilize.

Q2276

What organism is associated with hyperacute conjunctivitis?
Correct answer: A. Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Rationale
Neisseria gonorrhoeae

Bacterial conjunctivitis can be divided into these categories: (1)  Hyperacute onset (< 24 hrs), typically seen with Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Neisseria meningitidis; (2) Acute or subacute onset (days), typically seen with Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and Haemophilus influenzae; (3) Delayed onset (days to weeks), typically seen with Staphylococcus aureus and Moraxella spp.

Q2277
External Disease & Cornea
A 42-year-old man is referred for evaluation of red and irritated eyes. On examination, there are severe punctate erosions on the cornea and conjunctiva. Tears are noted to bead along the conjunctival surface in small, individual droplets. The patient's past medical history is significant for morbid obesity, for which he underwent gastric bypass surgery 6 months prior. Abnormalities in what cell type are responsible for patient's symptoms and examination findings?
Correct answer: B. goblet cells
Rationale
Vitamin A deficiency is associated with the loss of mucus production by goblet cells. This results in abnormal drying of the conjunctival surface, known as xerosis. In impoverished regions of the world, vitamin A deficiency results from low dietary intake. Gastric bypass surgery can result in vitamin A deficiency, due to decreased absorption.

Q2278
External Disease & Cornea
What clinical characteristic of a progressive corneal infiltrate is a contraindication for corneal biopsy?
Correct answer: B. the infiltrate is located in the posterior aspect of the cornea
Rationale
In the setting of a progressive cornea infiltrate that is unresponsive to appropriate antibiotics, has superficial corneal scrapings that are culture-negative, or is following an atypical course, the treating ophthalmologist may elect to obtain a corneal biopsy.  Corneal biopsy obtains greater amounts of material for analysis by culture or by pathological examination. Infiltrates that are located in the posterior cornea are not appropriate for corneal biopsy; only anterior material is used in a biopsy, as deeper dissection may lead to a corneal perforation.

Q2279
External Disease & Cornea
What corneal disorder would most likely lead to an increase in inferior to superior power (I-S ratio) on keratometry?
Correct answer: B. keratoconus
Rationale
An increased I-S ratio is a result of superior flattening and inferior steepening of the cornea classically seen in keratoconus. Corneal foreign body can cause changes in I-S ratio but depends on the extent and location of the foreign body. Fuchs endothelial dystrophy and cloudy central corneal dystrophy of François do not typically cause consistent changes in the I-S ratio or keratometry.

Q2280
External Disease & Cornea
What should be suspected as the cause of the fluorescein staining pattern shown in the figure?
Correct answer: D. incorrectly fit contact lens
Rationale
Fluorescein detects disruptions of intercellular junctions. If they are abnormal, it is important to consider the pattern of staining. If diffuse, consider keratoconjunctivitis sicca (severe), viral conjunctivitis, trauma, or toxicity. If inferior, consider lagophthalmos, blepharitis, trichiasis, or exposure keratopathy. If interpalpebral, consider exposure keratopathy, neurotrophic keratopathy, or dry eye syndrome. If superior, consider superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis, foreign body under upper lid, or trichiasis. If at 3 and 9 o'clock, consider contact lens abnormalities.

Q2281
External Disease & Cornea
Following unilateral chemical corneal burn with complete conjunctivalization of the cornea, what surgical option is most likely to result in improvement?
Correct answer: C. simple limbal epithelial transplantation (SLET)
Rationale
If total loss of limbal stem cells occurs unilaterally, an autograft of limbal epithelium from the fellow eye can repopulate the diseased cornea with normal corneal epithelium. The SLET technique is one in which minimal tissue is harvested from the donor eye to reduce the risk of damage to the ocular surface of the healthy eye. If total loss of limbal stem cells occurs bilaterally, options include harvesting stem cells from a living related donor (limbal stem cell allograft) or from an eye bank donor cornea (keratolimbal allograft). Cell culture (ex vivo expansion) of corneal stem cells has been shown to be an effective source for corneal surface repopulation; however, this technique remains experimental and is not available in the United States. Allogeneic limbal stem cell transplantation requires systemic immunosuppression as part of the postoperative regimen and is not needed when the unaffected eye can serve as a donor. Keratoprosthesis can be used in cases of limbal stem cell deficiency, but given its risks (glaucoma, endophthalmitis), this surgery is not the first-line choice for the clinical scenario described. PK is not the appropriate surgery to perform in eyes with significant limbal stem cell deficiency.

Q2282
External Disease & Cornea
A 50-year-old woman has the corneal appearance shown in the picture. She had long-standing phlyctenulosis. What is the likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. Salzmann nodular degeneration
Rationale
The image shown is a Salzmann nodule. Although some Salzmann nodules develop a leash of conjunctival vessels (a so-called "pseudopterygium"), the prominent feature is the nodule in this scenario. Conjunctival epithelial neoplasia can involve the cornea, but the appearance is typically that of a more prominent conjunctival mass with a more diffuse, lattice-like corneal involvement, rather than a discrete nodule. Herpes simplex keratitis can produce a similar-appearing scar, although the vessels would typically extend into the lesion rather than abut the peripheral margin. Furthermore, the corneal nodule is round, well-defined, and elevated, which would not be expected from herpetic stromal keratitis.

Q2283
External Disease & Cornea
Distichiasis is best distinguished from trichiasis by what finding on examination?
Correct answer: C. lashes originating from meibomian gland orifices
Rationale
Distichiasis is defined by the presence of aberrant eyelashes arising from the meibomian gland orifices. Although distichiatic lashes tend to be finer and lighter in color than normal eyelashes, this property is not sufficient to distinguish the 2 entities. Both distichiasis and trichiasis can result in corneal staining due to mechanical abrasion. Although distichiasis is generally bilateral, trichiasis can also be bilateral and thus does not differentiate the conditions.

Q2284
External Disease & Cornea
Patients with atopic keratoconjunctivitis are particularly susceptible to what type of infection?
Correct answer: C. herpes simplex virus keratitis
Rationale
Atopic keratoconjunctivitis is associated with increased susceptibility to chronic, sometimes bilateral, herpes simplex virus keratitis. Adenoviral conjunctivitis (including epidemic keratoconjunctivitis) is typically acquired by direct inoculation after contact with infected secretions. There is no known association with atopic disease. Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis typically occurs in profoundly immunosuppressed patients (eg, those with AIDS). While colonization with Staphylococcus aureus can occur in atopic keratoconjunctivitis, this does not always correlate with an increased incidence of blepharitis. Staphylococcal blepharitis is more common in younger patients and patients with Down syndrome.

Q2285
External Disease & Cornea
What is the most appropriate initial treatment of the ocular complications of Stevens-Johnson syndrome?
Correct answer: C. topical lubrication with artificial tears and ointments
Rationale
Stevens-Johnson syndrome is a hypersensitivity reaction to drugs or infectious diseases that results in an acute vesiculobullous reaction of the skin and mucous membranes. Initial ocular therapy for Stevens-Johnson syndrome should include frequent lubrication with preservative-free artificial tears and ointments. In cases of severe ocular surface involvement, amniotic membrane transplantation over the entire ocular surface can have long-term benefit.
Topical corticosteroids may decrease surface inflammation and corneal angiogenesis, but their efficacy has not been proven. Oral azathioprine and topical N-acetyl L-cysteine are not established ocular treatments for Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

Q2286
External Disease & Cornea
Why are pediatric corneal transplants more likely to fail than corneal transplants in adults?
Correct answer: A. There is a higher incidence of preexisting corneal neovascularization in pediatrics.
Rationale
Coexisting ocular abnormalities do occur in many adults who need corneal transplants (eg, glaucoma patients who may have shunt devices) and could compromise the integrity and survival of the graft. However, relatively speaking, most adult cases requiring corneal transplants are due to Fuchs dystrophy, pseudophakic bullous keratopathy (and the energy to phacoemulsify the lens and damage the endothelium would not be required again or threaten the new graft), and corneal scarring. Although repeat grafts often have the disadvantage of resulting in corneal neovascularization of the host cornea bed in adults, this is less common with the first graft.
In contrast, many pediatric cases requiring corneal transplant are for conditions such as Peters anomaly, which often have anterior segment findings including adhesions between surrounding structures (cornea, iris, lens), glaucoma, and untreated cataract, all of which make the surgical procedure longer, more extensive, and at higher risk for corneal graft failure due to increased handling of the tissue. Additionally, corneal neovascularization of the host bed is more common in pediatrics, and this is more likely to bring immune cells to the graft, which would lead to rejection.
Due to young age and lack of major medical comorbidities in most cases, re-epithelialization after a corneal transplant in a child is actually more likely to occur quickly, protecting the cornea from immune attack.
Pediatric patients have a higher risk of early loosening of sutures after penetrating keratoplasty. The sutures do not have to stay in longer in children; however, rapid neovascularization, especially along sutures, is particularly prevalent in corneal grafts in children under 2 years of age and can lead to rejection. As such, regular examinations under anesthesia are needed, with early suture removal and protection from self-induced trauma.
Astigmatism is not a reason for corneal transplant rejection. However, due to the high risk of amblyopia due to astigmatism in infants and young children, it is imperative to have the child fitted for a contact lens either at the time of surgery or shortly thereafter, and to use ocular occlusive therapy aggressively to prevent amblyopia.

Q2287
External Disease & Cornea
Tarsorrhaphy is indicated as a treatment for what type of corneal ulcer?
Correct answer: A. neurotrophic
Rationale
Common indications for tarsorrhaphy include severe, recalcitrant keratopathy, persistent epithelial defect, or corneal thinning resulting from (1) neurogenic exposure keratopathy (cranial nerve [CN] VII palsy), (2) neurotrophic corneal ulceration (CN V deficit, herpes simplex virus [HSV] or varicella zoster virus [VZV] keratitis), (3) eyelid abnormalities, or (4) exposure (thyroid eye disease). Active microbial (bacterial or fungal) keratitis is a contraindication to tarsorrhaphy.
In neurotrophic ulcer, there is damage to the trigeminal nerve, leading to reduced corneal sensation, spontaneous epithelial breakdown, and poor healing. Tarsorrhaphy enhances healing by reducing exposure. Autoimmune corneal ulcer, or peripheral ulcerative keratitis, occurs as white blood cells infiltrate the peripheral cornea and often needs systemic immunosuppression as a treatment, along with topical collagenase inhibitors such as N-acetylcysteine.

Q2288
External Disease & Cornea
A 25-year-old contact lens wearer has had 4 weeks of severe ocular pain (right eye) and photophobia. The figure demonstrates the examination at the slit lamp. What is the most likely causative organism?
Correct answer: D. protozoa
Rationale
A chronic corneal ulcer in the setting of contact lens wear can be caused by a variety of pathogens. In this case, the presence of radial perineuritis (arrows in photograph) should raise suspicion for keratitis caused by Acanthamoeba (a genus of free-living ubiquitous protozoa) species. Although radial perineuritis has been reported rarely in other infections (HSV, Pseudomonas), the clinical description, chronicity, and history of contact lens wear should elevate Acanthamoeba keratitis to the top of the differential diagnosis. Fungal infections in contact lens wearers can present insidiously or acutely, but radial perineuritis is atypical.

Q2289
External Disease & Cornea
What characteristic conjunctival finding is commonly seen in a patient presenting with herpes simplex virus (HSV) keratitis?
Correct answer: B. follicular conjunctivitis
Rationale
Papillae are conjunctival nodules with a central vascular core and are seen in allergic, vernal, atopic, or bacterial disease. Follicles are nodules without visible central vessels and are found with viral and chlamydial infections, as well as with toxins or medications. Thus, HSV infection would lead to a follicular conjunctivitis. A fine papillary reaction on the superior tarsal conjunctiva, and injection and thickening of the superior bulbar conjunctiva, are seen in superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis.

Q2290
External Disease & Cornea
A 35-year-old patient has chronic unilateral follicular conjunctivitis. Examination reveals the eyelid finding seen in the photograph. What would a biopsy of the eyelid lesion most likely show?
Correct answer: B. eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions within epidermal cells surrounding a necrotic core
Rationale
Chronic follicular conjunctivitis with an umbilicated eyelid nodule should raise suspicion for molluscum contagiosum. The classic histologic appearance of a molluscum lesion is a cup-shaped nodule with central necrosis surrounded by epidermal cells with large eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions (Henderson-Patterson bodies). Vacuolized cytoplasm with multinucleated cells is typical of a herpetic vesicle. Foamy histiocytes surrounding blood vessels describes xanthelasma. Hyperkeratosis and acanthosis with a papillary growth pattern are typical of verruca vulgaris caused by human papillomavirus.

Q2291
External Disease & Cornea
A patient presents with pruritis of the bilateral eyes. After everting the patient's upper eyelids and examining the palpebral conjunctiva, the ophthalmologist notes the findings shown in Figure 1, as well as the associated corneal findings shown in Figure 2. What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
Correct answer: C. vernal keratoconjunctivitis
Rationale
Clinical findings of palpebral vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) include large papillae on the palpebral conjunctiva and can also include corneal changes such as pannus and noninfectious, oval or shield-like epithelial ulcerations in the superior or central cornea.  Horner-Trantas dots are collections of eosinophils found at the hypertrophied limbus of patients with limbal vernal keratoconjunctivitis.
Seasonal allergic keratoconjunctivitis tends to have a shorter duration, with episodic clinical findings that can include itching, eyelid swelling, conjunctival hyperemia, chemosis, and mucoid discharge. While large papillae can be seen in palpebral vernal keratoconjunctivitis, giant papillary conjunctivitis is classically associated with contact lens wear. Atopic keratoconjunctivitis (AKC) occurs in approximately one-third of patients with atopic dermatitis, and features include year-round disease, small- to medium-sized papillae, milky conjunctival edema, extensive corneal vascularization and opacification, conjunctival scarring, subepithelial fibrosis, and posterior subcapsular and/or multifaceted or shield-shaped anterior subcapsular opacities. AKC may present with persistent epithelial defects as well, but shield ulcers are more typical of VKC.

Q2292
External Disease & Cornea
Evaluation of corneal and scleral donors includes required testing for what diseases?
Correct answer: A. hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus, and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)
Rationale
Donor evaluation must include serologic testing for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, and syphilis.
In addition, contraindications for donation include:
  • Death of unknown cause with likelihood of other exclusion criteria
  • Congenital rubella
  • Reye syndrome within the past 3 months
  • Active viral encephalitis of unknown origin or progressive encephalopathy
  • Active bacterial or viral encephalitis
  • Active bacterial or fungal endocarditis
  • Suspected rabies infection or history of being bitten by an animal suspected to be infected with rabies in past 6 months
  • Down syndrome
  • Intrinsic eye diseases
    • Retinoblastoma
    • Malignant tumor or known adenocarcinoma of the eye
    • Active ocular or intraocular inflammation
    • Congenital or acquired disorders that would preclude a successful outcome
  • Leukemias
  • Active disseminated lymphomas
  • High-risk behavior or incarceration
  • Prior refractive corneal surgery (except previous laser refractive may not disqualify)
Proven disease transmission
  • Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
  • Rabies
  • Hepatitis B
  • RB 
  • Bacterial or fungal keratitis
  • Bacterial or fungal endophthalmitis
Potential transmission
  • HIV
  • HSV
  • Prion diseases

Q2293
External Disease & Cornea
How is the diagnosis of mucous membrane pemphigoid confirmed?
Correct answer: C. tissue biopsy
Rationale
Biopsy specimens should be obtained from an actively affected area of the conjunctiva, or, if involvement is diffuse, from the inferior conjunctival fornix. Oral mucosal biopsies may be useful, especially in the presence of an active lesion. Pathologic support for a diagnosis of pemphigoid can be obtained from direct immunofluorescence or immunoperoxidase staining of conjunctival biopsy specimens.
Clinical appearance is important to the diagnosis but not sufficient for confirmation. Newer serologic tests may play an ancillary role in the diagnosis of MMP but have not replaced tissue diagnosis. Empiric treatment is not an appropriate way to diagnose MMP.

Q2294
External Disease & Cornea
What is the most common complication associated with this condition?
Correct answer: B. recurrent corneal erosions
Rationale
The picture is a classic example of epithelial basement membrane dystrophy (also termed anterior basement membrane dystrophy, map-dot-fingerprint dystrophy, Cogan microcystic epithelial dystrophy), characterized by geographic, gray lines and small dots corresponding to epithelial cysts. Most patients with this condition are asymptomatic, but the most common associated complication is recurrent corneal erosions (10%-33% incidence). Corneal edema, limbal stem cell deficiency, and corneal neovascularization are not typical features of epithelial basement membrane dystrophy.

Q2295
External Disease & Cornea
Topical corticosteroids are contraindicated for the treatment of what form of herpes simplex keratitis?
Correct answer: D. dendritic keratitis
Rationale
Dendritic keratitis represents active viral replication and may be significantly worsened by the use of topical corticosteroids. Patients with this disease who are using systemic corticosteroids for other indications should be treated aggressively with systemic antiviral therapy.
Herpetic interstitial keratitis, keratouveitis, and stromal keratitis all require the use of steroids to control the host immunologic response.Dendritic keratitis represents active viral replication and may be significantly worsened by the use of topical corticosteroids. Patients with this disease who are using systemic corticosteroids for other indications should be treated aggressively with systemic antiviral therapy.
Herpetic interstitial keratitis, keratouveitis, and stromal keratitis all require the use of steroids to control the host immunologic response.

Q2296
External Disease & Cornea
A 32-year-old man presents for evaluation for laser refractive surgery. His refraction is -5.50 D sphere in the right eye and -3.75 D sphere in the left. With full correction, he says his vision is still "not crisp," despite measuring 20/20 Snellen acuity in both eyes. His cornea appearance on slit-lamp examination is shown below. What intervention is recommended to improve visual results in this patient?
Correct answer: C. phototherapeutic keratectomy
Rationale
Careful slit-lamp examination must be performed when evaluating a patient for refractive surgery, and should include a careful examination for epithelial basement membrane dystrophy. Careful attention to a supportive history of corneal erosions and/or irregular astigmatism is also indicated in the assessment for refractive surgery candidacy. Epithelial basement membrane dystrophy increases the risk of flap complications during laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK). The use of a microkeratome increases such flap complications compared to the use of a femtosecond laser for flap creation, but both techniques increase the risk of flap complications (eg, epithelial ingrowth, irregular flap cuts, epithelial sloughing) compared to surface ablation. Phakic IOL placement may reduce the refractive error in this patient, but given that he already thinks that the vision is not crisp, he will still have visual symptoms after phakic IOL placement.
Dacryocystorhinostomy is not indicated in this situation, and would not help the patient's vision.
Patients with epithelial basement membrane dystrophy are better candidates for surface treatment—superficial keratectomy or phototherapeutic keratectomy can improve the irregular astigmatism from the basement membrane dystrophy in cases of significant irregular astigmatism—prior to consideration of refractive surgery to stabilize the epithelial layer and refractive status. In patients with minimal irregular astigmatism, but still presence of basement membrane dystrophy, photorefractive keratectomy may be attempted.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2297
External Disease & Cornea
A 63-year-old woman who has had poor vision in both eyes since early childhood presents for an examination. Her vision is 20/80 in the right eye and 20/50 in the left eye. Examination of the right cornea is remarkable for the findings in the Figure A (overview) and Figure B (magnified view). She has similar findings in her left eye. What is the likely pathogenesis of this condition?
Correct answer: D. immune-mediated response
Rationale
The figures depict stromal scarring and ghost vessels indicative of a prior episode of interstitial keratitis (IK). Congenital syphilis is the most likely cause of bilateral interstitial keratitis, although other organisms can cause IK, including herpes simplex virus, varicella zoster virus, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, M leprae, Borrelia burgdorferi, rubeola, Epstein-Barr virus, Chlamydia trachomatis, Leishmania spp, Onchocerca volvulus, and Cogan syndrome (nonsyphilitic interstitial keratitis, vestibuloauditory disease, and associated autoimmune vasculitis).
Syphilis that presents within the first 2 years of life is usually due to active infection. However, interstitial keratitis is a later, immune-mediated response that usually develops late in the first decade of life. The condition is a nonulcerative stromal interstitial keratitis and is bilateral in 80%. Sectoral superior stromal inflammation and keratic precipitates, as well as deep corneal stromal vascularization, may be seen. Complications of IK include corneal scarring, thinning, and ghost vessels (as seen in the figures). In severe cases, a corneal transplant may be required to improve vision. Other ophthalmic manifestations include uveitis, retinitis, optic neuritis, glaucoma, and cataract. Other systemic manifestations of congenital syphilis include notched (Hutchinson) incisors, mulberry molars, saddle nose, palatal perforation, saber shins, frontal bossing, cranial nerve VIII deafness, rhagades (circumoral radiating scars), and intellectual disability.

Q2298
External Disease & Cornea
Approximately what percentage of intact limbal stem cells is required to maintain a healthy ocular surface?
Correct answer: C. 30%
Rationale
To maintain a healthy ocular surface, approximately 25%-33% of the normal limbal stem cell population is required. For this reason, it is possible to transplant cells from a healthy fellow eye or living related donor without compromising the ocular surface of the donor eye.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2299
External Disease & Cornea
A 52-year-old woman presents with intermittent blurred vision. There is moderate astigmatism on refraction. Slit-lamp photos are shown in this figure. Similar findings are present in the contralateral eye. No other family members are affected. What condition is depicted?
Correct answer: A. epithelial basement membrane dystrophy
Rationale
Epithelial basement membrane dystrophy (EBMD) causes gray patches, pseudocysts, and fine lines in the corneal epithelium, resulting in either fingerprints, maps, or dots. Dots are round, oval, or comma-shaped opacities containing the debris of epithelial cells that have collapsed and degenerated before reaching the epithelial surface. Epithelial cell sloughing can occur spontaneously in patients with EBMD. Meesmann epithelial dystrophy causes tiny intraepithelial vesicles that look like minute bubble-like blebs; they appear throughout the entire surface of the cornea.
In Reis-Bücklers corneal dystrophy, confluent, coarse, and irregular geographic opacities of varying densities appear in the Bowman layer and superficial stroma usual in the central cornea. In lattice dystrophy, refractile branching lines appear in the corneal stroma. Although ovoid white dots may occur in lattice dystrophy, they are located in the subepithelial or stromal layer.

Q2300
External Disease & Cornea
In the United States, what is an acceptable donor cornea preservation time for corneal transplantation of corneas stored in Optisol?
Correct answer: D. 11-14 days
Rationale
Optisol GS (Bausch & Lomb, Bridgewater, NJ) is the most commonly used intermediate-term storage medium used in the United States today, allowing tissue to be stored up to 14 days after death. Originally, donor corneal tissue was preserved within the whole globe and refrigerated at 4 degrees Celsius, which allowed tissue to be stored for 24–48 hours. McCarey-Kaufman medium extended storage time to 4 days. In Europe, donor corneal tissue is incubated in organ culture storage that allows tissue to be stored for up to 35 days, but this requires a culture at the end of storage to confirm sterility, which can be complex, expensive, and labor intensive.

Q2301
External Disease & Cornea
In addition to antibiotics, what is the most appropriate management for a 3 mm central corneal perforation caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae?
Correct answer: A. corneal patch graft
Rationale
Large corneal perforations (> 2 mm) typically require emergent surgical closure with a corneal patch graft. Primary closure with nylon sutures is generally not feasible, especially in the setting of acute infectious keratitis in which the surrounding tissue is also likely necrotic. Similarly, amniotic membrane grafts and cyanoacrylate glue are best suited for impending perforations or small perforations, because they are unlikely to provide a watertight closure.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2302
External Disease & Cornea
A history of what refractive therapy precludes a cornea from use as penetrating keratoplasty tissue?
Correct answer: D. radial keratotomy
Rationale
There is a long list of exclusion criteria for corneal transplantation, including:
  • Death of unknown cause
  • Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, or family member with Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease
  • Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis
  • Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy
  • Congenital rubella
  • Down syndrome
  • Reye syndrome
  • Active viral encephalitis or encephalitis of unknown origin or progressive encephalopathy
  • Active septicemia (bacteremia, fungemia, viremia)
  • Active bacterial or fungal endocarditis
  • Active viral hepatitis
  • Rabies
  • Active and intrinsic eye disease (intraocular malignant tumors, infections, inflammatory diseases)
  • Leukemias and lymphomas
  • HIV
  • Previous refractive surgery (laser in situ keratomileusis/radial keratotomy [LASIK/RK])
Refractive procedures including RK, LASIK, photorefractive keratectomy (PRK) all are contraindications for corneal donor tissue for penetrating keratoplasty. However, previous uncomplicated cataract surgery and contact lenses are not contraindications.
