Q2303
External Disease & Cornea
Superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis causes what type of conjunctival reaction?
Correct answer: A. papillary
Rationale
Superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis is a chronic, recurrent condition of ocular irritation and redness that predominantly affects the superior cornea and conjunctiva. The superior bulbar conjunctiva can be injected and thickened, while a fine papillary reaction is often seen on the superior tarsal conjunctiva. Papillae are dilated vessels with surrounding edema and inflammatory cells producing raised elevations of the conjunctival epithelium. Papillary reactions are also seen in conditions such as allergic conjunctivitis and bacterial conjunctivitis, and in chronic contact lens wear.
In a follicular reaction, clusters of conjunctival lymphocytes become enlarged. Vessels surround the raised surface of follicles but are not prominent within the follicle. Follicular reactions are seen in conditions such as viral conjunctivitis, molluscum contagiosum, and chlamydial conjunctivitis.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2304
External Disease & Cornea
A 42-year-old man presents with severe right eye pain that began upon awakening this morning. Two weeks ago, he sustained an injury to the eye from a fingernail and was treated for a corneal abrasion. This is his second recurrence of pain since the initial injury. He denies additional trauma. What treatment would be the most appropriate next step to prevent recurrence of his condition?
Correct answer: B. hypertonic saline ointment
Rationale
This patient is presenting with recurrent corneal erosions following trauma. Hypertonic saline ointment can be helpful for this condition by facilitating epithelial adherence through creation of an osmotic gradient, drawing fluid from epithelial cells.
Although cyclopentolate can be utilized in the acute phase to reduce pain, it would have no role in preventing recurrence of this condition.
Surgical therapy with either anterior stromal puncture or phototherapeutic keratectomy should be reserved for patients with recurrent corneal erosions that have not responded to medical treatment.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2305
External Disease & Cornea
What should adult-onset varicella-zoster virus epithelial keratitis be treated with?
Correct answer: C. oral acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir
Rationale
Epithelial keratitis indicates the presence of live, replicating varicella-zoster virus within the corneal epithelium. Oral antiviral therapy with acyclovir, valacyclovir, or famciclovir is the preferred treatment for live, replicating zoster virus.
Topical medication such as trifluridine may be effective but has the disadvantage of only treating the ocular surface and conveying some degree of toxicity, which can limit or delay epithelial healing. Topical antivirals should be reserved for recurrent epithelial lesions or rare cases with contraindications to systemic therapy. Artificial tears provide lubrication, which aids in healing after ocular surface breakdown but does not inhibit replicating varicella-zoster virus. Intravitreal ganciclovir is an effective treatment for intraocular involvement of varicella zoster but is not effective in treating virus on the ocular surface.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2306
External Disease & Cornea
A 21-year-old male contact-lens wearer presents to the office with a report of severe right eye pain for 9 days. He currently works as a lifeguard. Vision in the right eye is 20/100, and his findings are shown in the figure. The ophthalmologist plans to take cultures. What media has the highest yield for the most likely pathogen in this case?
Correct answer: B. nonnutrient agar with E coli overlay
Rationale
E coli overlay

The figure shows radial perineuritis in a contact-lens patient exposed to water, making the likely diagnosis Acanthamoeba keratitis. Acanthamoeba species are ubiquitous protozoa found in freshwater and soil. Of the reported cases of Acanthamoeba keratitis, 70% are associated with contact-lens wear. Patients present with severe ocular pain and photophobia. Early presentation may be a diffuse punctate epitheliopathy or dendritic epithelial lesion. More advanced cases may present with a ring infiltrate or radial perineuritis (as in the figure). Diagnosis is made by corneal scrapings showing the cysts, or by culturing. The smears are stained with Giemsa or periodic acid-Schiff (PAS). The organism grows on nonnutrient agar with E coli or Enterobacter aerogenes, blood agar, and buffered charcoal-yeast extract agar.
Sabouraud agar is the preferred media when fungi are suspected. Lowenstein-Jensen agar is best used when atypical mycobacteria is suspected. Chocolate agar contains lysed, heated red blood cells, and is a non-selective growth media, but bacteria that typically grow on it include Neisseria and Haemophilus spp.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2307
External Disease & Cornea
A patient with keratoconus presents with new-onset eye pain and blurred vision. The slit-lamp appearance is shown below. What is the most appropriate treatment?
Correct answer: B. soft contact lens and topical hypertonic agent
Rationale
Acute hydrops occurs when Descemet membrane ruptures and causes corneal edema, often associated with pain, photophobia, and increased blurred vision. Typically, the edema will improve through re-endothelialization of the break, and so hypertonic agents and time can improve the situation. A soft contact lens and a cycloplegic can help reduce pain. Emergent transplant is not indicated. Intrastromal corneal ring segments (Intacs) are useful in keratoconus to center the cone and facilitate contact lens fit, but they are not a treatment for acute hydrops. Similarly, RGP contact lenses are not a treatment for acute hydrops.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2308
External Disease & Cornea
What corneal ectasia is characteristically bilateral, noninflammatory, not hereditary, and typically present at birth?
Correct answer: C. keratoglobus
Rationale
Keratoglobus is a rare, bilateral, noninflammatory condition and is not hereditary. The differential for keratoglobus includes keratoconus, pellucid marginal degeneration, megalocornea, and buphthalmos secondary to congenital glaucoma. Unlike keratoconus or pellucid marginal degeneration, keratoglobus is normally present at birth. Posterior keratoconus is a central or paracentral indentation of the posterior cornea that is present at birth and is classified as a congenital anomaly. Posterior keratoconus is most frequently unilateral and sporadic, although an autosomal recessive form of disease with bilateral corneal findings has been described that is also associated with other findings such as short stature, cleft lip and palate, vertebral anomalies, and intellectual disability.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2309
External Disease & Cornea
For the findings shown, what is the most likely causative organism?
Correct answer: D. Staphylococcus
Rationale
Staphylococcus

Staphylococcal blepharitis typically appears as matted crusts surrounding individual cilia on the anterior eyelid margin (Figure 1), which are often honey-colored. This is usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus but occasionally by other staphylococcal species. Marginal corneal infiltrates can develop in association with staphylococcal blepharitis (Figure 2). Other possible findings associated with staphylococcal blepharoconjunctivitis include ulceration of the anterior eyelid margin, inferior punctate keratopathy, papillary reaction of the inferior tarsal conjunctiva, conjunctival hyperemia, and phlyctenulosis. 
Moraxella can produce a crusting and ulceration of the skin in the lateral canthal angle; this is known as angular blepharoconjunctivitis. Angular blepharoconjunctivitis is frequently associated with concomitant staphylococcal blepharoconjunctivitis. Streptococcus and Corynebacterium species are commonly isolated from the external eye but are less likely causes of blepharitis in this case.
Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — External Disease & Cornea — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm
Q2310
External Disease & Cornea
What is the typical appearance of Thygeson superficial keratitis?
Correct answer: D. granular epithelial lesions with minimal conjunctival injection
Rationale
The classic presentation for Thygeson superficial keratitis is that of multiple, typically bilateral, gray, granular, or "crumblike" epithelial lesions and minimal or no conjunctival injection (reaction). The presence of significant conjunctival injection should raise suspicion for an alternative etiology (eg, adenoviral keratoconjunctivitis). This condition is usually very responsive to steroids, but often recurs when the steroid is stopped.

Q2311
External Disease & Cornea
By what mechanism can a corneal endothelial defect be covered?
Correct answer: C. enlargement and migration of endothelial cells
Rationale
The corneal endothelium is a single layer of mostly hexagonal-shaped cells that help maintain corneal transparency through a metabolic pump that maintains corneal deturgescence. Defective areas of endothelium may be covered by enlargement and spread of residual corneal endothelial cells, which can be observed through demonstration of polymegethism and polymorphism on specular microscopy. Although endothelial cells can divide in cell culture, they do not proliferate in vivo.

Q2312

What is a risk factor for the development of conjunctival melanoma?
Correct answer: A. primary acquired melanosis of the conjunctiva
Rationale
Primary acquired melanosis is a well-established risk factor for conjunctival melanoma. Conjunctival melanomas are rare in younger, Asian, and black individuals. Pterygium excision is not associated with conjunctival melanoma; however, local radiation applied following excision can be associated with later conjunctival squamous carcinoma.

Q2313
External Disease & Cornea
What pathogen can invade through an intact corneal epithelium?
Correct answer: A. Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Rationale
Neisseria gonorrhoeae

Although most pathogens require a defect in the corneal epithelial barrier in order to invade, Neisseria gonorrhoeae can penetrate through an intact corneal epithelium. Other organisms that can classically invade through intact corneal epithelium are Neisseria meningitidis, Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Listeria monocytogenes, Shigella species, Haemophilus influenzae, and Fusarium species.

Q2314
External Disease & Cornea
A patient presents for routine examination. He is asymptomatic and has been wearing rigid gas permeable lenses for many years for his "corneal condition." The slit-lamp photograph shown is representative of both eyes. What is the typical topographic finding in this condition?
Correct answer: B. high against-the-rule or oblique astigmatism
Rationale
Terrien marginal degeneration is a noninflammatory condition in which the peripheral cornea undergoes progressive thinning. The thinning typically begins superiorly and spreads circumferentially. Clinically, a fine vascular pannus extends across the area of thinning and there is often a line of lipid that deposits at the leading edge of the vascular pannus. Corneal topography reveals flattening of the peripheral thinned cornea, with steepening of the corneal surface approximately 90 degrees away from the midpoint of the thinned area. This pattern usually results in high against-the-rule or oblique astigmatism.

Q2315
External Disease & Cornea
What finding is specific for blepharitis caused by staphylococcus?
Correct answer: A. hard, matted crusting
Rationale
Blepharitis is an inflammation of the eyelid margins that causes ocular irritation. The most common cause of blepharitis is a staphylococcus infection, which typically presents with hard, brittle fibrinous scales and hard, matted crusts surrounding individual cilia (collarettes) on the anterior eyelid margin. The irritation from the infection can lead to eyelid ulceration, corneal vascularization, marginal infiltrates, or punctate erosions. Treatment modalities to decrease bacterial load and reduce inflammation include lid hygiene, lubrication, antibiotic ointment or pills, or anti-inflammatory drops.
Seborrheic blepharitis patients have increased oil secretion, with greasy scales along the lashes. Cylindrical sleeves around the lash bases occur in patients with Demodex colonization. Meibomian gland inspissations occur in posterior blepharitis or meibomian gland dysfunction. Rapid tear breakup is commonly found in patients with meibomian gland dysfunction. The tear breakup time will also be affected in aqueous tear deficiency (Sjögren and non-Sjögren etiologies).

Q2316
External Disease & Cornea
What mucopolysaccharidosis (MPS) has an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern?
Correct answer: A. MPS II (Hunter)
Rationale
The mucopolysaccharidoses (MPSs) are inborn errors of metabolism with impaired lysosomal storage. They typically are associated with corneal clouding due to the accumulation of incompletely degraded glycosaminoglycans. Most of the MPSs are autosomal recessive. The exception to this is MPS II (Hunter), which is X-linked recessive.

Q2317
External Disease & Cornea
What is the most typical appearance of corneal intraepithelial neoplasia?
Correct answer: B. translucent gray epithelial sheet with fimbriated margins
Rationale
Corneal intraepithelial neoplasia typically manifests as a translucent, sometimes granular, gray epithelial sheet that is based at the limbus and extends onto the cornea. The edges have characteristic fimbriated margins and pseudopodia-like extensions.
The presence of white opacities in a circinate pattern is more suggestive of a ring infiltrate, which is typically infectious in origin. A triangular fibrovascular mass is a description for a pterygium. A dense infiltrate with fluorescein uptake is characteristic of a corneal ulcer.

Q2318
External Disease & Cornea
A patient with dry age-related macular degeneration presents with new-onset decreased vision. The ophthalmologist orders fluorescein angiography. A few minutes later, the patient reports that he feels short of breath and starts wheezing. This is an example of what type of hypersensitivity?
Correct answer: A. type I
Rationale
Type I hypersensitivity is triggered by the activation of IgE. Presumably, the IgE producing B lymphocytes were "primed" by prior exposure to the antigen (in this case, fluorescein). The Fc portion of the IgE antibody binds to mast cells, causing them to degranulate and release interleukins and cytokines. This happens within several minutes of re-exposure. These inflammatory mediators can cause blood vessel dilation and massive edema, leading to reactions ranging from hives, urticarial, laryngeal edema, to ultimately, anaphylaxis.
Type II hypersensitivity is defined as a hypersensitivity reaction secondary to antibodies that are directly cytotoxic against human tissues. Examples of type II hypersensitivity include Goodpasture syndrome and cicatricial pemphigoid.
Type III hypersensitivity is defined as a hypersensitivity secondary to antibody-antigen immune complex reactions. Examples of type III hypersensitivity include systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis,
Type IV hypersensitivity is a delayed cell-mediated reaction. T lymphocytes are responsible for this hypersensitivity. Examples of type IV hypersensitivity include contact dermatitis, staph marginal keratitis, and purified protein derivative (PPD) placement.

Q2319
External Disease & Cornea
What corneal disorder is most amenable to a treatment by superficial keratectomy alone?
Correct answer: C. Salzmann nodular degeneration
Rationale
Of the choices displayed, Salzmann nodular degeneration is most amenable to superficial keratectomy alone. Common indications for superficial keratectomy include pterygium/pseudopterygium, epithelial basement membrane redundancy, and anterior corneal degenerations (Salzmann nodular degeneration). Although band keratopathy can be treated with superficial keratectomy, it is usually done along with ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA).
Contraindications for the procedure include corneal dystrophies or degenerations producing visual loss via stromal opacification.

Q2320

What surgical procedure is typically used to treat total unilateral limbal stem cell deficiency?
Correct answer: D. limbal stem cell transplant from the fellow eye
Rationale
If total unilateral limbal stem cell deficiency occurs, an autograft of limbal epithelium from the fellow eye is most commonly used.
Cases of bilateral limbal stem cell deficiency are generally treated with limbal allografts from living related donors or eye bank donor eyes. Epithelial cells of the oral mucosa have been used as a source of cultured corneal stem cells; however, this approach is still experimental.

Q2321
External Disease & Cornea
What histopathologic characteristic is associated most with melanoma transformation in primary acquired melanosis?
Correct answer: D. cellular atypia
Rationale
The main risk factor for progression of primary acquired melanosis (PAM) to melanoma is the presence of cellular atypia. Histopathologic characteristics of PAM with atypia, such as epithelioid cells, intraepithelial spread, and invasion into the substantia propria, further increase risk for transformation to melanoma. Hyperpigmentation can be a sign of malignant transformation, particularly if there has been increased pigmentation over time. Increased vascularity or inflammatory infiltration can also be a sign of malignant transformation.

Q2322
External Disease & Cornea
What is the appropriate adjunctive therapy for perilimbal conjunctival melanoma with suspected corneal epithelial involvement?
Correct answer: B. absolute alcohol to the adjacent corneal epithelium and scleral base
Rationale
Conjunctival melanoma is associated with a very high rate of local recurrence (up to 50%). In cases with perilimbal involvement and possible corneal epithelial extension, adjuvant local therapy should be strongly considered. Absolute alcohol epitheliectomy is one option to treat the epithelium selectively.
Tectonic penetrating keratoplasty is unwarranted, because the disease is confined the superficial cornea. External beam radiation cannot be targeted to the corneal epithelium specifically and may result in significant local complications. Observation alone is not recommended, based on the high-risk nature of these neoplasms.

Q2323
External Disease & Cornea
A 28-year-old man develops conjunctivitis after a recent upper respiratory infection. Ten days after the onset of conjunctivitis, he develops decreased vision and photophobia and the findings seen below. How should this condition be managed?
Correct answer: B. topical corticosteroid drops
Rationale
Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis is an adenoviral syndrome that may be preceded by an upper respiratory tract infection. Within 7-14 days after onset of ocular symptoms, multifocal subepithelial (stromal) corneal infiltrates (SEI) become apparent on slit-lamp examination, as seen in the photo. Photophobia and reduced vision from adenoviral subepithelial infiltrates may persist for months to years. Topical steroids are the first-line treatment for subepithelial infiltrates, although they can prolong viral shedding. Topical NSAIDs are ineffective for subepithelial infiltrates, although they can be helpful in preventing recurrence following tapering of steroids. Topical and oral antiviral therapies are not helpful for treating SEI.

Q2324
External Disease & Cornea
Meretoja syndrome (systemic amyloidosis associated with lattice corneal dystrophy) is found in patients who have a gene mutation that results in what abnormal protein product?
Correct answer: C. gelsolin
Rationale
Gelsolin type (type 2) lattice corneal dystrophy is associated with Meretoja syndrome (systemic amyloidosis with lattice dystrophy). Since Meretoja syndrome is a systemic syndrome, it is not classified as a corneal dystrophy by the International Committee for the Classification of Corneal Dystrophies (IC3D).
Classic lattice dystrophy (type 1) arises secondary to a conserved mutation in the transforming growth factor beta-induced gene (TGFBI). Iduronidase deficiency is associated with mucopolysaccharidoses. Carbohydrate sulfotransferase 6 (CHST6) deficiency is associated with macular corneal dystrophy.

Q2325
External Disease & Cornea
What location of conjunctival melanoma is associated with the best long-term prognosis?
Correct answer: C. bulbar conjunctiva
Rationale
Conjunctival melanoma-related mortality at 10 years ranges from 13% to 38%. Involvement of the caruncle, palpebral conjunctiva, or conjunctival fornix are all associated with a two-fold or greater risk for mortality compared to bulbar conjunctival involvement alone.

Q2326
External Disease & Cornea
How is the corneal dystrophy shown in the picture treated?
Correct answer: D. typically treatment is not required
Rationale
The photo demonstrates a patient with Meesmann corneal dystrophy affecting the corneal epithelium. The inheritance pattern is autosomal dominant and presents early in life with many small epithelial vesicles/cysts, most commonly found in the interpalpebral area. The cysts are filled with epithelial breakdown products ("peculiar substance"). Corneal sensation may be decreased and symptoms most commonly include mild irritation, glare, and mildly decreased visual acuity. Some patients are bothered by photophobia. In general, patients do not require treatment, but contact lenses may help with pain.

Q2327
External Disease & Cornea
For the condition shown, what blood test is most likely to reveal an associated systemic abnormality?
Correct answer: B. serum phosphate levels
Rationale
The figure demonstrates calcium deposition at the level of the Bowman membrane. This finding is consistent with band keratopathy, which may occur from a variety of causes, systemic or ocular. Ocular causes of band keratopathy include chronic uveitis, phthisis bulbi, and silicone oil toxicity. Systemic causes of band keratopathy include conditions that lead to serum calcium and phosphate deposition, such as hyperparathyroidism, excessive vitamin D intake, renal failure, Paget disease of bone, and sarcoidosis. The systemic work-up in patients with band keratopathy should include serum calcium and phosphate levels. Based on the clinical history, other potential evaluations may be useful, including tests of renal function, angiotensin-converting enzyme level, and parathyroid hormone level. Serum copper levels would be useful if the patient is suspected of having Wilson disease. Serum cysteine levels would be useful if the patient is suspected of having cystinosis. Serum cholesterol levels may be useful if the patient is suspected of having Schnyder crystalline corneal dystrophy.

Q2328
External Disease & Cornea
What intervention can help prevent pupillary block glaucoma after Descemet stripping automated endothelial keratoplasty (DSAEK)?
Correct answer: A. pharmacologic mydriasis
Rationale
In DSAEK (also referred to as DSEK), air is injected into the anterior chamber in order to promote graft attachment to the host cornea. If the air bubble obstructs aqueous flow through the pupil, acute pupillary block angle closure can occur. Interventions that prevent this complication include pharmacologic mydriasis, inferior peripheral iridectomy, and/or avoiding a large air bubble that might cover the pupil.
Face-down or prone positioning and pharmacologic miosis should be avoided because they increase the risk of pupillary obstruction by the air bubble. Ocular hypotensive agents may lower the intraocular pressure (IOP) if it is elevated post-DSEK, but they would not correct the underlying issue of pupillary block.

Q2329
External Disease & Cornea
A number of factors actively contribute to immune tolerance of corneal grafts. How does the cornea actively prevent rejection of corneal transplants?
Correct answer: D. triggering apoptosis through upregulation of Fas ligand
Rationale
Many factors actively contribute to "immunologic privilege" of transplanted corneal tissue, facilitating graft survival. These factors include:
  • absence of blood or lymphatic channels in graft and graft bed
  • absence of MHC class II antigen-presenting cells (APCs) in graft
  • reduced expression of MHC-encoded alloantigens on graft cells
  • increased expression of Fas ligand, which stimulates apoptosis of killer T cells
  • immunosuppressive cytokines in aqueous humor, including TGF-β2, vasoactive intestinal peptide, and α-melanocyte-stimulating hormone
  • development of suppressor T cells from aqueous humor antigens

Q2330
External Disease & Cornea
What is the primary cause of exposure keratopathy in patients with Parkinson disease?
Correct answer: C. decreased blink frequency
Rationale
The major cause of exposure keratopathy in patients with Parkinson disease is poor blink frequency. Patients may also suffer from reduced tear production as a result of anti-Parkinson medications. Parkinson is a degenerative neurologic condition.
Although progressive facial paralysis does occur, the mechanism of exposure is not cicatricial ectropion. Proptosis and upper-eyelid retraction are features of thyroid eye disease (TED), not Parkinson disease.

Q2331
External Disease & Cornea
What is the most common organism to cause the problem shown in the photograph in a contact lens wearer?
Correct answer: B. Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Rationale
Pseudomonas aeruginosa


Contact lens wear predisposes the cornea to infection through a number of mechanisms, including introduction of a contaminated foreign body to the corneal surface; interruption of the normal tear flow, which is essential to corneal immunity; induction of corneal epithelial microtrauma; alteration of ocular surface immunity; and induction of corneal hypoxia. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most common cause of bacterial keratitis in contact lens wearers. This organism becomes more pathogenic in lens-related biofilms, in turn enabling enhanced binding to molecular receptors exposed on injured epithelial cells. Once adherent, bacteria will proliferate and invade the corneal stroma, often with the aid of bacteria-specific proteases.

Q2332
External Disease & Cornea
In this post-cataract corneal optical coherence tomography (OCT) image shown, what abnormality is illustrated?
Correct answer: C. Descemet detachment
Rationale
This patient has centrally detached Descemet membrane with attachment in the peripheral cornea. This membrane may resemble a free-floating remnant of capsule, but closer inspection shows a whiter (more reflective), thicker cornea anterior to and co-localizing with the detachment, which would not be seen if the image represented a free capsular fragment. This complication is typically caused by an instrument or intraocular lens (IOL) delaminating Descemet membrane at the corneal wound. Addition of a viscoelastic gel may inadvertently detach Descemet membrane if the cannula is incompletely inserted and placed at the stromal-Descemet separation plane. Fluid inserted for hydration of the cornea may have a similar effect. If a small area is detached, the patient may have transient, localized, corneal microcystic edema. Involvement of a larger area may result in more persistent edema unless the endothelium can cover the defect over time. If the area is large enough and the edema is persistent, the patient may need a penetrating keratoplasty or other corneal procedure. Neither Fuchs endothelial dystrophy nor bullous keratopathy would have a layer visible that was separated from the remainder of the cornea.

Q2333
External Disease & Cornea
What type of device is best for detecting abnormalities in posterior corneal curvature?
Correct answer: D. Scheimpflug-based
Rationale
Scheimpflug-based imaging platforms (eg, Pentacam, Orbscan) are the most commonly employed devices for mapping posterior corneal curvature. These devices employ a scanning beam that "slices" through the cornea and generates maps based on the anterior-posterior dimensions of the cornea. Placido disk and videokeratoscopic imaging devices only provide information about the anterior surface (both devices use surface reflections and hence are unable to assess to the posterior cornea). Ultrasonic pachymetry can measure and detect areas of relative thickness disparity, but it is not typically employed to assess and monitor posterior corneal curvature.

Q2334
External Disease & Cornea
Six months ago, a 62-year-old man had penetrating keratoplasty performed on his right eye with interrupted corneal sutures. The current corneal topography is shown. The autorefraction is –9.00 +6.75 at 4°. The manifest refraction is –7.00 +5.00 at 4° and provides a best corrected visual acuity of 20/25. If the ophthalmologist were to remove 1 suture, at what axis should a suture be removed in order to best improve the astigmatism and visual acuity?
Correct answer: B. 4°
Rationale
In the past, corneal transplantation was considered a success if the donor cornea remained clear. In this day and age, the refractive outcome can determine whether a corneal transplant is successful or not, even if the cornea is completely clear. The primary method of minimizing astigmatism following a corneal transplant is to readjust a continuous suture or remove interrupted sutures.
The most critical step is to identify the steep axis (because sutures cause an axis to steepen, see below if further clarification is needed) using corneal topography, handheld keratoscopy, photokeratoscopy, or manual keratometry. The corneal topography here depicts high astigmatism, where the simulated keratometry readings show a steep axis of 49.93 diopters (D) at 11° and flat axis of 44.06 D at 101° (49.93-44.06=5.87 D of astigmatism at 11° ). Manifest refraction can aid in confirming the steep axis when using plus cylinder, as was done in this case. According to the BCSC, since autorefraction and manifest refraction identified the steep axis at 4°, this is where the suture should be removed to relax the cornea and hopefully decrease the astigmatism. The manifest refraction, autorefraction, and corneal topography are 3 methods that indicated the steep axis to be between about 2 and 3 o'clock and are in concordance with each other, which reassures the surgeon that removing a suture in this area (or 180 degrees away) should help the patient. The best answer is 4° or 184° because the manifest refraction achieves the best corrected visual acuity, and removing a suture where it indicates will likely have the most effect.
This question was written to test knowledge the correct axis on which to remove a suture (steep, never flat or in between steep and flat); however, when removing sutures, it is also important to confirm that the patient has regular astigmatism before a suture is removed. If there is irregular astigmatism, then suture removal should be deferred until clear and stable measurements are obtained. There are different clues to confirm regular astigmatism. In this case, the manifest refraction was able to correct the vision to 20/25, which is very good and would not have been possible if the astigmatism was irregular. Another tip is to look at the photokeratoscopic image with the topography and see if the mires or rings are clear and distinct (Figure 1). If they are irregular and indistinct, and a lubricating drop does not make them clear, then this may indicate irregular astigmatism and suture removal should be deferred until measurements are clear and stable.
After suture removal or manipulation of sutures, the patient should be placed on a topical antibiotic for 4 days and re-evaluated in 1 month for repeat corneal topography and manifest refraction.
Fifteen degrees (15°) is incorrect because it is not the best answer according to the manifest refraction, even though the topography does indicate that the cornea is steep at 15°.
Seventy-five degrees (75°) and 274° are incorrect because the cornea is flatter in these locations and suture removal is done where the cornea is steep.
Figure 2 demonstrates why a suture causes the cornea to steepen in the axis that it is located. The suture flattens where it is passed, but anterior to it, toward the central cornea, the cornea steepens. If one envisions the cornea as a dome sitting on its circular base and the rim of the base all remains the same except for the one spot where you put the suture, it is as if the suture is pushing the central cornea up by sliding the base of the cornea at that one spot (at the rim) in toward the center. By removing the suture, the rim/base can return back out to its original location, and the central cornea will decrease in height or flatten.

Q2335
External Disease & Cornea
Under physiologic conditions, what interface provides the majority of refractive power for the human eye?
Correct answer: B. air to tear film
Rationale
Owing to both the curvature as well as the large difference in index of refraction, the air to tear film interface provides the majority of refractive power for the normal human eye. As such, disorders that alter the corneal surface or tear film may produce significant visual aberrations, whereas a similar degree of pathology in the posterior cornea typically results in far fewer visual symptoms. Although the corneal endothelium to aqueous and aqueous to lens capsule transitions both contribute to the total refraction, the effect is greatly reduced by the relatively similar indices of refraction to the aqueous. Very little refraction takes places between the tear film and corneal epithelium, owing to the similar curvatures and indices of refraction.

Q2336
External Disease & Cornea
What clinical condition is caused by the organism shown?
Correct answer: C. blepharoconjunctivitis
Rationale
Shown in the photograph is a wet mount of Demodex species. Demodex folliculorum and Demodex brevis inhabit eyelash follicles and meibomian glands, which may result in blepharoconjunctivitis.
Among the causes of keratitis is the protozoan Acanthamoeba. Propionibacterium acnes is a major cause of chronic endophthalmitis. Neuroretinitis is usually an infectious or postviral autoimmune process, frequently associated with elevated antibody immunoglobulin M (IgM) titers for Bartonella quintana or Bartonella henselae.

Q2337
External Disease & Cornea
What condition is most closely associated with papillary conjunctivitis?
Correct answer: B. atopic keratoconjunctivitis (AKC)
Rationale
Patients with atopic keratoconjunctivitis show signs of type I immediate hypersensitivity, which manifests as a papillary conjunctivitis.
In contrast, adult inclusion, herpes simplex, and molluscum contagiosum typically demonstrate follicular conjunctivitis.

Q2338
External Disease & Cornea
In what clinical setting should empiric systemic antibiotics be considered to treat conjunctivitis?
Correct answer: A. acute purulent conjunctivitis with pharyngitis
Rationale
Generally speaking, conjunctivitis does not require systemic therapy. Indications for initiating systemic antibiotic therapy in the setting of conjunctivitis include acute purulent conjunctivitis with pharyngitis, conjunctivitis with concurrent otitis media, Haemophilus conjunctivitis in children, and culture-proven cases of chlamydial or gonococcal etiology.
Chronic intermittent conjunctivitis in a patient with sleep apnea should prompt the examiner to look for signs of floppy eyelid syndrome.
Giant papillary conjunctivitis caused by soft contact lens wear can be managed with topical anti-inflammatory medications or changing the composition of the contact lens material.
Serous conjunctivitis in the setting of a recent upper respiratory tract infection is likely to be viral in origin.

Q2339
External Disease & Cornea
What lens finding is most characteristic in a patient with atopic keratoconjunctivitis?
Correct answer: D. anterior subcapsular cataracts
Rationale
Anterior subcapsular cataracts are most commonly seen in patients with chronic atopic keratoconjunctivitis. Posterior polar cataracts are typically congenital and may be bilateral (often autosomal dominant inheritance) or unilateral (sporadic).
Anterior lenticonus is a very rare malformation of the anterior capsule that can be seen in patients with Alport syndrome (nephrotic hematuria and deafness), Lowe syndrome (oculocerebral renal syndrome), and Waardenburg syndrome (deafness and partial albinism). Posterior lenticonus may be associated with microcornea, hyperglycinuria, Duane syndrome, anterior lentiplanus, and MPPC (microcornea, posterior megalolenticonus, persistent fetal vasculature, coloboma).

Q2340
External Disease & Cornea
What is a contraindication to crosslinking in moderate keratoconus?
Correct answer: D. history of neurotrophic keratopathy
Rationale
Having a history of neurotrophic keratopathy may result in poor epithelial healing. Collagen crosslinking utilizes vitamin B2 (riboflavin) and ultraviolet A (UVA) light to strengthen the cornea and to stabilize the corneal curvature. The treatment leads to new physical crosslinks of the corneal collagen fibers. The procedure involves removing the corneal epithelium, placing frequent topical riboflavin drops, and exposing the cornea to UVA light for approximately 30 minutes. The effects take up to 6 months to peak. Complications can include corneal haze, decreased corneal sensitivity, sterile or microbial keratitis, corneal scarring, persistent corneal edema, and decreased vision.
Crosslinking is recommended in patients with progressive disease, especially in adolescents. Although crosslinking may not be as effective in patients post LASIK treatment or with severe disease, it is not contraindicated. It may be performed in concert with intrastromal ring insertion. It is currently contraindicated in concurrent ocular infection, severe corneal scarring, past history of poor epithelial wound healing, history of autoimmune diseases, pregnancy, and history of neurotrophic keratopathy. Hydrops occurs due to a tear in Descemet membrane, usually late in the course of keratoconus, and although following resolution with improvement in corneal edema, there is some stromal scarring, it is not an absolute contraindication to crosslinking.

Q2341
External Disease & Cornea
After completion of a penetrating keratoplasty shown in the photo, the surgeon elects to take a biopsy of the conjunctiva. What histological finding is expected?
Correct answer: D. loss of goblet cells
Rationale
This photo exhibits a severe case of xerophthalmia, due to Vitamin A deficiency. Note the severe drying of the conjunctiva with water beading on the surface. Histologically, loss of goblet cells can be seen, which contributes to the appearance. Abundance of giant cells can occur with sarcoidosis. Infiltration of small, basophilic cells with large nuclei would describe a salmon patch due to lymphoma. "Eosinophilic extracellular deposits that exhibit birefringence" describes amyloid deposits. Vitamin A deficiency due to malnutrition is a major cause of blindness in developing countries, whereas in the United States, this deficiency is usually caused by lipid malabsorption, chronic alcoholism, or unusual dietary practices. The first ocular manifestation is night blindness, but the disease eventually produces xerosis of the conjunctiva and then the cornea. Sometimes, Bitôt spots are seen; they contain Corynebacterium xerosis, which creates the classic foamy appearance. Finally, the disease can lead to corneal ulceration and necrosis. It is important to realize that systemic vitamin A deficiency has a mortality rate of 50% if left untreated, highlighting the importance of recognizing this disease.

Q2342
External Disease & Cornea
An obese 48-year-old man presents with irritation that is greater in his right eye than his left eye. There is scant discharge in both eyes. He states his symptoms are worse in the morning upon awakening. There is some punctate corneal staining and some corneal vascularization. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. floppy eyelid syndrome
Rationale
This clinical presentation is typical for floppy eyelid syndrome. Patients will demonstrate lid laxity, more commonly of upper eyelids than the lower eyelids. Disease can be unilateral or asymmetric, and patients can present with mild corneal epitheliopathy and papillae on upper lids. The syndrome is frequently seen in obese patients.
Vernal conjunctivitis does not present with lid laxity; it is a type of allergic conjunctivitis that presents with burning and itching. It has 2 forms, palpebral and limbal, and occasionally a combination of the 2 types.
Giant papillary conjunctivitis (GPC) is an allergic condition of the eyes seen most commonly in contact lens wearers. The upper lids show the formation of large papillae greater than .3 mm.
Thygeson superficial punctate keratitis is a condition marked by elevated corneal opacities, typically in both eyes, without inflammation; it tends to be chronic.

Correct answer: C. Sabouraud agar
Rationale
The mechanism of injury from vegetative material, along with the clinical findings of a white, fluffy infiltrate with satellite lesions, is highly suspicious for fungal keratitis. Sabouraud dextrose agar is used to culture fungal microorganisms. Blood agar and brain–heart infusion agar are other preferred media.
Löwenstein-Jensen medium is used to culture mycobacteria. Nonnutrient agar with E coli overlay is used to culture Acanthamoeba. Michel medium is used for preservation of specimens to be examined by immunofluorescence.

A 25-year-old woman complains of chronic, bilateral foreign-body sensation, which is worse at the end of the day. The slit-lamp examination of her left eye is abnormal, as shown. What blood test would suggest a specific etiology of this condition?
Correct answer: C. angiotensin-converting enzyme
Rationale
The slit-lamp photograph demonstrates rose bengal staining in the inferior conjunctivae, as well as ropy mucous discharge. These findings, along with the patient's symptoms, strongly suggest dry eye syndrome. In a young patient with severe dry eye symptoms, a search for an underlying systemic etiology should be considered. Sjögren syndrome is a systemic autoimmune condition that affects the exocrine glands that produce tears and saliva. Sjögren syndrome can present as a primary disease or in the setting of additional autoimmune disorders. Blood tests can determine if a patient has high levels of antibodies that are suggestive of systemic disease; the typical antinuclear antibody pattern found in Sjögren syndrome is a positive SSA/Ro and SSB/La, of which SSB/La is more specific. A biopsy of a minor salivary gland can also be performed to establish the diagnosis. Elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme levels can be found in patients with sarcoidosis, elevated rheumatoid factor levels can be found in patients with rheumatoid arthritis, and elevated antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody levels can be found in patients with systemic vasculitis. However, none of these are typically associated with keratoconjunctivitis sicca in a young patient.

Due to its virulence, epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (adenovirus serotypes 8, 19, 37; subgroup D) typically presents with bilateral corneal involvement that can include punctate epithelial keratitis associated with the severe follicular conjunctivitis. Rationale
Concretions are epithelial inclusion cysts filled with epithelial and keratin debris. Yellow-white deposits are sometimes found in the palpebral conjunctiva of patients who are elderly or who have chronic conjunctivitis. They are not a result of hypercalcemia, sun exposure, trachoma, rubbing, surgery, or dry eyes. They are usually asymptomatic, but they can be removed under topical anesthesia if they cause a foreign-body sensation.

Q2347

When evaluating a potential donor cornea for transplantation, a documented history of what procedure is an absolute contraindication for use in penetrating keratoplasty?
Correct answer: B. laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK)
Rationale
For the purpose of evaluating prospective corneal donor tissue, previous refractive surgery (LASIK, photorefractive keratectomy [PRK] and radial keratotomy [RK]) is an absolute contraindication for use in penetrating keratoplasty. LASIK and PRK, are, however, acceptable for use with endothelial keratoplasty (DSAEK or DMEK).
Intraocular surgery, including cataract surgery and vitreoretinal surgery, is a relative contraindication to corneal transplantation, but is acceptable if the endothelial cell density is normal and any surgical scars are outside of the area of trephination. Previous extraocular muscle surgery does not impact cornea transplantation eligibility.

Rationale
The fifth cranial nerve (CN V) is the cranial nerve most frequently affected by reactivation of latent varicella zoster, but CN V is also the most commonly inoculated nerve. Varicella zoster can be acquired as chickenpox or shingles either through direct contact with cutaneous lesions or by aerosolized respiratory droplets. The cornea and conjunctiva are moist, wet surfaces at risk of infection if inoculated by VZV. Varicella rarely infects cranial nerves II, III, or VII, so reactivation in those nerves is less likely.

A 58-year-old obese man presents with chronic ocular irritation and inflammation. On examination, there is significant eyelid laxity, and the upper tarsus everts with minimal upward force. What systemic workup is indicated?
Correct answer: D. sleep study
Rationale
Floppy eyelid syndrome is characterized by chronic ocular irritation, inflammation, and eyelid laxity. Upper eyelid eversion occurs with minimal upward force. It is most frequently seen in obese patients and is associated with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), which can be diagnosed with a sleep study. Floppy eyelid syndrome is not associated with abnormal brain imaging, abnormal buccal mucosa, or thyroid abnormalities.
In addition to floppy eyelid syndrome, OSA is also a risk factor for non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) and idiopathic intracranial hypertension. Less clear are the associations between OSA and glaucoma, central serous chorioretinopathy, retinal vein occlusion and diabetic maculopathy.

The figure shows Reis-Bücklers dystrophy (corneal dystrophy of the Bowman layer I), an autosomal dominant corneal dystrophy that often presents by late adolescence with recurrent corneal erosions and decreased vision.
Anterior basement membrane dystrophy (map-dot-fingerprint dystrophy) presents as a variable mix of epithelial and subepithelial "wavy" grayish lines and dots.
Avellino corneal dystrophy is characterized by well-demarcated granular stromal opacities and, often later in life, refractile gray lines typical of lattice corneal dystrophy.
Schnyder crystalline corneal dystrophy presents early in life with superficial, refractile crystalline opacities that, over time, coalesce to become diffuse central corneal opacification.

Correct answer: C. anterior lamellar keratoplasty
Rationale
Anterior segment OCT images the cornea as a cross-section and readily identifies interfaces of a cornea that has been cut. This patient has undergone anterior lamellar keratoplasty: A lamellar dissection is seen with additional cuts at the edge of the graft, extending anteriorly. Superficial keratectomy would leave the deep stroma intact. Penetrating keratoplasty would lack a lamellar cut parallel to the surface and would have peripheral full-thickness cuts perpendicular to the ocular surface. Endothelial keratoplasty also leaves the stroma intact, and one may observe the graft on the posterior aspect of the cornea.

Rationale
Scleritis is often associated with systemic disease, especially rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, seronegative spondyloarthropathies, polyarteritis nodosa, and giant cell arteritis. Infectious and metabolic causes (such as gout) should also be considered in the differential diagnosis.
Necrotizing scleritis is the most destructive form of scleritis and can cause either ocular or systemic complications in up to 60% of affected patients. It is further subdivided into necrotizing scleritis with or without inflammation.

What is a common clinical finding in persistent corneal epithelial defects?
Correct answer: C. elevated rounded edge
Rationale
Persistent corneal epithelial defects are areas of chronic nonhealing epithelium. They frequently have elevated, rounded edges or scalloped borders and are round or oval in shape. A dendritiform shape is uncharacteristic and should prompt further evaluation for herpetic keratitis. The most common location for a persistent epithelial defect is inferior or inferonasal as a result of the protective effect of Bell phenomenon on the superior cornea. Persistent epithelial defects are commonly seen in neurotrophic keratopathy, so corneal hypoesthesia or anesthesia is often present.

Q2354
External Disease & Cornea
What is the next step in the treatment of this Seidel-positive corneal ulcer?
Correct answer: B. cyanoacrylate glue
Rationale
Although not approved by the FDA for use on the cornea, cyanoacrylate tissue adhesives have been used for the repair of corneal perforations for over 30 years. Cyanoacrylate adhesive is most effective in treating corneal perforations of < 2 mm. Because the surface of the adhesive is usually irregular, a bandage contact lens is employed for patient comfort.
While a corneal patch graft or scleral patch graft may be needed, attempting to seal the wound with cyanoacrylate adhesive would be a more reasonable first option. A tarsorrhaphy can be very helpful in the treatment of corneal disease; however, a complete tarsorrhaphy would not allow for monitoring to ensure that infection is being controlled. Intravitreal antibiotics would not be indicated without evidence of endophthalmitis.

What is the most appropriate surgical therapy for a patient with painful band keratopathy?
Correct answer: B. debridement with topical ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA)
Rationale
EDTA chelation is a rapid and effective method for removing calcium from the anterior corneal stroma.
Anterior stromal micropuncture is a treatment that can be used for recurrent corneal erosions due to previous trauma or anterior basement membrane dystrophy (ABMD), but it has no role in the management of band keratopathy.
Deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty is unnecessarily invasive for the treatment of band keratopathy, which is limited to the anterior stroma and more effectively treated with EDTA chelation.
LASIK is not an appropriate treatment for band keratopathy.

Q2356

On slit-lamp examination, a patient is found to have an elevated pterygium with an adjacent area of corneal thinning. The epithelium is intact. What is the best treatment option for the corneal thinning?
Correct answer: A. lubrication
Rationale
The answer is lubrication. The case is describing a dellen at the leading edge of an elevated pterygium. A dellen occurs when there is focal thinning from dehydration of the stroma due to adjacent elevation (pinguecula, pterygium, filtering bleb) in the area. There are 2 appropriate treatment options for this patient. The first step should be to try aggressive lubrication. If this does not completely alleviate the condition, surgical excision of the pterygium should be considered. Pterygium excision will restore the normal tear film to this area and prevent further formation of the dellen. Since the dellen is neither an inflammatory nor infectious process, corticosteroids and topical antibiotics would not help treat the condition. A penetrating keratoplasty is not necessary for this condition.

Q2357

What surgical intervention can be performed to alleviate chronic pain associated with a chronic sterile corneal ulcer in an eye with poor vision potential?
Correct answer: B. conjunctival flap
Rationale
Conjunctival flap surgery (Gundersen flap) is an effective procedure to control chronic pain in the setting of a non-healing corneal defect. Although retrobulbar alcohol injection can be used for pain relief, it would not be a suitable choice in the setting of a chronic epithelial defect, as a corneal perforation can ensue. A limbal stem cell autograft would subject the fellow eye to unnecessary risk in the setting of poor visual potential. Penetrating keratoplasty is unlikely to provide a long-term solution and is also unnecessarily invasive.

Q2358
External Disease & Cornea
What refractive procedure would be preferred for restoring functional vision in a patient with keratoconus?
Correct answer: B. intrastromal corneal ring segments
Rationale
Intrastromal corneal ring segments have been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for use in reducing or eliminating myopia and astigmatism in keratoconus patients who are no longer able to achieve adequate vision with their contact lenses or spectacles. The intent of intrastromal corneal ring segment placement is to restore functional vision and defer the need for corneal transplantation.
Corneal collagen crosslinking combines riboflavin, a naturally occurring photosensitizer, and ultraviolet A light to strengthen the biomechanical properties of the cornea. Although there may be a slight flattening of the cornea, the most important effect of this treatment is that it appears to stabilize the corneal curvature. The primary clinical application is as a treatment to prevent the progression of keratoconus and postrefractive ectasia.
Keratoconus is generally considered a contraindication to laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) and surface ablation; weakening of the cornea, as a result of the loss of structural integrity in LASIK flap creation and tissue removal, increases the risk of progressive ectasia. Although early case reports suggested that combining collagen crosslinking treatment with surface ablation or conductive keratoplasty may offer some benefit to keratoconus patients, the clinical evidence remains very preliminary.

Corneal epithelial stem cells reside at the corneal limbus. Conjunctival and corneal epithelial cells are replaced in 1-2 weeks.

Acanthamoeba keratitis is a protozoal infection that can present in various ways, but is often associated with severe ocular pain, radial perineuritis, or a ring infiltrate. A number of cell types contribute to ocular immunological defense mechanisms. What cells function as dendritic antigen-presenting cells in the conjunctiva and cornea?

Rationale
Langerhans cells are major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II+ dendritic antigen-presenting cells found in the conjunctiva and cornea. These cells uptake antigens and present them to CD4+ T cells, priming them to form an immune response. Corneal Langerhans cells are predominantly located in the limbus and corneal periphery.
Touton cells are multinucleated giant cells with foamy cytoplasm from high lipid content that can be seen in xanthogranulomas.

Q2363

What technique is the most useful in evaluating for lipid-deficient tear film?
Correct answer: B. tear breakup time
Rationale
A poor lipid layer can lead to tear film instability and increased tear evaporation. Measuring tear breakup time is a way to quantify tear film stability. To measure tear breakup time, the practitioner instills fluorescein in the patient's eyes and holds the eyelids open after a blink, counting the seconds until a dry spot appears. The appearance of a dry spot in less than 10 seconds is considered abnormal.
Schirmer testing uses filter paper to measure the amount of aqueous tear production over a period of time. Rose bengal and lissamine green stain epithelial cells of the cornea and conjunctiva when a disruption occurs in the protective mucin coating.

What meibomian gland appearance is the final stage of severe chronic ocular rosacea?

Rationale
The end stage of chronic ocular rosacea or severe meibomian gland dysfunction is involution and atrophy of the gland orifices and failure to produce expressible oil secretions. Transillumination or direct visualization of the palpebral conjunctiva may reveal shortened or absent vertical lines corresponding to the atrophied ducts. Increased thickness, turbidity, and inspissation of the meibomian gland secretions are all indicators of ongoing inflammation, but these represent earlier stages of the disease compared to gland atrophy.

Q2365

A 42-year-old man presents for a routine examination. Correct answer: A. patching and topical lubrication
Rationale
A dellen is a small depression that occurs at the corneal limbus due to dehydration of the epithelium and stroma. Conjunctival elevation causes irregularity of the tear film, disrupting distribution from blinking in the involved area of cornea and leading to desiccation. Patching followed by topical lubrication can restore hydration of the stroma.
Systemic immune suppression along with topical lubrication can be considered for peripheral ulcerative keratitis. Although this may also result in thinning adjacent to the limbus, patients usually have an epithelial defect and corneal infiltrate. Additionally, the presence of raised conjunctiva may suggest dellen.
Lid scrubs, warm compresses, and topical lubrication can be used in the treatment of marginal keratitis, which is characterized by focal sterile infiltrates at the limbus from lid margin disease.

In the case of corneal opacities from traumatic scars, infectious scars, and Peters anomaly type I, the pathology is generally limited to the cornea, with an otherwise normal anterior segment. This improves the prognosis for pediatric keratoplasty.
In the case of Peters anomaly type II, anterior segment findings can be more severe, including adhesions among cornea, iris, and lens. These associated anterior segment abnormalities lead to a higher chance of failure in pediatric keratoplasty.

The pattern of staining in this patient is consistent with LSCD. This whorl-like pattern is caused by migration to the ocular surface of conjunctival cells that are usually inhibited by limbal stem cells. What gram-negative bacterium can penetrate an intact cornea epithelium?

Neisseria gonorrhoeae

The answer is Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Only a few organisms are able to invade an intact epithelium. They include Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Neisseria meningitides, Corynebacterium diphtheriae, Shigella species, Haemophilus aegyptius, and Listeria monocytogenes.

Q2370

A 57-year-old woman with a history of penetrating keratoplasty for a herpetic corneal scar presents with an endothelial rejection line, inferior graft edema, and a 2+ anterior chamber reaction. What is the most appropriate initial therapy?
Correct answer: B. frequent use of topical prednisolone with suppression dose of an oral antiviral agent
Rationale
The presentation given is most consistent with corneal allograft rejection. The most appropriate therapy for new-onset endothelial rejection is hourly topical steroids, which may be combined with systemic steroids in severe cases. (Either dexamethasone 0.1% or prednisolone 1% eyedrops are used, as often as every 15 minutes to 2 hours, depending on the severity of the episode.) It is important to concurrently administer antiviral prophylaxis because of the known history of herpetic keratitis. As such, the most appropriate therapy is hourly topical prednisolone acetate 1% with oral acyclovir 400 mg BID. Topical prednisolone acetate 1% QID and oral acyclovir 400 mg 5 times daily is inadequate for suppressing the inflammation and endothelial cell damage caused by acute rejection. Topical steroids or oral acyclovir alone fail to address both problems in this scenario.
Bacterial, fungal, viral, or amebic keratitis can recur in a graft in the early postoperative period. In recurrent infections, medical treatment directed at the causative agents is the initial form of therapy.

Factitious disorders include a spectrum of self-induced injuries with symptoms or physical findings that the patient intentionally produces. In factitious ocular surface disorder, there is usually evidence of mechanical injury to the inferior and nasal quadrants of the cornea and conjunctiva. The areas of involvement show sharply delineated borders. The conjunctival tissues usually show no evidence of inflammation of pathologic examination. Mucus-fishing syndrome and topical anesthetic abuse are common presentations of factitious ocular surface disorder.

Wide ciliary body band, especially if sectoral or unilateral, is highly suggestive of angle recession. Other gonioscopic findings may include iris root tear or avulsion of the ciliary body. Patients with angle recession are at lifelong risk for developing glaucoma.
Neovascularization is not a common finding after blunt trauma. It is seen in ischemic disorders such as proliferative diabetic retinopathy and retinal vein occlusions.

By what mechanism do oral antihistamines cause dry eye?

Rationale
Many systemic medications, including antihistamines, antihypertensives such as propranolol and clonidine, decongestants such as pseudoephedrine, and antidepressants such as amitriptyline cause dry eye by decreasing aqueous tear production.
Increased (not decreased) tear film osmolarity can be associated with aqueous tear deficiency. Increased rate of tear evaporation, or evaporative dry eye, is caused by meibomian gland dysfunction. Decreased blink rate can be seen during some activities such as extensive reading or driving and in some neurologic conditions such as Parkinson disease.

Q2375
External Disease & Cornea
What property of adenovirus makes it resistant to routine disinfection precautions (eg, swabbing a tonometer tip with ethyl alcohol)?
Correct answer: A. absence of a viral envelope
Rationale
In contrast to herpes simplex virus (HSV), human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), and influenza virus, adenoviruses, and many other viruses responsible for infectious outbreaks, do not have a viral envelope. Viral envelopes are composed primarily of lipids and proteins, which render them more susceptible to heat, acids, and drying. Alcohol swabbing is sufficient to inactivate enveloped viruses. Adenoviruses, however, are surrounded only by a capsid of primarily glycoproteins, which are intrinsically more resistant to these same environmental stressors. For this reason, alcohol swabbing of a reusable tonometer tip is insufficient to prevent inoculation of subsequent patients in the setting of adenoviral exposure. Diluted bleach cleaning solution or disposable tonometer tips are necessary. Both HSV and adenovirus are characterized by a double-stranded DNA genome. Acanthamoeba, not adenovirus, can prolong survival by encysting itself in a dormant form.

Q2376

Rationale
Initial treatment of adenovirus may include cool compresses and artificial tears. Topical steroids can lengthen viral shedding and predispose to more severe corneal infections. Therefore, topical steroids should only be used for clear indications, such as EKC conjunctival membranes and bilateral reduced visual acuity from subepithelial infiltrates. Oral steroids are not recommended for this limited ocular inflammation. Topical and oral antivirals have no role in the treatment of adenovirus.

External Disease & Cornea
An ophthalmologist who has been following a patient closely for traumatic hyphema notices the finding shown in the photo. The patient's course has been complicated by elevated intraocular pressure, which is being treated with topical timolol. The intraocular pressure measures 31 mm Hg today. What is the best next course of action?
Correct answer: D. perform anterior chamber washout
Rationale
An anterior chamber washout should be performed at the earliest sign of corneal blood staining, as is the case with this patient. There is an increased risk for corneal blood staining in cases with intraocular pressure elevation and endothelial damage. Slit-lamp examination may reveal early yellow granular changes in the posterior corneal stroma. Because this finding may be visually significant and permanent, early surgical intervention with anterior chamber irrigation is warranted.
Adding topical brimonidine may help to further reduce intraocular pressure, but would not address corneal blood staining. Antifibrinolytics such as aminocaproic acid are thought to have a theoretical risk of reducing rebleeding, but are controversial and have systemic side effects, in addition to having no effect on corneal blood staining. Aqueous shunt implantation would also address intraocular pressure, but it may be premature and would not address corneal blood staining.

Q2378
External Disease & Cornea
What is the most appropriate first-line treatment for mild to moderate scleritis?
Correct answer: C. oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory therapy
Rationale
Scleritis is typically treated with oral agents. Several options are available: Mild-moderate scleritis can be treated with oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). Severe scleritis or diseases not responsive to NSAIDs are treated with systemic corticosteroids (1 mg/kg/day with slow taper). In select cases, systemic immunosuppressive agents are needed, and should be used in consultation with an internist, oncologist, or rheumatologist.

Q2379
External Disease & Cornea
Long-term administration of what oral medication can produce the conjunctival changes shown?
Correct answer: C. minocycline
Rationale
Adrenochrome deposits (oxidation products of epinephrine) appear as a dark-brown or black granular pigmentation of the conjunctiva or cornea. The most common causes of these deposits are the long-term administration of tetracycline antibiotics (including minocycline) and topical epinephrine-containing drops (rarely used now). The deposits are harmless but can be mistaken for a pigmented neoplasm.
Amiodarone and tamoxifen can produce cornea verticillata: brown-pigmented, whorl-like corneal epithelial changes. Ethambutol can cause optic neuropathy but is not known to cause ocular surface deposits.

Q2380
External Disease & Cornea
What systemic condition is associated with superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis?
Correct answer: D. thyroid disease
Rationale
Superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis (SLK) is thought to result from mechanical trauma transmitted from the upper eyelid to the superior bulbar and tarsal conjunctiva. The condition is associated with autoimmune thyroid disease. It is typically seen in adult women (3:1 female to male), 20 to 70 years of age, with a median age of 50 years. It has also been associated with graft-vs-host disease and following blepharoplasty. Medical treatment is generally considered to be less effective than surgical treatment.

Q2381
External Disease & Cornea
What is the most common clinical manifestation of primary ocular herpes simplex?
Correct answer: D. blepharoconjunctivitis
Rationale
The most common presentation for primary ocular herpes is blepharoconjunctivitis. It is usually follicular in nature and accompanied by vesicles on the skin or eyelid margin that progress to blistered, crusted lesions. While epithelial keratitis can occur, stromal keratitis and uveitis are rare.

Q2382
External Disease & Cornea
What is thought to be the reason that pterygia occur more often on the nasal rather than the temporal side of the interpalpebral zone?
Correct answer: D. The nose casts a shadow to the temporal interpalpebral zone.
Rationale
The predominance of pterygia on the nasal side in the interpalpebral zone is theorized to result from light passing medially through the cornea, focusing on the nasal limbal area, while the shadow of the nose reduces the intensity of light transmitted to the temporal limbus.

Q2383
External Disease & Cornea
If hypertonic saline solution (5% sodium chloride) fails to provide symptomatic relief from epithelial basement membrane dystrophy, what would be an appropriate next step?
Correct answer: A. epithelial debridement
Rationale
Corneal epithelial basement membrane dystrophy or map-dot-finger or Cogan microcystic dystrophy is characterized by an abnormality in epithelial turnover, maturation, and production of basement membrane. Initial therapy involves use of hypertonic (5%) saline, but this alone may be insufficient. Debriding the epithelium, or, if recalcitrant, stromal puncture or phototherapeutic keratectomy (PTK, not LASIK) could be considered. Acanthamoeba is an unlikely complication unless a chronic contact lens has been applied. A penetrating keratoplasty would be resurfaced by host epithelium, likely leading to recurrence.

Q2384
External Disease & Cornea
For a patient with conjunctival melanoma, what clinical feature increases the risk of regional lymph node metastasis?
Correct answer: C. involvement of palpebral conjunctiva
Rationale
Conjunctival malignant melanoma that involves the palpebral conjunctiva is associated with an increased risk of lymphatic metastasis. Involvement of the limbus and bulbar conjunctiva is common and is not predictive of metastasis. Breslow score refers to the thickness of invasion of a cutaneous melanoma, and an increased Breslow score is associated with a higher chance of metastasis.

Q2385
External Disease & Cornea
What blood test should be ordered if on slit-lamp examination, the lens reveals reddish-brown pigment in the anterior capsule and subcapsular cortex in a stellate shape?
Correct answer: D. serum ceruloplasmin
Rationale
Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disease of copper metabolism. A "sunflower cataract" is sometimes seen as a result of cuprous oxide deposition in the anterior lens capsule and cortex. Another finding of Wilson disease is a Kayser-Fleischer ring, which is a golden brown coloration of the Descemet membrane. Cataracts may occur in any condition that causes hypocalcemia. The cataract is typically focal iridescent opacities within the cortex.
Other metabolic conditions known to cause cataract include diabetes mellitus, galactosemia, and myotonic dystrophy. Young patients with poorly controlled diabetic mellitus may develop an acute diabetic cataract or snowflake cataract consisting of bilateral, multiple gray-white subcapsular opacities. Vacuoles and clefts are also common in the lens of a person with diabetes. As diabetic patients age, they develop age-related changes similar to those in patients without diabetes, but the changes occur at a faster rate.
Galactosemia is an autosomal recessive disease that results in a lack of production of glucose from galactose. It is due to one of 3 enzyme deficiencies: galactose 1-phosphate uridyltransferase, galactokinase, or UDP galactose 4-epimerase. The most commonly involved enzyme is galactose 1-phosphate uridyltransferase. Patients develop an accumulation of galactose in the lens, which drives in water osmotically and causes an "oil droplet" cataract in the cortex on retroillumination. Other findings of this disease include hepatomegaly, malnutrition, jaundice, and intellectual deficiency.
Myotonic dystrophy is an autosomal dominant condition causing generalized muscle weakness, cardiac conduction defects, and frontal balding. Patients may develop iridescent opacities in the lens cortex with posterior subcapsular cataract.

Q2386
External Disease & Cornea
A 27-year-old woman presents with a complaint of eye irritation. She reports that she was using a tanning bed yesterday and removed her eye protection. On examination, she has eyelid edema, conjunctival hyperemia, and diffuse punctate keratitis of the right eye. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
Correct answer: D. patching with cycloplegia and topical antibiotic ointment
Rationale
Ultraviolet (UV) radiation can be damaging to the corneal epithelium. Exposure to sunlamps and tanning beds can cause UV-induced injury. Treatment involves use of topical antibiotic ointment, cycloplegia, and patching to reduce discomfort from eyelid movement. Topical steroids or antihistamines are not indicated for this condition.

Q2387
External Disease & Cornea
A 70-year-old man presents with chronic unilateral crusting and discharge from the right lateral canthus. Gram stain of the discharge reveals numerous gram-negative cocci in pairs. What is the most likely pathogen?
Correct answer: C. Moraxella lacunata
Rationale
Moraxella lacunata

The description is consistent with angular blepharitis, a relatively uncommon entity that may be mistaken for other forms of chronic lid margin inflammation. Angular blepharitis is classically caused by Moraxella lacunata (consistent with the Gram stain result of gram-negative cocci in pairs), although Staphylococcus aureus and herpes simplex virus are other possible etiologies. Chlamydia trachomatis is a potential cause of chronic follicular conjunctivitis, but it is not associated with angular blepharitis. Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Haemophilus influenzae can cause acute conjunctivitis, but they are not known to cause angular blepharitis.

Q2388
External Disease & Cornea
What would be an appropriate initial management of marginal corneal infiltrates associated with blepharoconjunctivitis?
Correct answer: B. topical antibiotic/corticosteroid combination
Rationale
Marginal corneal infiltrates associated with blepharoconjunctivitis are usually due to Staphylococcus aureus. Use of topical corticosteroids or a corticosteroid/antibiotic combination can be useful for treating acute inflammation. Management should also include therapy for blepharitis with warm compresses, lid scrubs, antibiotic ointment to lid margins, or topical antibiotics. Also, oral tetracyclines or erythromycin can be considered.
Topical cyclosporine would not be a good option, as it is not an ideal agent to treat acute inflammation. Surgery or laser procedures should be avoided in patients with an acute inflammation. Artificial tears would not be useful for treatment of the inflammation.

Q2389
External Disease & Cornea
A patient with history of a chronically inflamed chalazion presents with the findings shown below. What is an appropriate treatment for this condition?
Correct answer: B. topical corticosteroids
Rationale
Pyogenic granulomas are reactive hemangiomas consisting of granulation tissue and proliferating capillaries as part of a healing response to minor trauma, surgery, or a chronically inflamed chalazion. These lesions are nonsuppurative, do not contain giant cells, and can bleed easily. Treatment may involve topical or intralesional corticosteroids, as well as excision with cauterization to the base (with postoperative topical corticosteroids).

Q2390
External Disease & Cornea
For 3 days, a 30-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has had poor vision and pain in her left eye. Her slit-lamp examination is abnormal, as shown. Bacterial and fungal cultures of the peripheral cornea are negative. What is the likely definitive treatment?
Correct answer: C. systemic steroids
Rationale
The figure depicts a patient with peripheral ulcerative keratitis. After a negative infectious workup result, an autoimmune etiology must be considered, and a thorough workup should be conducted to look for associated systemic conditions. In this case, the patient is known to have an autoimmune condition. Noninfectious, immune-mediated peripheral ulcerative keratitis necessitates systemic therapy with corticosteroids and may require subsequent immunosuppressant therapy, as well. It is important to recognize this condition, obtain the appropriate systemic workup, and recognize the need for systemic treatment in this potentially blinding condition.
Early mortality can occur in patients with untreated systemic illnesses. Vancomycin and tobramycin would be used to treat a bacterial keratitis, which is an unlikely diagnosis, considering the negative cultures. Lamellar and penetrating grafts used in corneal transplantation are susceptible to melting unless systemic immunosuppression is instituted; thus, this is not a definitive treatment. Observation is not appropriate with an underlying active inflammatory process.

Q2391
External Disease & Cornea
What clinical finding makes the diagnosis of mucous membrane pemphigoid more likely than pseudopemphigoid?
Correct answer: B. oral ulcers
Rationale
Mucous membrane pemphigoid (MMP) is a chronic cicatrizing conjunctivitis of autoimmune reaction etiology. It primarily involves the conjunctiva; however, it frequently affects other mucous membranes including the mouth and oropharynx, genitalia, and anus.
Pseudopemphigoid has been associated with long-term use of certain topical medications. Case reports have implicated pilocarpine, epinephrine, timolol, idoxuridine, echothiophate iodide, and demecarium bromide.
Pemphigoid and pseudopemphigoid share several features, including conjunctival hyperemia, papillary conjunctivitis, conjunctival erosions, conjunctival subepithelial fibrosis, symblepharon, tear deficiency, and abnormal position of the eyelids and eyelashes, including entropion, trichiasis, and distichiasis. However, it would not be typical for pseudopemphigoid to have other (nonocular) findings, such as skin lesions and/or oral or respiratory lesions.

Q2392
External Disease & Cornea
What systemic antibiotic can be given as a single dose to treat adult chlamydial conjunctivitis?
Correct answer: D. azithromycin
Rationale
Azithromycin 1g PO administered once is an acceptable treatment for adult chlamydial conjunctivitis (it may be necessary in some cases to retreat at 1 week). For this reason, it may be a preferable choice for patients with a history of poor compliance. The other 3 antibiotic choices are also effective therapies, but they must be administered over a 7-day period. Sexual partners should be treated concurrently to prevent reinfection.
Currently, 1 of the following oral antibiotic regimens is recommended:
  • azithromycin 1000 mg  PO single dose
  • doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x 7days
  • tetracycline 250 mg PO QID x 7 days
  • erythromycin 500 mg PO QID x 7 days
