Q2393
External Disease & Cornea
A 20-year-old, otherwise healthy patient presents with severe pain, photophobia, and blurry vision 5 days after bilateral photorefractive keratectomy (PRK). Examination reveals an 8 mm epithelial defect with a faint ring infiltrate and small hypopyon in both eyes. Gram stain and potassium hydroxide (KOH) prep are negative for organisms. Cultures are negative and there is minimal improvement on topical fortified antibiotics over the next several days. What is the most important history to obtain?
Correct answer: B. use of any nonprescribed eye drops
Rationale
This history is concerning for anesthetic abuse. Patients may be reluctant to reveal this information, but it is critical to ask the patient directly and nonjudgmentally in suspected cases. The most suspicious elements are the patient's young age, the bilateral involvement of the eyes, and the description of a non-healing defect with an early ring infiltrate.
Although herpetic disease could present with a non-healing ulcer after a surface procedure, it would be unlikely to present bilaterally. A history of showering with contact lenses is important when considering Acanthamoeba, but in this case the rapid onset makes a toxic etiology more likely. Use of oral pain medications is an important part of the medical history, but it does not help to narrow the differential diagnosis.

Q2394
External Disease & Cornea
A 60-year-old woman complains of pain upon awakening for many years, increasing in frequency over the last few months. Some days she cannot open her left eye for hours because of pain and light sensitivity. She tried hypertonic saline drops and ointment without improvement. On a follow-up visit, a 3 mm area of left cornea epithelium has fluorescein staining indicating an area of recurrent corneal erosion. What is her recommended treatment?
Correct answer: D. epithelial debridement
Rationale
The patient has basement membrane dystrophy, showing thick geographic map lines, or "putty marks." Epithelial debridement of the central area of recurrent erosion followed by patching or bandage soft contact lens to promote reepithelialization would be recommended. This strategy is the most efficacious with the least risk of complication. Phototherapeutic keratotomy (PTK) may be helpful for this type of epithelial disorder, but radial keratotomy has no role is this disease. Stromal puncture may be helpful in cases where the erosion is outside the visual axis, but not appropriate in this patient's central lesion. A soft bandage lens may have a role in her treatment, but a rigid contact lens may not be tolerated, exacerbating her symptoms.

Q2395
External Disease & Cornea
Neurotrophic keratopathy is most frequently encountered as a long-term consequence of what type of infectious keratitis?
Correct answer: B. viral
Rationale
Viral keratitis, specifically herpes simplex and herpes zoster keratitis, is most commonly associated with long-term corneal hypoesthesia and neurotrophic keratopathy. Although some degree of corneal hypoesthesia can occur after other forms of infectious keratitis, viral keratitis is by far the most common. Other causes of neurotrophic keratopathy are listed in Table 4-2.

Q2396
External Disease & Cornea
What is the most appropriate initial management of a patient with an acute corneal injury involving tree sap?
Correct answer: D. sterile saline irrigation
Rationale
Ocular contact with tree sap (particularly those from the pencil tree and manchineel tree) may result in keratoconjunctivitis, epithelial defects, stromal infiltration, and opportunistic infection. The most important initial management is copious irrigation, similar to management of a chemical injury.
To minimize the risk of potentiating a fungal infection, topical corticosteroids are not recommended in the acute setting. Empiric fungal therapy, however, is not routinely recommended unless evidence of infectious keratitis develops, and at that point culture and/or biopsy should be performed to determine the infectious agent. Occlusive patching is not routinely recommended in the setting of vegetative trauma.

Q2397
External Disease & Cornea
A 42-year-old man with a history of eczema reports itchy eyes and mucoid discharge. His eyes have actually bothered him all year; however, he has been busy at work and unable to come to the clinic. On examination, his eyelid margins are irregular and thickened with crusting. He has bilateral papillae in the upper and lower palpebral conjunctiva, as shown in the photo of his upper tarsal conjunctiva. The ophthalmologist also notes a symblepharon in the lower fornix, corneal neovascularization, and a posterior subcapsular cataract. To what ocular infectious diseases is this patient more susceptible compared to the average patient?
Correct answer: D. herpes simplex virus (HSV) keratitis and colonization of eyelids with Staphylococcus aureus leading to secondary infections
Rationale
Staphylococcus aureus leading to secondary infections

The history of older age, eczema, and symptoms year-round, with findings of lid hypertrophy and cicatrization, chronic conjunctivitis (small papillae with a milky conjunctival edema and possible subepithelial fibrosis, shown in the question stem photo, and symblepharon), corneal vascularization, and posterior subcapsular cataract are consistent with a diagnosis of atopic keratoconjunctivitis. Patients with atopy have type 1 hypersensitivity responses plus depressed systemic cell-mediated immunity, making them more susceptible to herpes simplex virus (HSV) and colonization of the eyelids with Staphylococcus aureus (S aureus). These patients need careful monitoring for complications, especially findings of keratitis, from these 2 infections. HSV keratitis is also more likely to be bilateral in AKC patients. For a review of signs of AKC see below.
AKC patients may be more susceptible in general to infectious diseases; however, for testing purposes staphylococcal and HSV infections should be associated with a higher incidence than the normal population in AKC. Additionally, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) usually affects humans in early adulthood. This patient is outside the usual age range (15-24 years of age). Adenoviral infections are not necessarily more common in AKC patients than normal patients. It may be in the differential in a patient with early AKC. Facial and eyelid lesions from molluscum contagiosum virus can be more extensive in AIDS patients.
Findings particular to AKC (differentiating it from vernal keratoconjunctivitis or VKC)
History
  • Year-round disease with minimal seasonal exacerbation
  • Older age
Clinical signs
  • Small or medium-sized papillae
  • Papillae in the upper and lower palpebral conjunctiva
  • Milky conjunctival edema, with variable subepithelial fibrosis (shown in the photo in the question)
  • Occasional symblepharon formation
  • Corneal vascularization (can be extensive) and opacification due to chronic epithelial disease (likely from direct trauma from eyelid changes and/or limbal stem cell dysfunction)
  • Other corneal findings: persistent epithelial defects, ectatic diseases (eg, keratoconus and pellucid marginal degeneration), and increased incidence of staphylococcal and herpes simplex infections
  • Cataract: Posterior subcapsular and/or multifaceted or shield-shaped anterior subcapsular
Pathology
  • Fewer eosinophils in conjunctival cytology specimens, which are less often degranulated

Q2398
External Disease & Cornea
What topical treatment regimen is recommended for ocular surface squamous neoplasia?
Correct answer: C. topical interferon-a2b 1 million IU/mL 4 times daily for 3–4 months
Rationale
2b 1 million IU/mL 4 times daily for 3–4 months

Several topical therapies can be used to treat ocular surface squamous neoplasia. Topical interferon-α2b (IFN-α2b) 1 million IU/mL is typically given 4 times daily until clinical resolution occurs, usually within 2 to 4 months. Several additional months of treatment might be beneficial; recent evidence indicates that residual tumor might be present for up to 3 months following clinical resolution. Subconjunctival/perilesional IFN-α2b (3 million IU in 0.5 mL) can be given weekly in addition to, or as an alternative to, topical drops, especially if patient adherence is an issue. Subconjunctival IFN-α2b is associated with flulike symptoms in 10% of patients.
Mitomycin C (MMC) can be used for a shorter duration — typically weeks rather than months — but might have greater adverse effects, including surface toxicity and potential stem cell deficiency. Topical MMC 0.02% or 0.04% is typically administered 4 times daily for 1 week, followed by a 1-week structured treatment interruption (drug holiday), for a maximum of 3 or 4 treatment cycles.
Topical 5-fluorouracil 1% can be given 4 times daily for 1 month, with at least several months off if repeated; alternatively, it can be given 4 times daily for 1 week, followed by a 3-week structured treatment interruption, until resolution, for a maximum of 3 cycles.
Application of topical corticosteroids may help with the surface toxicity. Placement of punctal plugs reduces the likelihood of systemic absorption and helps prevent punctal stenosis.

Q2399
External Disease & Cornea
A 54-year-old man on amiodarone for cardiac arrhythmia is found to have yellow-white deposits in a whorl-like pattern in the inferocentral corneal epithelium of both eyes. What is the most appropriate management of the corneal deposits?
Correct answer: A. no treatment
Rationale
Cornea verticillata, or vortex keratopathy, manifests as a whorl-like pattern of golden brown or gray deposits in the inferior interpalpebral aspect of the cornea. Some systemic medications can bind with the cellular lipids of the basal epithelial layer of the cornea to cause this appearance. The anti-arrhythmic medication amiodarone is the most common cause of corneal verticillata. It is unusual for these deposits to result in reduction of vision or ocular symptoms; therefore, treatments such as superficial keratectomy with excimer laser are not necessary. It is acceptable for the patient to continue on the recommended dose of systemic medication.

Q2400
External Disease & Cornea
One week after undergoing epithelial debridement for chronic recurrent corneal erosions, a patient returns with persistent pain. The examination reveals a 7 mm nonhealing epithelial defect without any visible corneal infiltrate or anterior chamber reaction. The patient's current medications are topical ofloxacin 0.3% QID and topical ketorolac 0.5% QID. What is the most appropriate management?
Correct answer: D. discontinue topical ketorolac
Rationale
The most important first step in this scenario is to discontinue the topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drop (ketorolac), which may delay epithelialization in some patients. Topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can even cause corneal melts or even corneal perforations.
Topical ofloxacin is unlikely to be the cause of the persistent epithelial defect and should not be discontinued without starting an alternative prophylactic antibiotic.
Anterior stromal micropuncture may be an effective treatment for recurrent erosions but is better performed through loose, intact epithelium than to the bed of an abrasion.
Muro 128 drops are another treatment for preventing recurrent erosions, but they have limited benefit in the setting of a nonhealing epithelial defect.

Q2401
External Disease & Cornea
A patient with keratoconus presents with acute pain and a decrease in vision. The slit-lamp examination is shown in the picture. What is the characteristic associated histologic feature?
Correct answer: A. disruption of the Descemet membrane
Rationale
Acute corneal hydrops develops when a rupture (typically spontaneous) of the Descemet membrane occurs and aqueous rapidly saturates the stromal collagen, producing profound edema. Fragmentation of the Bowman layer, iron deposition in the basal epithelium, and focal corneal thinning are also features of keratoconus, but not specific to corneal hydrops.

Q2402
External Disease & Cornea
What material would be found on pathology in the patient with the corneal dystrophy shown in the photo?
Correct answer: B. hyaline
Rationale
The photo shows a patient with granular corneal dystrophy, a dominantly inherited stromal dystrophy. Pathology demonstrates hyaline deposits when stained with Masson trichrome. The deposits in macular dystrophy are glycoaminoglycans or acid mucopolysaccharides, which stain with colloidal iron and alcian blue. In lattice dystrophy, Congo red dye is used to stain the amyloid. "Peculiar substance," an electron-dense accumulation of fibrogranular material surrounded by tangles of cytoplasmic filaments, is found in epithelial cells of Meesmann epithelial dystrophy. The cellular debris is periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) positive and fluoresces.

Q2403

For the patient shown, a conjunctival biopsy is most likely to show what findings?
Correct answer: C. linear immunoglobulin on the epithelial basement membrane
Rationale
Mucous membrane pemphigoid (MMP), formerly called ocular cicatricial pemphigoid, is a chronic cicatrizing conjunctivitis, with biopsy revealing immunofluorescent staining disclosing C3, IgM, IgA, and/or IgG at the level of the basement membrane zone.
Touton giant cells are multinucleated cells that can be seen in granulomatous inflammation. While follicles are seen in follicular conjunctivitis (associated with toxic conjunctivitis, viral conjunctivitis, and certain bacterial infections including Moraxella and Chlamydia), these do not characterize MMP. Giant papillary conjunctivitis will show both an eosinophilic and plasma cell infiltrate.

Q2404
External Disease & Cornea
What is the best way to manage uveal prolapse when it occurs during an acute open-globe repair?
Correct answer: D. reposit tissue
Rationale
If uvea or retina (seen as translucent, tan tissue with extremely fine vessels) protrudes, the surgeon can reposit it, using a gentle sweeping technique through a separate limbal incision, with the assistance of viscoelastic injection to keep the anterior chamber formed. Only in cases of frankly necrotic, macerated, or contaminated tissue should prolapsed uveal tissue be excised.
Cauterization of uveal tissue would not be appropriate. Reconstruction of iris tissue, using techniques such as the McCannel suture, may be indicated in a follow-up surgery, but not during the repair of an acute open globe.

Q2405
External Disease & Cornea
What is the appropriate microscope cell staining technique to confirm the diagnosis of adult chlamydial conjunctivitis?
Correct answer: B. Giemsa stain
Rationale
Chlamydia trachomatis is an obligate intracellular bacterium that is best visualized with Giemsa staining. The characteristic appearance is intracytoplasmic basophilic inclusion bodies within epithelial cells.
Acid-fast staining aids in the identification of Mycobacteria species.
Calcofluor white stain is useful for visualizing fungal elements.
Gram staining is appropriate for typical bacterial infections but does not readily identify atypical bacteria, including Chlamydia species.

Q2406
External Disease & Cornea
The refractive correction of the intrastromal corneal ring devices (INTACS) procedure is titrated by choosing what factor of the implant?
Correct answer: D. thickness of the implant
Rationale
The amount of correction achieved is related to the thickness of the ring segments, not to their diameter (they have a fixed outer diameter), nor their material (they are all made of polymethylmethacrylate [PMMA]), and not to their implantation depth.
When performing INTACS, increasing the ring thickness will achieve a reduced corneal arc length (flattening effect) and thus greater correction of myopia. An advantage of INTACS is that the effect of myopia correction can be titrated. For example, if a patient remains undercorrected with a 0.325 mm ring, it can be exchanged for a thicker ring (eg, 0.350 mm or 0.400 mm); if a patient is overcorrected, a thinner ring can be exchanged to reduce the amount of myopia correction. The depth of the ring segments must always be between 68% and 70% for this procedure and is not varied.

Q2407
External Disease & Cornea
A 67-year-old man visits the ophthalmologist for an examination. He has a history of hypercalcemia, renal failure, and a recent work-up including serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP), which demonstrated a monoclonal spike. What ocular finding is associated with his underlying condition?
Correct answer: A. corneal crystalline deposits
Rationale
Hypercalcemia, renal failure, and monoclonal spike on SPEP are associated with multiple myeloma. Ocular findings associated with multiple myeloma include crystalline deposits in all layers of the cornea (or in the conjunctiva), hyperviscosity of retinal vasculature, pars plana cysts, or proptosis from orbital bony invasion.
Sea-fan retinal neovascularization is a characteristic of sickle cell retinopathy. Blue sclera is characteristic of osteogenesis imperfecta, a condition caused by a mutation in type I collagen. Corneal verticillata are seen in Fabry disease, an X-linked recessive condition characterized by deficiency of α-galactosidase A. Verticillata can also be caused by multiple medications, such as amiodarone or phenothiazines or netarsudil.

Q2408
External Disease & Cornea
In order to be considered acute graft-versus-host disease, within what time period following bone marrow transplantation do symptoms need to present?
Correct answer: C. within 3 months
Rationale
Graft-versus-host disease is a complication that can occur following allogeneic bone marrow transplantation, wherein the grafted cells attack the host tissue. Ocular surface manifestations can include conjunctival inflammation and severe keratoconjunctivitis sicca. Acute graft-versus-host disease occurs within 3 months of transplantation, although most ocular manifestations are seen in chronic graft-versus host-disease (greater than 3 months from transplantation).

Q2409
External Disease & Cornea
A 65-year-old farmer complains of a spot on his left eye that has been present for 2 years. He is concerned about the spot and would like it to be surgically removed. His slit-lamp photograph is shown. What technique of removal should be avoided as it has a high rate of "spot" recurrence?
Correct answer: D. Excise the lesion, allow spontaneous epithelialization.
Rationale
The photograph depicts a pterygium. Removing the pterygium and allowing the bed to reepithelialize results in a high rate of recurrence. Adjuvant techniques are now used to decrease the risk of pterygium recurrence after surgery and include placing a conjunctival autograft or amniotic membrane over the sclera bed, or treating the area with mitomycin C or beta radiation. All these adjunctive techniques have decreased the incidence of pterygium recurrence after surgery.

Q2410
External Disease & Cornea
For what type of corneal scarring is phototherapeutic keratectomy (PTK) contraindicated?
Correct answer: B. deep central scarring from herpes simplex keratitis
Rationale
Phototherapeutic keratectomy (PTK) is indicated for the treatment of visually significant anterior (limited to the superficial one-third) stromal opacity or irregular astigmatism due to anterior scarring. Deeper scars are not amenable to PTK, due to the necessity of tissue destruction and the resulting corneal destabilization and severe hyperopic shift. Previous herpetic keratitis is also a relative contraindication to excimer laser smoothing. Anterior scars caused by previous bacterial keratitis, central islands following refractive surgery, and subepithelial scarring secondary to ABMD are all acceptable candidates for PTK.

Q2411
External Disease & Cornea
What is the most common etiology of isolated episcleritis?
Correct answer: D. idiopathic
Rationale
The majority of cases of isolated episcleritis are idiopathic. Autoimmune conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and Wegener granulomatosis have all been associated with episcleritis, but a serologic workup is rarely indicated in the absence of other systemic findings.

Q2412
External Disease & Cornea
What is the most appropriate initial treatment for Candida keratitis?
Correct answer: B. topical amphotericin
Rationale
Topical amphotericin B, and more recently voriconazole, has been advocated for treating keratitis caused by yeasts such as Candida. Topical amphotericin B is also recommended for Aspergillus keratitis. Natamycin 5% is more effective against filamentous fungi such as Fusarium species and is thus first-line treatment for most fungal keratitis in the southern United States. Because of its systemic toxicity and irregular penetration to the cornea, intravenous amphotericin B should be avoided for keratitis.

Q2413
External Disease & Cornea
What organism causes ocular toxocariasis?
Correct answer: B. Toxocara canis
Rationale
Toxocara canis

Ocular toxocariasis (also termed ocular larval migrans) is a rare condition resulting from tissue invasion by the second-stage larvae of Toxocara canis or cati. Ocular larval migrans, with sparing of the viscera, often occurs in older children. In contrast, visceral larval migrans typically occurs in younger children.
Toxoplasma gondii causes toxoplasmosis, which is a much more common retinochoroiditis and may be acquired or congenital.
The Brucella species may cause a systemic infection in humans after exposure to infected animals, typically via ingestion of unpasteurized milk or cheese products.
Onchocerciasis, caused by the filarial parasite Onchocerca volvulus, is one of the leading causes of blindness in sub-Saharan Africa. The flies that carry the parasite breed in fast-flowing streams, giving the disease its common name, "river blindness."

Q2414
External Disease & Cornea
What is the appropriate surgical therapy for visually significant Salzmann nodular degeneration?
Correct answer: B. superficial keratectomy
Rationale
Salzmann nodular degeneration refers to grayish subepithelial nodules that typically occur following previous inflammatory or mechanical insult to the cornea. They can also be idiopathic. These changes are typically confined to the very superficial anterior stroma and are amenable to debridement with superficial keratectomy.
LASIK would not be a good option, as flap creation would preserve the pathologic changes. Deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty is unnecessarily invasive for a superficial condition. Limbal stem cell resection is reserved for the treatment of focal limbal stem cell deficiency causing visual impairment. This treatment would not be indicated for Salzmann nodular degeneration.

Q2415
External Disease & Cornea
For a patient with an intraocular pressure (IOP) of 18 mm Hg measured by applanation tonometry and a central corneal thickness of 490 μm, what is the most likely IOP upon entering the anterior chamber (ie, the manometric IOP)?
Correct answer: A. greater than 18 mm Hg
Rationale
Applanation tonometry assumes certain properties of the cornea when IOP is calculated. Measurement with the Goldmann tonometer is most accurate when the central corneal thickness (CCT) is 520 μm. Thicker corneas resist the deformation inherent in most methods of tonometry, resulting in an overestimation of IOP, while thinner corneas may give an artificially low reading. Although the exact conversion factor is not universally agreed upon (typically around 1 mm Hg of deviation for every 10 to 15 μm deviation from normal corneal thickness), the pattern has been well established.
The most likely IOP upon entering the anterior chamber can be predicted with the information provided in the stem about CCT and intraocular pressure measured by applanation. The given CCT is less than 520 μm, and thus will give a falsely low reading on applanation. The most likely IOP upon entering the anterior chamber would be less than 18 mm Hg if the CCT were thicker or greater than 520 μm and applanation measured a higher-than-true IOP.

Q2416
External Disease & Cornea
A 58-year-old man returns from vacation with 4 days of asymmetrically red eyes, worse on the right. He has light sensitivity and bilateral foreign body sensation. Because of his fear of worsening the situation, he has not used eyedrops. His vision best corrects to 20/20 OU. Given his slit-lamp examination (photo), what is the likely cause of his diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. enterovirus type 70
Rationale
This patient has a severe form of acute conjunctivitis, most likely acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis (AHC). Sudden onset of follicular conjunctivitis associated with multiple petechial hemorrhages of bulbar and tarsal conjunctiva characterizes AHC. AHC is most commonly caused by enterovirus or coxsackievirus, and, less commonly, adenovirus.
IgE-mediated activation and degranulation of mast cells can cause allergic conjunctivitis. Types I and IV hypersensitivity reaction with infiltrate of eosinophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells, and monocytes can cause vernal conjunctivitis. Allergic and vernal conjunctivitis are chronic conditions that usually have a predominant symptom of itching or pruritus, and do not typically present with conjunctival hemorrhages. Contact lens solution containing benzalkonium chloride (BAK) can cause toxic conjunctivitis. Patients with toxic conjunctivitis usually admit to using an ocular medication known to cause conjunctivitis such as an adrenergic agonist or neomycin. They may also have a toxic reaction to preservatives in contact lens solution.

Q2417
External Disease & Cornea
For a patient with acute Stevens-Johnson syndrome and conjunctival involvement, what surgical treatment is the most beneficial?
Correct answer: A. amniotic membrane transplantation
Rationale
Amniotic membrane grafting has been established as an effective therapy for patients with conjunctival inflammation secondary to Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS). Conjunctival resection is indicated in some cases of severe peripheral ulcerative keratitis or Mooren ulcer, but it plays no role in the management of SJS. Punctal cauterization can be employed as a long-term strategy for severe dry eye resulting from SJS, but it would not be indicated in the acute setting. A Gunderson flap can be employed for select nonhealing corneal ulcers, but it would not be a good choice in the setting of SJS.

Q2418
External Disease & Cornea
When performing cataract surgery in patients with endothelial dystrophy, what step should be taken to reduce operative risks?
Correct answer: C. frequent use of a dispersive viscoelastic
Rationale
Endothelial dystrophy (or Fuchs endothelial dystrophy) ranges from asymptomatic to a decompensated corneal edema.  The condition shows variable autosomal dominant transmission and can be sporadic.  Endothelial cell counts of less than 1000/mm2 or the presence of epithelial edema suggests caution and the possibility that the cornea might decompensate with surgery.  Techniques during cataract surgery would be aimed at reducing the amount of ultrasound power used and optimizing the distance of the ultrasound from the corneal endothelium.  Using the pulse-and-burst mode of phacoemulsification reduces overall ultrasound power used.  Frequent use of viscoelastic will help protect the endothelium. Using hyperosmotic topical drops is sometimes used to aid in corneal edema, but not hyperosmotic BSS during surgery.  Using a capsule dye is a technique used for dense cataracts, not a technique for endothelial dystrophy.

Q2419
External Disease & Cornea
The instrument shown here allows quantification of what ophthalmic property?
Correct answer: B. corneal sensation
Rationale
Corneal esthesiometry is the measurement of corneal sensation, which may be quantified by the length of a fixed diameter fiber required to induce a corneal response (shorter length indicates diminished sensation). The handheld esthesiometer (Cochet-Bonnet) is a contact device that provides this information.
Tear osmolarity can be measured by a tear osmometer. Aberrometry can be measured using the principle of wavefront optics (eg, Shack-Hartmann aberrometry). Contrast sensitivity can be measured with the Pelli-Robson chart.

Q2420

For the initial management of early and peripheral contact lens-related microbial keratitis, what topical antibiotic is most appropriate as monotherapy?
Correct answer: A. moxifloxacin
Rationale
Initial treatment of a contact lens-related microbial keratitis should include a broad-spectrum activity against gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria. Fluoroquinolones, particularly fourth-generation fluoroquinolones, have good coverage against most gram-positive and gram-negative organisms implicated in contact lens-related microbial keratitis. Sulfonamides, penicillins, and first-generation cephalosporins lack adequate coverage against gram-negative organisms, most notably Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

Q2421
External Disease & Cornea
At what level of the cornea are the deposits in the condition depicted (figure) primarily found?
Correct answer: C. Bowman layer
Rationale
Band keratopathy results from the deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite at the level of the Bowman layer. Aside from chronic inflammation associated with uveitis, other causes of calcific band keratopathy include systemic disorders that cause hypercalcemia or elevated serum phosphorus, as well as silicone oil (particularly in an aphakic eye), exposure to mercurial vapors or preservative, and primary hereditary band keratopathy. In ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) chelation to treat band keratopathy, the epithelium must be removed before the chelating solution is applied.

Q2422

What condition is phlyctenulosis usually associated with?
Correct answer: C. staphylococcal blepharitis
Rationale
Phlyctenules are a delayed or cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction to staphylococcus or other microbial antigens, not meibomian gland dysfunction, seborrheic blepharitis, or vernal conjunctivitis. They are characterized by focal gray or yellow elevations in cornea, limbal region, or conjunctiva.

Q2423
External Disease & Cornea
In herpes zoster ophthalmicus, what is the most typical location of vesicular lesions?
Correct answer: D. the upper eyelid
Rationale
The presence of vesicular involvement of the upper eyelid (CN V1) is 1 feature that can distinguish herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO) from other dermatomal involvement. One would expect to see involvement of the forehead and upper lid as part of V1 zoster dermatitis, but the lower eyelid is supplied by V2 and is not as commonly associated with HZO. The cheek and scalp are also not generally involved in HZO. In immunosuppressed patients, more than 1 branch of CN V may be affected simultaneously.

Q2424
External Disease & Cornea
When an inheritance pattern is present in Fuchs endothelial dystrophy, what type of pattern is most common?
Correct answer: C. autosomal dominant
Rationale
Fuchs endothelial dystrophy is characterized by corneal guttae and decreased endothelial cell function, which lead to decreased vision. Cases without known inheritance are common, but when an inheritance pattern is present, it is usually autosomal dominant.
To manifest an autosomal recessive dystrophy, an individual must receive a genetic mutation from both parents who, although carriers of the mutation, are usually unaffected. Macular corneal dystrophy is an example of autosomal recessive inheritance.
X-linked dominant inheritance occurs when a genetic mutation is carried on the X chromosome and manifests in both male and female carriers. Incontinentia pigmenti is an example of X-linked dominant inheritance.
Mitochondrial inheritance occurs when a genetic mutation found on mitochondrial DNA is passed from mother to offspring. Leber hereditary optic neuropathy is an example of mitochondrial inheritance.

Q2425
External Disease & Cornea
What is the most effective immediate treatment for a symptomatic corneal infiltrate caused by staphylococcal marginal keratitis?
Correct answer: C. topical corticosteroids
Rationale
The limbus plays an important role in immune-mediated corneal disorders. The limbus has a population of antigen-presenting cells (APCs) that constitutively express MHC class II antigens and are capable of efficient mobilization and induction of T-cell responses. Therefore, immune-related corneal changes often occur in a peripheral location adjacent to the limbus. In addition, because the peripheral cornea is adjacent to the vascularized (posterior) limbus, circulating immune cells, immune complexes, and complement factors tend to deposit adjacent to the terminal capillary loops of the limbal vascular arcades, thereby producing a variety of immune phenomena that manifest in the corneal periphery.

Q2426
External Disease & Cornea
What test is most appropriate to confirm the presence of corneal guttae?
Correct answer: D. specular microscopy
Rationale
Imaging of the corneal endothelium can be accomplished by specular microscopy or confocal microscopy. Typically, a slit-lamp examination is sufficient to diagnose corneal guttae, but either of these tests may be useful in equivocal cases.
Pachymetry may be elevated in patients with corneal guttae, but it does not confirm the diagnosis. Ultrasound biomicroscopy is better suited for imaging larger structures of the angle or the ciliary body and cannot identify corneal guttae. Anterior segment OCT can provide corneal thickness and curvature measurements, but it is not suitable for identifying corneal guttae.

Q2427
External Disease & Cornea
What culture media is best suited for identifying mycobacterial infections?
Correct answer: A. Löwenstein-Jensen medium
Rationale
Mycobacterium can be cultured on Löwenstein-Jensen medium for identification as the causative agent of a corneal infection. Thioglycollate broth is useful for culturing aerobic and anaerobic bacteria. Chocolate agar is most effective for identifying aerobic bacteria. Buffered charcoal-yeast extract agar can be used to identify Acanthamoeba infections.

Q2428
External Disease & Cornea
What systemic disease does this 67-year-old patient most likely have?
Correct answer: D. rheumatoid arthritis
Rationale
The image shows findings consistent with peripheral ulcerative keratitis (PUK). The inferior sector of the cornea, within 2 mm of the limbus, shows an area with stromal thinning and likely absent epithelium overlying this thinned area. There is also moderate inflammation of the adjacent conjunctiva. PUK occurs most often in the setting of rheumatoid arthritis.
PUK may occur in many other conditions, including sarcoidosis, Sjögren syndrome, and tuberculosis. However, these are incorrect answers for this question, which asks for the most likely systemic disease.
Peripheral Ulcerative Keratitis Associated with Systemic Immune-Mediated Diseases
Pathogenesis:
  • Occurs most often in association with rheumatoid arthritis (RA)
  • Biopsy of conjunctival tissue adjacent to corneal disease shows evidence of immune-mediated vaso-occlusive disease (biopsy not standard diagnostic procedure)
Clinical Presentation:
  • History of connective tissue disease almost always (but not always) present
  • Peripheral corneal infiltration or stromal melting (called keratolysis if significant, often rapid) could be first sign of underlying systemic disease
  • Generally correlates with exacerbations of systemic disease activity
  • Usually unilateral and limited to 1 sector of peripheral cornea (as seen in the figure)
  • Can be bilateral and extensive
  • Early corneal findings: Epithelial involvement patchy and stroma still near-normal thickness
  • Beyond early corneal findings: Lesions within 2 mm of the limbus, accompanied by vaso-occlusion of the adjacent limbal vasculature. Epithelium absent and stroma thinned in the affected area. Possible significant cellular infiltrate in stroma.
  • Conjunctiva: minimally or severely inflamed
  • Sclera: May be involved if patient has systemic immune-mediated disease, such as necrotizing scleritis in patients with RA
Management:
  • Goal to decrease melting (will stop or slow if epithelium made to heal) 
  • Epithelial healing: Lubricants, patching, bandage contact lens
  • Topical collagenase inhibitors: sodium citrate 10%, acetylcysteine solution 20%, medroxyprogesterone 1%, corticosteroids (can have variable effects; weigh benefits against risks of impaired healing)
  • Systemic collagenase inhibitors: tetracyclines (doxycycline) of potential value
  • If central melting: topical cyclosporine may be effective due to T-cell-mediated process instead of occlusive vasculitis
  • Procedures: Excision or recession of adjacent limbal conjunctiva
If uncontrolled:
  • Systemic immunosuppression (oral prednisone), cytotoxic agents (cyclophosphamide), immunomodulatory agents (methotrexate or cyclosporine), biologics (infliximab)
  • If rapid melting: intravenous treatment with high-dose cyclophosphamide + corticosteroid
  • Threatened perforation: cyanoacrylate glue and bandage contact lens until systemic therapy started, occasionally multiple tectonic grafts required while systemic therapy adjusted
  • Visual restoration: keratoplasty, after underlying disease controlled
  • Partner with rheumatologist - morbidity and death risk is significant

Correct answer: C. conjunctival resection
Rationale
Medical therapies for conjunctivochalasis include ocular lubricants, topical corticosteroids, topical antihistamines, and patching at bedtime with ointment to protect the exposed conjunctiva. Surgical approaches include excision of the redundant conjunctiva or thermal cautery to shrink the tissue.

Q2430
External Disease & Cornea
What vital dye is most likely to produce symptoms of ocular irritation?
Correct answer: C. rose bengal
Rationale
Ocular surface damage is commonly assessed by staining with fluorescein, rose bengal, and/or lissamine green. Of these, rose bengal staining is the most poorly tolerated and frequently causes some irritation and reflex tearing. Rose bengal stains the conjunctivae to a greater extent than the cornea and signifies areas of devitalized epithelial cells. Trypan blue is used in vivo for staining of anterior capsule during cataract surgery, assessing trabeculectomy bleb function, and staining of trabecular meshwork during angle-based minimally invasive glaucoma surgery (MIGS) procedures. Fluorescein sodium dye is most commonly clinically used and is relatively well tolerated. Fluorescein stains the cornea to a greater extent than the conjunctiva and signifies areas where the epithelial cells have desquamated. Lissamine green is usually well tolerated.

Q2431
External Disease & Cornea
What is the best noninvasive way to visualize the cysts pathognomonic of Acanthamoeba keratitis?
Correct answer: A. confocal microscopy
Rationale
Confocal microscopy has demonstrated efficacy in the early diagnosis of patients with Acanthamoeba. It allows rapid identification of acanthamoebal cysts with a relatively high sensitivity and specificity, although it requires a skilled observer to interpret the images.
Sclerotic scatter is useful for demonstrating subtle pathology but is inadequate to resolve microscopic cysts. Specular microscopy allows imaging of the corneal endothelium, but is not considered useful in the diagnosis of Acanthamoeba keratitis. Optical coherence tomography can provide cross-sectional information about corneal pathology but is inadequate to resolve microscopic structures the size of Acanthamoeba cysts.

A 69-year-old woman developed varicella-zoster infection involving the nasociliary branch of the trigeminal nerve (V1), with Hutchinson sign. Three months following oral antiviral treatment for a corneal pseudodendrite, she returns with decreasing vision, redness, and a chronic dull ache involving the right eye. Given her corneal fluorescein staining shown, what diagnosis is most consistent with her course?
Correct answer: C. neurotrophic ulceration
Rationale
This patient has neurotrophic ulceration. Long-term complications from severe varicella-zoster keratitis include trigeminal nerve damage and resulting neuropathy. The photography shows the classically rounded edge of the ulcer, indicating the chronicity of this condition. Calcific band keratopathy is not seen in this patient, but it can occur in many long-standing forms of keratitis. Bacterial keratitis and corneal perforation are not found in this patient, but she is at risk for these complications as well.

Q2433

What rheumatologic condition is most frequently associated with peripheral ulcerative keratitis?
Correct answer: A. rheumatoid arthritis
Rationale
Rheumatoid arthritis is the condition most frequently associated with peripheral ulcerative keratitis, and testing for rheumatoid factor (RF) is warranted as part of the systemic evaluation. Systemic lupus erythematosus, granulomatosis with polyangiitis (also termed Wegener granulomatosis), and ulcerative colitis are also associated with peripheral ulcerative keratitis, but they are less commonly present.

Q2434
External Disease & Cornea
A 32-year-old woman visits the ophthalmologist for an urgent same-day appointment. She sustained a corneal abrasion 2 weeks ago, and it developed into a keratitis that has not been responding to topical antibiotics. She reports excruciating pain. The examination is shown in Figure 1. Multiple cultures have been negative. What is the most likely cause of this patient's findings?
Correct answer: A. surreptitious use of topical anesthetic
Rationale
This patient is presenting with a necrotic corneal ring infiltrate. This infiltrate can be caused by topical anesthetic overuse, as well as bacterial, fungal, herpetic, and amebic infection. However, as this patient has been treated appropriately for bacterial keratitis and has had multiple negative cultures, suspicion should be raised for topical anesthetic use, use of which can inhibit epithelial cell migration and division, inhibiting healing of the corneal surface.
Topical antibiotics (like aminoglycosides) can be associated with toxic keratoconjunctivitis, but are not classically associated with a corneal ring infiltrate.
Epidemic keratoconjunctivitis, caused by adenoviral serotypes 8, 19, and 37, can be associated with conjunctival injection, chemosis, follicles, and membrane/pseudomembrane formation; 7–14 days following the initial infection, patients can develop multifocal subepithelial, not ring, infiltrates.

An asymptomatic patient presents for a routine examination. The ophthalmologist discovers longstanding traumatic mydriasis. What is the appropriate next step?

Rationale
Given that the patient is asymptomatic, observation is the best choice. If the patient were to develop symptoms, a trial of medical therapy would involve less risk than surgery.

Q2436
External Disease & Cornea
What is a contraindication for using corneal tissue for transplantation?
Correct answer: D. history of leukemia
Rationale
The Eye Bank Association of America has a list of exclusion criteria regarding donation of tissue for corneal transplantation. Leukemia, active disseminated lymphoma, and malignant tumors of the anterior segment or known adenocarcinoma in the eye of primary or metastatic origin are contraindications for donation. Lung adenocarcinoma that has not metastasized to the eye is not on the list of exclusion criteria. A history of sarcoidosis without active ocular or intraocular inflammation would not be a contraindication. Psychiatric disorders are not part of the criteria contraindicating donor cornea use.
Criteria for exclusion include:
  • Death of unknown cause
  • Congenital rubella
  • Reye syndrome within the past 3 months
  • Neurodegenerative conditions including prion disease (eg, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy)
  • Infectious conditions including human immunodeficiency virus, hepatitis, and active bacterial/viral encephalitis or bacterial/fungal endocarditis, suspected rabies or history of being bitten within the past 6 months
  • Down syndrome (exclusion criterion for penetrating and anterior lamellar keratoplasties)
  • Intrinsic eye disease including retinoblastoma, malignant tumors of the anterior segment, or known adenocarcinoma in the eye of primary or metastatic origin, active ocular or intraocular inflammation, congenital or acquired disorders of the eye that would preclude a successful outcome
  • Leukemias
  • Active disseminated lymphomas
  • Behavioral criteria: High-risk behavior (eg, intravenous drug use or incarceration in prison)
  • Prior refractive corneal surgery with the exception that previous laser refractive surgery may not disqualify for use in endothelial keratoplasty
  • Positive test for anti-HIV-1/anti-HIV-2, nonreactive for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and anti-HCV antibody

Q2438
External Disease & Cornea
The diagnosis of seasonal allergic conjunctivitis can be confirmed by finding a predominance of what cell types in a conjunctival scraping?
Correct answer: A. eosinophils
Rationale
All 3 specific types of ocular allergy: seasonal allergic conjunctivitis, vernal conjunctivitis, and atopic keratoconjunctivitis, have some element of type 1 hypersensitivity reaction caused by the interaction between an allergen and specific immunoglobulin E (IgE) antibodies on the surface of mast cells in the conjunctiva. In seasonal allergic conjunctivitis, conjunctival scrapings reveal eosinophils, a finding that is almost diagnostic of an allergic response.

Q2439
External Disease & Cornea
A 56-year-old man with decreased vision has a markedly enlarged corneal diameter and visually significant cataract; the dilated exams are normal for both eyes. Preoperative measurements for cataract surgery show normal axial length with white-to-white measurements of 14.5 mm in both eyes. During cataract surgery, what complication is the patient at increased risk for?
Correct answer: A. zonular instability
Rationale
Megalocornea is a condition with bilateral, nonprogressive corneal enlargement that usually shows X-linked inheritance. In this condition, the cornea is histologically normal, but its diameter is greater than 13 mm. Megalocornea is associated with zonular instability, so there are additional risks for these eyes during cataract surgery. Megalocornea is not associated with an increased risk of bleeding or malignant glaucoma. Nanophthalmic eyes are associated with an increased risk of choroidal effusion during cataract surgery.
Lens instability and subluxation, iridodonesis, and poor zonular integrity are also associated with megalocornea and present additional risks and challenges in the management of cataracts, particularly in terms of the selection and placement of an intraocular lens (IOL) after cataract surgery. If the lens is of normal size, an IOL can be inserted in the capsular bag. A capsular tension ring may be placed to reduce stress on the zonular fibers. Standard-sized posterior chamber lenses are typically too short to be fixated in the ciliary sulcus, and anterior chamber lenses are similarly problematic in the enlarged anterior chamber. If zonular support is insufficient or capsular volume too great to allow stable IOL centration, an iris clip or iris-sutured lens may be the best option.

Q2440
External Disease & Cornea
A 43-year-old woman presents with an iris elevation and corresponding pigmented mass visible on gonioscopy. What is the best imaging modality to further investigate this lesion?
Correct answer: C. ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM)
Rationale
High-frequency ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) provides high-resolution in vivo imaging of the anterior segment. Tissues visualized include the cornea, anterior and posterior iris, ciliary body, zonules, angle structures, and anterior lens capsule. UBM allows a view through an opaque cornea and total hyphema. UBM is helpful in the assessment of ciliary body pathology, including cysts and tumors. Its major advantage is in visualizing structures behind the iris.
B-scan ultrasonography is more useful in detailing posterior segment pathology. A CT scan images structures external to the globe, and is used in assessing, for example, orbital and facial pathology. Anterior segment OCT provides high-resolution imaging of the anterior segment but is best used for structures anterior to the iris plane.

Q2441
External Disease & Cornea
A 73-year-old woman presents with decreased vision over the past 6 months. A photo of her anterior segment examination is shown. The condition is localized to what layer of the cornea?
Correct answer: A. Bowman layer
Rationale
This is an image of band keratopathy. Band keratopathy (the deposition of calcium in the cornea) can result from multiple causes, including chronic inflammatory ocular disease, hypercalcemia from systemic disorders such as renal failure, elevated serum phosphorus, chronic exposure to mercurial preservatives or vapors, silicone oil in the anterior chamber, and other rare causes. Band keratopathy can also be hereditary. The keratopathy begins as basophilic deposits in the Bowman layer. The band typically starts peripherally and then coalesces inwards. The band generally runs horizontally in the interpalpebral fissure, but in advanced cases can involve the entire cornea.
The treatment of band keratopathy involves the use of disodium ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) chelation. The corneal epithelium is removed and the chelating agent is then applied to the calcium. Agitation with a cellulose sponge may enhance calcium release from the Bowman layer. Occasionally, residual anterior stromal opacification is present following removal of calcium, which may be amenable to additional treatment such as phototherapeutic keratectomy (PTK).

Q2442

For 2 weeks, a patient with past ocular herpes simplex keratitis has had ocular redness and irritation. What slit-lamp finding is most strongly suggestive of an active epithelial herpes simplex infection?
Correct answer: A. terminal bulbs on linear epithelial lesions
Rationale
Herpes simplex virus (HSV) epithelial keratitis typically presents as a linear lesion with dichotomous branching and terminal bulbs at the ends of branches. Ciliary flush and conjunctival injection usually coincide with the corneal findings. With worsening, the terminal bulbs can coalesce into a geographic ulcer.
The other presentations are not typical for HSV epithelial keratitis. Mucous epithelial plaques and filaments with punctate staining are consistent with dryness, while a hypopyon suggests severe intraocular inflammation, often seen with infection

Q2443
External Disease & Cornea
What finding would support the decision for pterygium excision?
Correct answer: C. increased with-the-rule astigmatism
Rationale
The most widely accepted indications for pterygium excision include induced astigmatism and chronic symptomatic irritation. Induced astigmatism is most commonly with-the-rule, with relative flattening occurring in the axis of the pterygium.
A history of pterygium excision in the contralateral eye may indicate a propensity for progression but is not, in and of itself, an indication for surgery.
Deposition of iron at the leading edge (Stocker line) is indicative of relative stability and is not an indication for excision.
Increased thickness on pachymetry may be observed, owing to the pterygium's added thickness on the underlying cornea.

Q2444
External Disease & Cornea
How can the technique of specular reflection with a slit lamp be optimized to evaluate endothelial cell morphology?
Correct answer: A. Set the slit-beam arm at an angle of 60° from the viewing arm and use a short slit.
Rationale
Specular reflection is mainly used to examine the corneal endothelium (second Purkinje light reflex), although it can also examine corneal epithelium and lens epithelium. Endothelial cell morphology is typically viewed under high magnification using only 1 ocular.
The examiner can enhance this specular reflection by placing a light beam at an appropriate angle, revealing the corneal endothelium. Following are the steps for examining the corneal endothelium with specular reflection:
  • Begin by setting the slit-beam arm at an angle of 60° from the viewing arm and using a short slit or 0.2-mm spot.
  • Identify the very bright mirror image of the lightbulb’s filament and the paired epithelial and endothelial Purkinje light reflexes.
  • Superimpose the corneal endothelial light reflex onto the filament’s mirror image, giving a bright glare.
  • Use the joystick to move the biomicroscope slightly forward in order to focus the endothelial reflex.
A wide diffuse beam is used to optimize diffuse illumination. A tall wide beam directed onto the limbal area is used to optimize sclerotic scatter.

The ends of herpes zoster dendritiform lesions are typically what shape?
Correct answer: C. blunt
Rationale
The dendritic epithelial keratitis common in ophthalmic zoster is actually caused by herpes zoster pseudodendrites. These pseudodendrites, as distinguished from true dendrites in herpes simplex virus epithelial keratitis, have blunt ends rather than terminal bulbs, have little epithelial ulceration, and stain poorly with fluorescein and rose bengal. Additionally, pseudodendrites typically have a more raised, plaque-like appearance.

Q2447

Combined hearing loss and corneal findings are seen in what clinical entity?
Correct answer: A. Cogan interstitial keratitis
Rationale
Stromal interstitial keratitis can be associated with a variety of systemic diseases including autoimmune (systemic lupus erythematosus, polyarteritis nodosa), protozoan (trypanosomiasis [sleeping sickness]), plasmodium [malaria], leishmaniasis), worms (onchocerciasis [river blindness], schistosomiasis [bilharzia], taenia solium [cysticercosis]), viral (herpes zoster, rubeola, vaccinia, herpes simplex virus, mumps, influenza, Epstein-Barr virus), bacterial (Treponema pallidum, Mycobacterium spp, Borrelia spp, Leptospira spp), and in conditions with unknown underlying etiology, such as Cogan interstitial keratitis. The latter clinical entity is associated with interstitial keratitis, vertigo, and hearing loss. Early diagnosis of Cogan syndrome is vital because the syndrome can include systemic vasculitis as one of its findings, which can lead to death if not adequately treated.

Correct answer: C. observation
Rationale
The photo depicts a pinguecula, a yellow-white conjunctival lesion that is most commonly located nasally, but may be temporal, in the interpalpebral space; it is usually adjacent to the limbus. Pingueculae do not involve the cornea but may be associated with an adjacent dellen. No treatment is generally needed in asymptomatic patients. If patients are symptomatic, artificial tears or ocular lubricants can be used. Topical corticosteroids can be used briefly in inflamed lesions. Surgical removal is usually not needed but can be considered for chronically inflamed lesions.

Q2449
External Disease & Cornea
For the finding shown, what is the most appropriate management?
Correct answer: D. topical lubricant
Rationale
The pictured finding is a subconjunctival hemorrhage. Typically, there is no antecedent trauma. Occasionally, a history of Valsalva maneuver, use of anticoagulants, or rarely, systemic disorders such as bleeding diathesis may be elicited as a potential cause. Observation and topical lubrication are the most appropriate treatment options.
When there is associated elevation of the limbal conjunctiva, disruption of the normal tear film can cause corneal dellen, which represents focal corneal thinning due to stromal dehydration. Topical steroids could be indicated for inflammatory conditions such as episcleritis or scleritis, but not in the setting of subconjunctival hemorrhage. Similarly, topical nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications would not be indicated in this scenario. Prophylactic antibiotics would only be warranted in the setting of a significant conjunctival abrasion or associated corneal epithelial defect.

Q2450

What best describes the origin of conjunctival melanoma?
Correct answer: B. It always arises from conjunctival melanocytes.
Rationale
Conjunctival melanomas may arise from PAM (70%) or nevi (5%) or may arise de novo (25%). A PAM lesion should be removed if it involves greater than 2 clock-hours, or has progressive enlargement, a nodular component, feeder vessels, or thickening. It should then be biopsied to identify whether atypia is present and whether it has converted to melanoma.

Q2451
External Disease & Cornea
A 75-year-old patient presents for evaluation of blunt trauma to the right eye from a fall sustained one day previously. Vision is 20/50 in the affected eye. The slit-lamp examination is remarkable for a formed anterior chamber with a teardrop-shaped pupil. Two clock hours of iris are prolapsed through the previous temporal clear corneal phacoemulsification incision. The extruded iris tissue appears viable but is noted to have a thin translucent membrane adherent to the stromal surface. In addition to surgical repair of the laceration, what is the most appropriate management?
Correct answer: A. Reposit the prolapsed iris tissue, with removal of the membrane.
Rationale
Whenever possible, viable uveal tissue should be reposited during surgical repair of a ruptured globe. In this case, the description is consistent with iris prolapse and early epithelialization of the iris surface from the cornea or conjunctival epithelium. As the iris tissue is noted to be viable and the injury is recent, the most appropriate option is to peel off any adherent membranes and reposit the iris tissue. Repositing the tissue without peeling off the membranes would increase the risk of developing epithelial ingrowth. Similarly, culturing the membrane without excising it would also be inappropriate. Excision of the prolapsed iris tissue should only be performed when the iris tissue is visibly necrotic or macerated beyond repair.

Moraxella lacunata

Moraxella lacunata is a common cause of angular blepharoconjunctivitis. Propionibacterium acnes is a slow-growing organism that can be seen in pseudophakic chronic endophthalmitis. Streptococcus pneumoniae and Chlamydia trachomatis are both causes of bacterial conjunctivitis.

Q2453

In a patient with fungal keratitis, what finding confers the most guarded (ominous) prognosis?
Correct answer: A. scleral extension
Rationale
Invasion of fungus into the sclera is a potentially globe-threatening complication. Scleral extension can precede intraocular infection and is particularly concerning because infected tissue may no longer be cleared by surgical grafting. Extension into the sclera or anterior chamber lowers the prognosis for globe salvage. Satellite lesions, ring infiltrates, and endothelial plaques can be seen in moderately severe fungal keratitis.

Q2454
External Disease & Cornea
What is distichiasis?
Correct answer: C. growth of accessory eyelashes posterior to the normal row of eyelashes
Rationale
Distichiasis, both congenital and acquired, refers to an accessory row of eyelashes posterior to the normal anatomic location. These can be coarse or fine, and they can occur as a result of numerous inflammatory conditions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome, ocular rosacea, and chemical burns. Misdirected eyelashes arising from the normal anatomic location that curve toward the ocular surface describes trichiasis, not distichiasis. Direction of the eyelashes away from the ocular surface is a normal phenomenon, although it may be exaggerated in the setting of eyelid ectropion.

Q2455
External Disease & Cornea
What class of virus causes molluscum contagiosum?
Correct answer: A. poxvirus
Rationale
Poxviridae are large, enveloped, double-stranded DNA viruses. Molluscum contagiosum is a poxvirus infection that produces one or more umbilicated nodules on the skin and eyelid margin and, less commonly, on the conjunctiva. These nodules release viral particles that can be found in the tear film and are spread by direct contact with infected individuals.
Ocular manifestations of adenovirus include a follicular conjunctivitis and, less commonly, corneal epithelial keratitis or subepithelial infiltrates. Adenoviruses can cause a broad spectrum of systemic disease, and ocular manifestations most commonly include a follicular conjunctivitis.
Herpesviruses establish latency in their natural host and have a wide variety of ocular manifestations caused by primary infection, recurrent infection, or host inflammatory response. 
The most commonly known parvovirus to infect humans is parvovirus B19, or "fifth disease," which has been associated with some ocular inflammatory manifestations.

Q2456
External Disease & Cornea
A patient presents with bilateral stromal infiltrates without epithelial ulceration. On review of systems, the patient reports a recent viral upper respiratory tract infection (URI) and difficulty with balance and tinnitus. Rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test and microhemagglutination assay (FTA-ABS) results are negative. What treatment is indicated in addition to the typical therapeutic regimen for this condition?
Correct answer: D. systemic corticosteroid
Rationale
This patient's presentation with bilateral nonulcerative stromal inflammation is suggestive of interstitial keratitis, which is an inflammatory, nonulcerative condition primarily involving the corneal stroma. Herpes simplex and syphilis are the most common etiologies of interstitial keratitis in the US. In this case, the negative RPR and FTA-ABS results and a review of systems suggesting vestibuloauditory pathology are consistent with Cogan syndrome, a rare autoimmune disease often precipitated by a viral illness, with features that overlap with polyarteritis nodosa. Cogan syndrome can be associated with vertigo and can lead to permanent deafness if not treated promptly with systemic corticosteroids.

Q2457
External Disease & Cornea
A 35-year-old man presents with a 2-day history of decreased vision and of pain in the right eye after being struck by a tree branch while hiking. Vision is 20/50, with an intraocular pressure of 8 mm Hg. Slit-lamp examination is remarkable for a 5-mm vertical conjunctival laceration near the semilunar fold. Examination of the wound is attempted at the slit lamp, but significant bullous subconjunctival hemorrhage limits the examination. What is the best course of management?
Correct answer: B. exploration of the wound with conjunctival peritomy in the operating room
Rationale
The principal requirement in this setting is to evaluate the wound to its full depth. Since adequate examination in the clinic is halted by subconjunctival hemorrhage, the patient should be taken to the operating room to explore the wound and, if necessary, close an open globe. In addition, the patient's 2-day history of pain and decreased vision should also warrant additional investigation.
Primary closure of the conjunctiva is not advisable without exploration in the setting of trauma with a possible ruptured globe or foreign body: By closing the surface defect, a definitive diagnosis is potentially obscured.
Ultrasonography of an eye should not be performed if there is concern for an open globe, as pressure on the eye could expulse intraocular contents. One could order a computed tomography (CT) scan to examine for any scleral irregularity; however, this is not one of the answer choices.
Treating with antibiotics followed by re-examination in 3 to 5 days is insufficient.

Q2458
External Disease & Cornea
One day following penetrating keratoplasty with 16 interrupted sutures, a patient is noted to have an aqueous leak originating from the suture track of the 12 o'clock suture. The suture is not visibly loose or malpositioned. The anterior chamber is deep and the pressure is 17 mm Hg. The patient's medications are topical prednisolone acetate 1% QID and topical gentamicin sulfate 0.3% QID.  What is the most appropriate initial management?
Correct answer: A. Place a bandage contact lens and start timolol 0.5%.
Rationale
Suture track leaks generally resolve without surgical intervention and may be monitored closely for spontaneous resolution. Placement of a bandage contact lens and the use of an aqueous suppressant may encourage more rapid closure of the leak. Persistent small wound leaks (those failing to improve after several days of conservative management) or larger wound leaks (those causing significant shallowing of the anterior chamber or iris prolapse) should be repaired in the operating room. Discontinuing topical steroids for a small wound leak is not advisable, and graft rejection may ensue. Unless a suture is broken or overtly loose, it is generally inadvisable to remove the suture in the early postoperative period following penetrating keratoplasty, as doing so may trigger a larger wound dehiscence.

Q2459

A 32-year-old man has painless, slowly progressive decreased vision in both eyes. His anterior segment examination is abnormal as illustrated in the left eye shown. What would be the preferred management for this patient?
Correct answer: D. polycarbonate lenses and a discussion that the vision loss may slowly progress with time
Rationale
The figure demonstrates superior limbal thinning with an intact epithelium and without inflammation. These findings, as well as the history of painless vision loss, support the diagnosis of Terrien marginal degeneration. Over time the degeneration often progresses in a circumferential fashion, and may result in a slowly progressive increase in astigmatism. Oral corticosteroids would be appropriate in a patient with peripheral ulcerative keratitis. Aggressive topical lubrication and a discussion that the condition should resolve with time would be appropriate in a patient with corneal dellen. Surgical correction is indicated when perforation is imminent because of progressive thinning, or when marked astigmatism significantly limits vision. Crescent‑shaped lamellar or full‑thickness corneoscleral patch grafts may be used; they have been reported to arrest the progression of severe against‑the‑rule astigmatism for up to 20 years. Annular lamellar keratoplasty grafts may be required in severe cases of 360° marginal degeneration.

Q2460

When considering phototherapeutic keratectomy (PTK) for a corneal scar, what test provides the most objective measurement of the depth of the lesion?
Correct answer: D. anterior segment optical coherence tomography (AS-OCT)
Rationale
Anterior segment optical coherence tomography (AS-OCT) provides extremely high-resolution cross-sectional imaging of the corneal layers, which may be beneficial in assessing the depth of a scar prior to attempting phototherapeutic keratectomy. Confocal microscopy can provide in vivo images of different depths of the cornea, but it is not helpful in determining the depth of a scar. Slit-lamp examination is always indicated for the evaluation of a corneal scar but cannot provide the same degree of accuracy with regard to measuring depth as AS-OCT. Ultrasonic pachymetry is useful for measuring total corneal thickness, but it does not allow direct measurement of the depth of a scar.

Q2461

In a patient with posterior scleritis, what is the most likely finding on B-scan echography?
Correct answer: B. choroidal and scleral thickening
Rationale
Choroidal and scleral thickening are the initial and most consistent findings of posterior scleritis on B-scan ultrasonography. With enough inflammation, patients can also manifest the classic "T-sign," which reflects fluid in sub-Tenon space. Patients with posterior scleritis can also manifest subretinal fluid accumulation with exudative retinal detachments, but this is not as common as choroidal and scleral thickening. Similarly, patients can have optic nerve head edema, but this is not as common on choroidal and scleral thickening. Vitreous opacities are not a finding typically associated with posterior scleritis.

Q2462

What change in the filament of a handheld (Cochet-Bonnet) esthesiometer is required to elicit sensation from a patient with worsening neurotrophic keratopathy?
Correct answer: B. shorter filament length
Rationale
Corneal esthesiometry is used to evaluate corneal sensation. The handheld (Cochet-Bonnet) esthesiometer contains a thin, retractable, nylon monofilament that contacts the patient's cornea. Adjusting the length of the monofilament changes the pressure applied by the device. When the filament is shortened, more pressure is applied to the cornea, and less corneal sensation is required to detect the stimulus. When the filament is lengthened, less pressure is applied and more corneal sensation is required to detect stimulus. The thickness of the filament does not change during testing.

Correct answer: C. renal failure

Nephropathy is most common in the infantile form of cystinosis (and least common in the adult-onset form). Corneal symptoms are often present by 2 years of age and manifest as photophobia. Renal damage is the major medical morbidity and can lead to kidney failure by 10 years of age. Corneal symptoms are managed with topical application of cysteamine. Oral administration of cysteamine might be beneficial for posterior segment manifestations (retinopathy, optic neuropathy).

Q2464

Incubation of both blood agar and Sabouraud agar media at 25 degrees Celsius can facilitate recovery of what organism?
Correct answer: B. fungi
Rationale
Several recovery techniques are available in cases of suspected fungal infection, including:
  • Staining the specimen with potassium hydroxide, Gram, Giemsa, Gomori-methenamine silver, acridine orange, and/or calcofluor white
  • Plating the specimen on Sabouraud agar in addition to blood agar, chocolate agar, and thioglycollate broth; incubation of media at room temperature (25 degrees Celsius or 77 degrees Fahrenheit) may facilitate fungal recovery as noted specifically by Table 9-4 of the BCSC series. Brain-heart infusion agar can also be used.
  • Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
Sabouraud agar is specifically meant for fungal organism detection, so it would not detect the other organisms listed. Acanthamoeba would require nonnutrient agar with bacterial overlay, blood agar, or buffered charcoal-yeast extract agar. Neisseria is a gram-negative diplococcus normally seen inside neutrophils on a smear with gram stain, grows on chocolate agar, or can be detected by PCR amplification of its DNA. Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular parasite and is best detected with Giemsa stain, immunofluorescent antibody tests, or by PCR.

Q2465

A patient has 24 hours of severe, copious conjunctival discharge without a corneal ulcer. Conjunctival gram stain shows numerous neutrophils with gram-negative intracellular diplococci. What is the most appropriate treatment?
Correct answer: C. intramuscular ceftriaxone
Rationale
Hyperacute conjunctivitis with gram-negative intracellular (or extracellular) diplococci is diagnostic of gonococcal conjunctivitis caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae. If corneal ulceration is present, the patient should be admitted to the hospital to receive intravenous ceftriaxone. In the absence of corneal involvement, outpatient therapy with intramuscular ceftriaxone 1 g and close observation is appropriate. Intravenous penicillin G is indicated for treatment of neurosyphilis. Oral azithromycin is indicated for the treatment of chlamydial conjunctivitis. Topical gentamicin ointment can be used as an adjunctive treatment for gonococcal conjunctivitis, but the mainstay of treatment is systemic ceftriaxone.

For acute Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) with conjunctival involvement, what intervention is indicated to reduce long-term formation of symblepharon?
Correct answer: A. amniotic membrane transplantation
Rationale
Early amniotic membrane transplantation has been shown to reduce the formation of symblepharon and minimize the long-term ocular surface complications for patients with conjunctival inflammation from SJS. Symblepharon rings and forniceal debridement have been largely supplanted by amniotic membrane grafting (repeated forniceal debridement may actually worsen conjunctival scarring, owing to mechanical trauma). Temporary tarsorrhaphy may be indicated for non-healing epithelial defects, but it is not directly beneficial to preventing the formation of symblepharon.

Rationale
Conjunctival resection is indicated for progressive rheumatologic corneal melting disorders that are not responsive to immunosuppression. The presumptive mechanism is distancing the conjunctival vasculature from the area of corneal inflammation. In this case, the focal area of sectoral injection with adjacent corneal thinning allows for relatively easy identification and resection of the responsible tissue.
Limbal stem cell transplantation plays no role in the management of acute corneal melting. Systemic antifungal treatment is not indicated in the absence of a confirmed (or strongly suspected) fungal sclerokeratitis. Penetrating keratoplasty may be indicated in progressive corneal melts, but typically should be delayed unless there is impending (eg, descemetocele) or existing perforation.

A foreign body that enters the corneal stroma deep to the Bowman layer always results in some degree of scar formation. Optimal management of a corneal foreign body therefore includes minimal disruption of the Bowman layer to avoid further scarring and obstruction of the visual axis.

In patients with renal failure, what elevated serum electrolyte can cause the condition shown in the photograph?

Rationale
Band keratopathy refers to the characteristic appearance of calcium hydroxyapatite deposited in a horizontal band across the cornea. The keratopathy commonly occurs in the presence of elevated levels of serum calcium (eg, due to hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D toxicity, sarcoidosis), although elevated levels of serum phosphate also drive the precipitation of calcium hydroxyapatite, even in the setting of normal calcium levels. This can occur in patients with renal failure, particularly if they are not receiving appropriate treatment to lower serum phosphate concentrations. This is why laboratory workup for unexplained band keratopathy should include calcium and phosphate tests. Sodium, chloride, and potassium serum levels are not associated with development of band keratopathy.

Q2475
External Disease & Cornea
What is the appropriate initial management of a pyogenic granuloma?
Correct answer: A. topical corticosteroid eyedrops
Rationale
A pyogenic granuloma is an inflammatory, reactive hemangioma that typically occurs as an exuberant healing response to inflamed chalazia, minor trauma, ocular surgery, or retained suture.  Its name is a misnomer as it is neither suppurative nor does it contain giant cells. Topical steroids may be curative in these lesions and should be the first treatment option. Intralesional corticosteroid injections are minimally invasive and can also quickly shrink lesion or be curative. In some cases, excision of the lesion with cauterization to the base may be required. Since pyogenic granulomas are not microbial in etiology, topical antibiotics have little role in treatment.

Q2476
External Disease & Cornea
What is the most common causative organism of the condition shown in the photograph?
Correct answer: A. Streptococcus
Rationale
Streptococcus

The long-term use of topical corticosteroids, loss of corneal sensation after transplantation, uneven tear film, and suture exposure or erosion all predispose the patient to infectious keratitis, sometimes caused by unusual organisms. Culture of the infiltrate and the exposed suture is recommended, and initiation of broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy can help avoid graft failure. A peculiar form of keratitis, infectious crystalline keratopathy (shown in the figure), is occasionally seen in grafts and other immunocompromised corneas. Branching colonies of organisms proliferate in the deep corneal stroma with minimal or no inflammatory response. Many organisms have been implicated, but Streptococcus viridans is seen most frequently.

Q2477
External Disease & Cornea
A 34-year-old woman was treated for herpes simplex virus (HSV) epithelial keratitis with trifluridine 8 times daily for 2 weeks. She reports that the ocular discomfort improved, but that shortly afterward she developed new onset of redness, tearing, and discomfort. What is the most likely cause of her newer symptoms?
Correct answer: A. toxic epithelial keratopathy
Rationale
While trifluridine is effective in treating HSV epithelial keratitis, it is important to remember that continued use of trifluridine can lead to toxicity, which can manifest with symptoms similar to those of the original HSV episode. The corneal finding is most often diffuse punctal epithelial erosions, as opposed to the classic petaloid epithelial pattern of HSV.
Of note, oral acyclovir has been reported to be as effective as topical antivirals for the treatment of epithelial keratitis and does not cause ocular toxicity. For this reason, oral therapy is preferred by an increasing number of physicians.

Q2478

For a small conjunctival laceration without scleral involvement, what is the most appropriate treatment in addition to prescribing topical antibiotics?
Correct answer: B. observation
Rationale
The majority of conjunctival lacerations do not require operative closure and can be observed, with a covering of prophylactic topical antibiotic drops or ointment. Initial closure with thermocautery or sutures is typically only recommended for large lacerations with displacement of a conjunctival pedicle flap. In the absence of a ruptured globe, systemic antibiotics have no role in treating conjunctival lacerations.

Q2479

A 19-year-old woman with anorexia nervosa presents with severe dry eye. A loss of what tear film component is thought to be primarily responsible?
Correct answer: C. mucin
Rationale
Examination findings suggest conjunctival xerosis (abnormal dryness of the conjunctiva), which in this case is most likely due to vitamin A deficiency. The deficiency is in the mucin component of the tear film, caused by degeneration/dysfunction of the goblet cells. Mucin is produced by the goblet cells within the conjunctiva. Lipid, another component of the tear film, is produced by the meibomian glands. A reduced level of lactoferrin, a protein found in tears, can be a marker for dry eye. Immunoglobulin E levels in tears are elevated in allergic conjunctivitis.

Q2480
External Disease & Cornea
What infectious agent has an association with conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia?
Correct answer: D. human papillomavirus
Rationale
Ocular surface squamous neoplasia (OSSN) represents a spectrum of disease, ranging from mild dysplasia to invasive squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), and is the most common nonpigmented tumor of the ocular surface. Persistent viral infection by human papillomavirus (HPV) of susceptible epithelial cells induces cellular proliferation and can lead to malignant transformation. Neoplastic transformation due to HPV 6 or 11 is very rare. In contrast, HPV 16 and 18 stereotypically integrate their viral genome into host chromosomal DNA, and this in turn is associated with malignant transformation and squamous cell carcinoma.
Scott and Karp previously found HPV DNA and mRNA in 10 out of 10 OSSN specimens (5 HPV 16 and 5 HPV 18); neither HPV was detected in control specimens or in any clinically uninvolved conjunctival specimens from OSSN eyes.
