Q2481
External Disease & Cornea
What treatment for recurrent epithelial erosions may be suitable for peripheral erosions but not central erosions?
Correct answer: D. anterior stromal micropuncture
Rationale
Recurrent epithelial erosions can occur after corneal trauma, with dystrophies of the stroma and the Bowman layer, and can be associated with diabetes. Both peripheral and central erosions can be treated conservatively with bandage contact lenses (often with concurrent antibiotic drops) and hypertonic saline/lubrication. Frequent recurrences can sometimes require surgical therapy. While phototherapeutic keratectomy (PTK) and superficial keratectomy can be used on central lesions, stromal micropuncture is often avoided centrally, due to stromal scarring.

An excisional biopsy of a conjunctival lesion is performed, showing positive margins for primary acquired melanosis (PAM) without atypia. What is the most appropriate treatment?
Correct answer: B. careful follow-up of lesions every 6-12 months
Rationale
PAM without atypia has a low risk of becoming conjunctival melanoma and can be carefully observed every 6 to 12 months. PAM with atypia should be completely excised, and when excision is not possible, adjuvant chemotherapy may be used. Lymph node biopsy is not a part of the management of PAM.

Q2483

What dye, used for examination of the cornea epithelium, is most likely to cause irritation?
Correct answer: B. rose bengal
Rationale
Rose bengal (RB) can cause significant postexamination irritation, as compared with fluorescein and lissamine green (LG) dyes. LG and RB dyes stain dead and devitalized cells, mucus, and epithelial cells that are inadequately protected by ocular surface mucins. Fluorescein stains are used for epithelial erosions and exposed basement membrane. Trypan blue is a dye used in cataract surgery to stain the anterior capsule. It is not used in the evaluation of the corneal epithelium.

Q2484
External Disease & Cornea
What is the most significant risk factor for the condition shown?
Correct answer: A. chronic sun exposure
Rationale
The pictured lesion is a pinguecula, a benign degenerative lesion of the temporal or nasal conjunctiva. These are most frequently encountered in patients with chronic ultraviolet (UV) light exposure. The lesion is typically yellow-white and does not involve the cornea. Focal injection can be present, especially when the eye is irritated.
Bitôt spots are plaque-like white lesions occurring in the interpalpebral zone in patients with severe vitamin A deficiency (malnutrition). Conjunctival lymphoma can occur in patients with systemic lymphoma. Lesions in conjunctival lymphoma are typically salmon colored and generally arise from caruncle or fornix. A limbal dermoid can occur at the temporal limbus, but typically has a denser nodular yellow-white appearance and can have associated hair follicles. These can occur in patients with Goldenhar syndrome (in which a pre-auricular skin tag can be present).

Q2485
External Disease & Cornea
What illumination technique is based on the property of total internal reflection?
Correct answer: A. sclerotic scatter
Rationale
Sclerotic scatter is used to detect subtle corneal abnormalities that distort the total internal reflection property of the normal cornea. Decentering the isocentric light beam so that an intense beam shines on the limbus and scatters off the sclera causes a very faint glow of the cornea. Reflective opacities stand out against the dark field, whereas areas of reduced light transmission in the cornea are seen as shades of gray. This technique is effective in demonstrating epithelial edema, mild stromal infiltration, nebulae, and cornea verticillata.
Specular reflection is mainly used to examine corneal endothelium, although it can also be used to examine corneal epithelium and lens epithelium. Direct focal illumination and slit illumination allow detection and localization of structures, including differences in refractive index. Indirect, proximal illumination and lateral illumination purposely focus or reflect the illuminator's light beam at a different, though adjacent, site than the corneal microscope. This technique is useful to highlight abnormalities that have a refractive index similar to their surroundings and that are difficult to discern by direct illumination.

Q2486
External Disease & Cornea
A 50-year-old restaurant worker was mixing cleaning products when some liquid splashed into his right eye. His slit-lamp photograph is shown. What finding is the best predictor of late corneal neovascularization and pannus formation?
Correct answer: A. amount of scleral and limbal ischemia
Rationale
Although all these clinical features are pertinent when documenting the extent of ocular surface injury after a chemical burn, the degree of limbal ischemia is the most important predictor of progression to limbal stem cell deficiency (which results in corneal neovascularization/pannus formation). In this picture, almost 100% of the limbus is ischemic (manifested by blanching), and the patient is therefore at high risk for developing late limbal stem cell deficiency. Treatments to improve prognosis include mechanisms to minimize ongoing exposure to the agent (eg, immediate irrigation with water or normal saline, removal of any particulate matter), decrease inflammation (topical corticosteroids, oral tetracyclines), and promote healing (oral vitamin C, amniotic membrane transplantation).

Q2487

A 62-year-old man with no previous ocular surgery has painless slowly progressive visual loss, with best-corrected visual acuity of 20/60 OD and 20/60 OS. His slit-lamp examination of one cornea is as shown. His pachymetry is 607 µm OD and 610 µm OS. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. Fuchs dystrophy
Rationale
The presence of bilateral thickened corneas and guttata support the diagnosis of Fuchs corneal dystrophy. Iridocorneal endothelial syndrome may have corneal thickening, but guttata are not a characteristic finding in this typically unilateral disease. Similarly, Meesmann corneal dystrophy presents with corneal epithelial cysts, but not corneal endothelial guttae. Also, Meesmann dystrophy is associated with a slightly thinned cornea, not thickening. Pseudophakic bullous keratopathy is not possible, because he has not had ocular surgery.

Q2488

What is an indication for the implant shown?
Correct answer: D. multiple corneal graft failures
Rationale
The figure demonstrates a Boston Type 1 keratoprosthesis. Indications for its use include treatment of patients who have experienced multiple corneal graft failures or patients with other causes of corneal scarring in which a traditional corneal transplant has a poor prognosis. Aphakic bullous keratopathy would typically be treated with either a full-thickness corneal transplant or a Descemet stripping automated endothelial keratoplasty procedure. Patients with high myopia may be candidates for phakic intraocular lenses. Patients with active ocular infections are not candidates for this procedure.

Q2489

Where is the deposition of copper seen in the Kayser-Fleischer ring associated with Wilson disease?
Correct answer: D. Descemet membrane
Rationale
Wilson disease is an autosomal recessive disease that affects copper metabolism. Copper gets deposited first in the liver, then in the kidneys, and later in the brain and the cornea. The Kayser-Fleischer ring (which is not seen in all patients with Wilson disease) is characterized by posterior copper deposition at level of Descemet membrane in the peripheral cornea. The deposition of the copper pigment starts superiorly.

Q2490
External Disease & Cornea
What is a known risk factor for floppy eyelid syndrome?
Correct answer: B. obstructive sleep apnea
Rationale
Risk factors for floppy eyelid syndrome are obesity, obstructive sleep apnea, and face-down sleep position. If a patient has more laxity on one side than the other, it may be due to sleeping on the side with more laxity. Floppy eyelid syndrome must be distinguished from other diagnoses, including vernal conjunctivitis, giant papillary conjunctivitis, atopic keratoconjunctivitis, infectious conjunctivitis, and toxic keratopathy.

Q2491
External Disease & Cornea
A 70-year-old patient presents with right lower eyelid entropion and trouble swallowing. A bilateral blunting of the fornices and a symblepharon are noted on the right side. What is the most appropriate test for this ocular disorder?
Correct answer: D. conjunctival biopsy with immunofluorescent staining
Rationale
Mucous membrane pemphigoid (MMP), formerly called ocular cicatricial pemphigoid, is a chronic cicatrizing conjunctivitis of autoimmune etiology. Although it is a vesiculobullous disease primarily involving the conjunctiva, it frequently affects other mucous membranes, including those of the mouth and oropharynx, genitalia, and anus. Difficulty swallowing may be an important early symptom. Patients with MMP are usually older than 60 years at the time of diagnosis. They often present with recurrent attacks of mild and nonspecific conjunctival inflammation with an occasional mucopurulent discharge. Patients with early MMP may present with conjunctival hyperemia, edema, ulceration, and tear dysfunction. Transient bullae of the conjunctiva rupture, leading to subepithelial fibrosis. Loss of goblet cells, shortening of the inferior fornices, symblepharon formation, and, on occasion, restricted ocular motility with extensive adhesions between the eyelid and the globe, can follow. Entropion and trichiasis may develop as scarring progresses, leading to abrasions, corneal vascularization, further scarring, ulceration, and epidermalization of the ocular surface. Although MMP is a bilateral disease, one eye may be more severely involved than the other. Pathologic support for a diagnosis of pemphigoid is obtained from direct immunofluorescence or immunoperoxidase staining of conjunctival biopsy specimens. 
Thyroid eye disease often presents with lid retraction, but never causes symblepharon. Although ocular myasthenia can be associated with systemic symptoms of weakness such as dysphagia, this patient's ocular clinical findings are not associated with myasthenia.

Q2492
External Disease & Cornea
When attempting to culture Haemophilus species, what is the preferred culture medium?
Correct answer: A. chocolate agar
Rationale
Haemophilus species are a gram-negative coccobacillus. They require an enriched media such as chocolate agar. Of note, Haemophilus and streptococci are associated with bleb infections after glaucoma filtering surgery.
Blood agar is a versatile agar for bacteria and fungi; however, Haemophilus is unlikely to grow on blood agar. Of note, streptococci were historically classified based on their ability to hemolyze blood-containing agar media, and their cell wall carbohydrates (Lancefield groups).
Nonnutrient agar with bacterial overlay (Enterobacter aerogenes, Escherichia coli) is used only for Acanthamoeba. The trophozoites leave trails in both blood agar and nonnutrient agar with an overlay of killed Enterobacter; however, the latter is optimal.
Sabouraud agar is used to culture fungi (at 25 degrees Celsius).

Q2493
External Disease & Cornea
A 35-year-old man complains of blurry vision in his right eye. Although he has no other symptoms, he has had prior recurrent episodes of pain and redness. He is not currently using any medications. His abnormal slit-lamp examination is shown. What would be the preferred treatment for this patient?
Correct answer: B. acyclovir 400 mg 2 times daily
Rationale
The symptoms and signs on examination suggest a diagnosis of scarring from inactive herpes simplex virus (HSV) stromal keratitis. Acyclovir has been proven to reduce recurrences of HSV keratitis in a large clinical trial funded by the National Institutes of Health, but this agent may not always be considered in the treatment of patients with recurrent herpes simplex ocular disease. The prophylactic dose of acyclovir is 400 mg bid and should be considered in any person with multiple recurrences. Stromal keratitis may also require topical corticosteroids to suppress inflammation, but this treatment should never be used without antiviral coverage. Trifluridine can be used to treat acute episodes of HSV epithelial keratitis but is not used for prophylaxis. Valacyclovir, a prodrug of acyclovir, can also be used for treatment and prophylaxis. The dose of valacyclovir for acute disease is 1000 mg 2 times daily; the prophylactic dose is 500 mg once daily.

Q2494
External Disease & Cornea
For a patient with bilateral, chronic conjunctivitis as shown, what diagnostic test is most likely to establish the diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. conjunctival biopsy with direct immunofluorescence
Rationale
The photograph shows conjunctivitis, forniceal shortening, and subconjunctival fibrosis. This is cicatrizing conjunctivitis, and the diagnosis of mucous membrane pemphigoid (MMP) is secured by performing a conjunctival biopsy with direct immunofluorescence.
Indirect immunofluorescence for circulating antibodies in the serum is not performed to determine the nature of a chronic, cicatrizing conjunctivitis. Conjunctival biopsy with H&E stain will not demonstrate the antibodies directed against the basement membrane in MMP. Serum ANA is not relevant in the diagnosis for MMP.

Q2495
External Disease & Cornea
A 4-day-old infant has the examination findings shown below and a normal intraocular pressure. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. birth trauma
Rationale
The photo shows corneal edema and vertical striae or breaks in Descemet membrane, characteristic of birth trauma. Congenital glaucoma can also cause corneal edema and breaks in Descemet membrane, but these breaks are typically curvilinear or horizontal and intraocular pressure would be elevated.
Peters anomaly is characterized by a central or paracentral corneal opacity due to localized absence of the corneal endothelium and Descemet membrane. Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome is characterized by an anteriorly displaced Schwalbe line (posterior embryotoxon) with iris strands, iris hypoplasia, and corectopia. Posterior keratoconus is characterized by a central or paracentral indentation of the posterior cornea without protrusion of the anterior corneal surface. None of these disorders have vertical breaks in Descemet membrane.

Q2496
External Disease & Cornea
A follicular conjunctivitis with presence of follicles on the bulbar conjunctiva (rather than only the palpebral conjunctiva) is most suggestive of what condition?
Correct answer: D. toxic conjunctivitis
Rationale
Follicular conjunctivitis generally involves both the upper and lower palpebral conjunctivae but is usually most prominent inferiorly. Bulbar follicles are uncommon, but when present, they are highly suggestive of a toxic etiology. The most common medications to cause a toxic conjunctivitis are atropine, antiviral agents, miotics, sulfonamides, alpha-adrenergic agonists, and vasoconstrictors.
Adenovirus and molluscum contagiosum are associated with follicular reactions, but not involving the bulbar conjunctiva specifically. Atopic keratoconjunctivitis causes a papillary reaction, not a follicular reaction.

An 85-year-old male complains of a growing lesion on his left eye as shown. What histologic feature is a poor prognostic factor for this patient?

Rationale
The figure demonstrates an elevated, irregular, pigmented lesion most consistent with a conjunctival melanoma. Clinical features that portend a poor prognosis include increased tumor thickness, unfavorable location (caruncle, palpebral conjunctiva, fornix), and invasion into deeper ocular structures. Histologic features that portend a poor prognosis include mixed cell type, lymphatic invasion, moderate-to-severe atypia, greater than 5 mitotic figures per 10 high-power fields, and lack of an inflammatory response induced by the tumor.

What clinical appearance of a corneal ulcer is most suggestive of fungal etiology?
Correct answer: A. multiple discrete infiltrates
Rationale
In the setting of a corneal ulcer, the presence of multiple infiltrates or smaller "satellite" infiltrates is very suspicious for fungal etiology, especially filamentous fungi (eg, Fusarium, Aspergillus, etc.).
Perineural inflammation may be seen in infections caused by Acanthamoeba.
"Soupy" or wet stromal necrosis and thinning is usually caused by bacterial pathogens, particularly Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Stromal edema with keratic precipitates is suggestive of herpes simplex disciform keratitis.

A 75-year-old woman has constant irritation and foreign body sensation in both eyes. Artificial tears have not helped. A slit-lamp examination reveals conjunctiva overhanging her lower eyelid, as shown. What would be the preferred management to treat her symptoms?

The photograph depicts redundant bulbar conjunctival tissue, a finding consistent with conjunctivochalasis. The definitive management of this condition involves resecting the redundant conjunctiva. Using topical cyclosporine or inserting punctal plugs would be appropriate in a patient with dry eye syndrome unresponsive to artificial tears. Applying a bandage contact lens would be a consideration in a patient with superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis.

Q2500
External Disease & Cornea
A 20-year-old patient presents with a best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) in eyeglasses of 20/100 OU and fine vertical lines in the posterior central cornea on slit-lamp examination. What is the most useful test to confirm the diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. corneal topography
Rationale
The clinical description is most consistent with keratoconus (the fine vertical lines describe Vogt striae), which is best diagnosed with corneal topography. The expected pattern would be that of asymmetric inferior steepening with high regular and irregular astigmatism.
Specular microscopy allows imaging and quantification of the corneal endothelium, which would be expected to be normal in the setting of keratoconus.
Glare testing may show a decrease in BCVA but is not useful in diagnosing the underlying etiology. It is very helpful for quantifying glare from cataracts, posterior capsule opacity (PCO), and other opacities.
Wavefront analysis would likely show a large degree of lower- and higher-order aberrations. It is mostly used for refractive surgery planning, but it is less often used in the diagnosis of keratoconus, compared to topography.

Q2501
External Disease & Cornea
What finding is the most common slit-lamp finding in a patient with adult chlamydial conjunctivitis?
Correct answer: A. follicular conjunctival response
Rationale
Adult chlamydial conjunctivitis is a sexually transmitted disease characterized by a primarily follicular conjunctival response, mild keratitis, and a superiorly located micropannus. In contrast to neonatal forms, inflammatory membranes are not observed in adult chlamydial conjunctivitis. Interstitial keratitis, corneal ulceration, and thinning are not commonly seen in this disease. Syphilis and HSV are the most common infectious causes of interstitial keratitis. Corneal ulcer due to chlamydia is infrequent. Gonorrhea, which can often co-infect with chlamydia, can cause a rapidly necrotizing corneal ulcer.

Q2502

For a corneal ulcer with suspected mycobacterial etiology, what is the most appropriate culture medium?
Correct answer: D. Löwenstein-Jensen medium
Rationale
Löwenstein-Jensen medium is the best choice for growing mycobacterial species. Malachite green, which gives the media its distinctive appearance, is present to inhibit the growth of most other bacteria.
Blood agar is useful for culturing normal and fastidious (special nutrient-requiring) bacteria and differentiating them based on the hemolysis pattern. Chocolate agar is similar to blood agar but also allows growth of Neisseria and Haemophilus species. Sabouraud dextrose is designed for culturing fungi.

Q2503

What is the immunoglobulin involved in atopic keratoconjunctivitis (AKC)?
Correct answer: B. IgE
Rationale
Atopic individuals show signs of type I hypersensitivity responses, increased serum levels of IgE, and depressed systemic cell-mediated immunity. As a consequence of this altered immunity, they are susceptible to herpes simplex virus keratitis and colonization of the eyelids with Staphylococcus aureus. Complications related to this predisposition to infection may contribute to, or compound, the primary immunopathogenic manifestations. AKC is primarily a type IV reaction; therefore, the use of mast-cell therapy may not be effective.

Q2504

A 10-year-old girl complains of unilateral pain, redness, and photophobia following a bee sting injury on the eyelid. The figure shows a slit-lamp photograph of her cornea. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. tarsal foreign body
Rationale
The figure demonstrates vertical linear superficial corneal abrasions. This presentation is most consistent with a retained tarsal foreign body, which in this case may be a bee's stinger. Eversion of the upper and lower tarsus is important in such cases in order to locate and remove the foreign body. If no foreign body is seen in the presence of vertical linear corneal abrasions, the conjunctival fornices should be irrigated and wiped with a moistened cotton-tipped applicator. The corneal manifestation of toxic and allergic keratoconjunctivitis is most often diffuse punctate epithelial erosions. The corneal manifestations of keratouveitis include opacities, neovascularization, edema, and/or keratic precipitates in the setting of intraocular inflammation. In addition to this presentation, bee stings to the cornea or conjunctiva may cause conjunctival hyperemia and chemosis sometimes associated with severe pain, corneal edema, and infiltration. Rarely, other sequelae including hyphema, lenticular opacities, iritis, secondary glaucoma, and heterochromia may occur. In addition to attempting to remove externalized stingers, initial therapy with cycloplegics and topical (and occasionally systemic) corticosteroids is beneficial.

Q2505

What gene is associated with the corneal finding in the photo?

Rationale
PITX2

The corneal finding depicted is posterior embryotoxon, or an anteriorly displaced Schwalbe line. This can be found in Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome. Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome can also include ocular findings of glaucoma, corectopia, and peripheral iris strands. It can be associated with systemic symptoms such as developmental defects in teeth, maxillary hypoplasia, redundant periumbilical skin, pituitary abnormalities, and hypospadias. It is associated with the pituitary homeobox 2 gene PITX2 and forkhead box C1 gene FOXC1 or PAX6.
LOXL1 is associated with pseudoexfoliation syndrome. ABCA4 is associated with Stargardt disease. FOXL2 is associated with blepharophimosis syndrome.

A 52-year-old woman with a history of Descemet membrane endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK) 5 days ago presents with poor vision. An anterior segment optical coherence tomography (OCT) scan is shown. What intervention would be best for this patient?
Correct answer: A. injection of gas into the anterior chamber
Rationale
The patient presents with focal corneal edema after DMEK from a peripheral graft detachment. DMEK detachments that do not involve the visual axis or that involve less than 30% of the graft area can be managed by observation over several weeks, as a large percentage will seal without any intervention. Otherwise, patients can be managed with rebubbling, which involves injection of additional gas to tamponade the graft back into place. If persistent edema is seen 1 to 2 months after surgery, repeat endothelial keratoplasty is indicated.

Rationale
This patient has meibomian gland dysfunction (MGD), which causes abnormalities of the lipid layer of tear film and increased evaporative loss of tears. Sjögren syndrome and aqueous deficient DES have normal meibomian gland architecture and poor tear volume production. Ocular allergy may exacerbate DES but does not cause changes in the meibomian glands.

A 75-year-old man complains of decreased vision and redness in his left eye. Best-corrected visual acuity is 20/20 in the right eye and 20/150 in the left eye. His intraocular pressure (IOP) is 19 mm Hg in the right eye and 37 mm Hg in the left eye. His slit-lamp examination is abnormal as shown. What is the preferred first-line therapy for this case?
Correct answer: D. topical corticosteroids and oral acyclovir
Rationale
The photographs demonstrate central stromal edema with underlying keratic precipitates. This presentation, along with the elevated IOP, is most consistent with herpes simplex virus endotheliitis. The condition is believed to represent an immunologic response to viral antigens. The most appropriate first-line treatment consists of topical corticosteroids in combination with an antiviral agent (oral or topical). The other choices (topical corticosteroids and topical moxifloxacin, topical trifluridine and oral valacyclovir, oral corticosteroids and topical moxifloxacin) do not represent a combination of a corticosteroid and an antiviral agent and are therefore not appropriate as first-line management options.

What complication can be prevented if the condition shown is perceived prior to cataract surgery?

Rationale
The image shows the typical appearance of epithelial basement membrane dystrophy (EBMD), also termed anterior basement membrane dystrophy. The presence of EBMD, especially when near the visual axis, can create keratometric and topographic irregularities, which reduce the accuracy of intraocular lens calculations. The surgeon may need to perform epithelial debridement in these patients prior to cataract surgery to ensure accurate measurements. EBMD has no association with any of the other listed complications (bacterial endophthalmitis, pseudophakic bullous keratopathy,  posterior capsule rupture).

Q2510

In what layer of the cornea is copper deposited in Wilson disease?
Correct answer: A. Descemet membrane
Rationale
Wilson disease is an inherited autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism. It is caused by multiple allelic substitutions or deletions in a copper-ATPase-transporting beta-polypeptide, linked to mutations in the ATP7B gene on chromosome 13.
The ocular manifestation is a Kayser-Fleischer ring, which is a golden-brown discoloration of the Descemet membrane around the periphery of the cornea. In addition, a characteristic sunflower cataract often develops. The corneal deposit is not in the Bowman membrane, posterior stroma, or anterior stroma.

Q2511

When repairing a full-thickness traumatic corneoscleral laceration, what area of the wound should be approximated first?
Correct answer: D. limbus
Rationale
Reapproximating the limbus is the most important first step in closing a corneoscleral laceration. This allows the surgeon to distribute the remaining corneal tissue evenly for the remaining wound closure. After the limbus is repaired, the corneal component of the wound should be repaired to allow reformation of the anterior chamber. The scleral component is subsequently closed, followed by any conjunctival laceration.

Q2512

What is the primary treatment for filamentary keratopathy to reduce the severity of recurrence?
Correct answer: D. preservative-free artificial tears
Rationale
Treatment of filamentary keratopathy associated with severe aqueous tear deficiency (ATD) can be challenging. Filaments should be debrided with a jeweler’s forceps or a cotton swab soaked with topical anesthetic. Treatment directed at enhancing the tear film reduces the severity of recurrence. In addition to tear supplementation and punctal occlusion, acetylcysteine 10%, dispensed with an eyedrop container, can serve as a mucolytic agent and may further reduce filament formation. Topical low-dose corticosteroids, cyclosporine, and therapeutic soft contact lenses may be helpful.
While therapeutic soft contact lenses may be beneficial for treatment of filamentary keratitis due to other causes, bandage soft contact lenses are rarely used to reduce symptoms in patients with ATD, because they may be associated with an increased risk of infection. Patients who use them should therefore be observed carefully. Scleral contact lenses have been found to be extremely helpful in patients with advanced dry eye symptoms.
Hypertonic saline (5% sodium chloride) solution is used for the treatment of recurrent corneal erosions. The drops provide lubrication and may transiently produce an osmotic gradient, drawing fluid from the epithelium and theoretically promoting the adherence of epithelial cells to the underlying tissue.

Q2513

What role does cryotherapy play in the treatment of the pictured condition?
Correct answer: C. decreases recurrence
Rationale
For the treatment of conjunctival neoplasia, excision with cryotherapy of the margin is a recommended strategy to reduce recurrence at the wound margin. Depending on the type of the lesion, systemic chemotherapy or radiation therapy may be combined with surgical excision. Cryotherapy does not play a significant role in the prevention of distant metastasis, diagnostic yield, or wound closure.
Options for first-line therapy for squamous lesions are topical interferon-alpha 2b, or topical mitomycin C (MMC), or wide-margin surgical excision with cryotherapy. Cryotherapy at time of ocular surface surgery has been shown to improve prognosis.

Q2514

Neurotrophic keratopathy is caused by a dysfunction of what cranial nerve?
Correct answer: A. cranial nerve 5
Rationale
Neurotrophic keratopathy is caused by corneal anesthesia due to an abnormality in cranial nerve 5. Patients may develop corneal edema, nonhealing epithelial defects, and conjunctival injection secondary to the disruption of the reflex between CN V1 and the lacrimal gland. These patients are at higher risk of secondary bacterial infiltrates in the cornea. Patients should be tested for corneal sensation by using either a cotton-tipped applicator or an anesthesiometer. Other diseases associated with decreased corneal sensation include familial dysautonomia, topical anesthetic abuse, herpes simplex keratitis, and crack-cocaine abuse. Treatment for neurotrophic keratopathy should focus on improving the lubrication on the anesthetic cornea by using artificial tears, lubricating ointment, bandage contact lens, punctal plugs, and tarsorrhaphy.

Rationale
The image illustrates a slit-lamp examination using rose bengal stain to demonstrate devitalized conjunctiva. Lissamine green demonstrates a similar staining pattern of the injured conjunctival epithelial cells, but has a blue color. Rose bengal and lissamine green stain not only dead and devitalized cells and mucus but also epithelial cells that are inadequately protected by ocular surface mucins. The answer choices "exposed Bowman membrane" and "epithelial defects" refer to staining using fluorescein. Fluorescein does not readily stain conjunctival cells and is better for visualization of corneal epithelial defects with cobalt blue-filtered illumination. Although rose bengal can be used to detect viral dendrites in the cornea, this pattern of staining on the conjunctiva does not represent active viral particles.

Q2517

What ocular procedure is contraindicated in a patient with forme fruste keratoconus?
Correct answer: D. laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK)
Rationale
Intracorneal ring segments and phakic IOLs do not subtract corneal tissue, and therefore can be used to treat forme fruste keratoconus. Photorefractive keratectomy (PRK) may play a role in the treatment of these patients because there is no flap construction (flap construction can hasten the onset of keratoconus). However, LASIK involves the construction of a flap, which can affect the integrity of the cornea and cause the onset of keratoconus in a patient with previous forme fruste keratoconus. There have been reported cases of ectasia development after PRK, but it is not clear whether this is progression of the underlying disease, or actual hastening because of tissue removal. If the patient shows signs of progression, corneal crosslinking may be an option for stabilization of their corneal condition.
Phakic intraocular lenses may be considered off-label treatment for patients with irregular topographies from forme fruste or frank keratoconus. When indicated, intracorneal ring segment implantation flattens the cone and regularizes the topography and may be combined with crosslinking.

What type of glue is typically used to seal small corneal perforations?

Cyanoacrylate glue is used to seal small corneal perforations. Some brands include 1. Indermil, butyl-2-cyanoacrylate, Henkel Corporation; 2. Histoacryl, butyl-2-cyanoacrylate, Aesculap, Inc.; 3. Nexacryl, N-butyl-cyanoacrylate, Closure Medical; 4. Dermabond, 2-octyl-cyanoacrylate, Ethicon.
The adhesive plug has a rough surface, so a bandage contact lens should be used to protect the upper tarsal conjunctiva and to prevent the plug from being dislodged by blinking.
Fibrin sealant is often used in the operating room to help with ocular surface reconstruction, such as after pterygium surgery. An example of this glue is Evicel fibrin sealant (Ethicon). Polyethylene glycol hydrogel is in ReSure (Ocular Therapeutix, Inc.) and is used to help seal cataract wounds. Polyvinyl acetate is a widely used component of glue, such as wood glue. Q2519

A 40-year-old man complains of chronic itching and watering eyes as illustrated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. atopic keratoconjunctivitis
Rationale
This patient presents with several features of atopic keratoconjunctivitis (AKC), including lichenification of the skin, stringy discharge, and thickening, crusting, edema, and ptosis of the eyelids. While not pictured here, small or medium papillae (giant papillae are more often found in vernal keratoconjunctivitis than AKC) are found on the palpebral conjunctivae along with hyperemia on the bulbar and palpebral conjunctivae. Other features that may be seen in this condition include cicatrization; symblepharon and corneal changes, including punctate epitheliopathy; persistent epithelial defects; shield ulcers; and micropannus.
Rosacea, on the other hand, would typically present with a malar rash and telangiectasias of facial skin and eyelid margin, papules, pustules, hypertrophic sebaceous glands, rhinophyma, and/or meibomian gland dysfunction.
Seborrheic blepharitis affects primarily the anterior eyelid margin, with oily or greasy eyelid crusting. These patients may have evidence of seborrhea elsewhere on the body.
Psoriasis would present as red patches with silvery scales. Patches usually present on the elbows, knees, scalp, back, face, palms, and feet, but they can show up on other parts of the body.

A 25-year-old adult has 1 day of pain, redness, and copious purulent discharge in the right eye as shown. The responsible microbe is transmitted in what fashion?
Correct answer: B. sexual intercourse
Rationale
The image demonstrates a hyperpurulent conjunctivitis, a presentation most commonly seen in the setting of gonococcal- or Neisseria-associated conjunctivitis. Gonococcal conjunctivitis is typically a sexually transmitted ocular disease, although newborn infants may acquire the infection by passing through an infected birth canal. Management involves obtaining appropriate cultures and treating the patient and affected sexual partners with 1 gram of intramuscular ceftriaxone. Given the potential for concomitant chlamydial disease, a 10- to 14-day course of erythromycin or doxycycline should also be administered. Parinaud oculo-glandular syndrome may be caused by Bartonella henselae, which can be transmitted through a scratch from a kitten. Herpetic ocular disease can occur as a primary infection or as a reactivation of latent virus from the trigeminal ganglion.

Inflammatory membranes can form with gonococcal conjunctivitis, but the discharge is extremely purulent, not watery. Herpes simplex conjunctivitis is typically unilateral and does not cause inflammatory membranes.

Other risk factors include ultraviolet light exposure, fair complexion, and immunosuppression. Prior conjunctival surgery, alcohol consumption, and diabetes mellitus are not known risks.

The description of this patient's condition is consistent with marginal corneal infiltrates associated with blepharoconjunctivitis. These are believed to arise as a toxic/immune response to staphylococcal antigens that are found on the lid margin. As such, it is important to evaluate the eyelid for evidence of staphylococcal blepharitis. What is the histological composition of the lesion pictured?
Correct answer: B. lipid
Rationale
The figure shows lipid keratopathy occurring in the setting of Terrien marginal degeneration. The deposits occur adjacent to corneal neovascularization, are well-defined, and typically have a yellowish hue. Glycosaminoglycans are normal constituents of the corneal stroma, although in dystrophic corneas their accumulation can result in visually significant opacities. Protein deposits in the cornea are generally gray and refractile and may be seen in specific conditions (eg, amyloidosis, lattice). Protein deposits in the cornea are not typically associated with neovascularization. Carbohydrate deposits are not associated with corneal opacification.

What virus family includes cytomegalovirus (CMV)?

Cytomegalovirus is a DNA virus from the herpes family. In the eye, it is most commonly associated with sectoral necrotizing retinitis that is seen almost exclusively in AIDS and other immunocompromised states. It can also cause anterior uveitis and corneal endotheliitis.
Molluscum contagiosum is an example of a poxvirus with ocular manifestations. Parvovirus B19 can have ocular manifestations such as anterior uveitis. Hepadnaviridae such as hepatitis B and C have rare ocular manifestations.

Rationale
Corneal changes due to birth trauma are most commonly the result of forceps delivery that leads to linear ruptures of Descemet membrane.
Corneal changes related to birth trauma are extremely rare, but when present, they manifest as symptomatic, progressive corneal edema in the first few postnatal days. Sequelae include hypertrophic ridges of Descemet membrane, persistent corneal edema, high astigmatism, and amblyopia.

What is the most common anatomical source of infection in microbial scleritis?

Infectious scleritis usually arises as a result of local extension from adjacent tissues, most commonly from the cornea. The causative organism is usually bacterial (Pseudomonas is the most common). What is the most common treatment for conjunctival lymphoma without systemic involvement?

Rationale
Conjunctival lymphoma is a neoplastic lymphoid lesion that is most commonly composed of a monoclonal proliferation of B-cells. It usually appears as a salmon pink, mobile mass on the conjunctiva. Local external-beam radiation is usually curative for lesions confined to the conjunctiva and is the mainstay of treatment. More recently described treatments include intralesional interferon-alpha 2b and intralesional or systemic rituximab.
Systemic lymphoma develops in about 31% of patients and systemic chemotherapy is required to treat this.
Topical 5-fluorouracil can be used to treat ocular surface squamous neoplasia but is not used for conjunctival lymphoma. While surgical excision and cryotherapy can be used to treat some types of ocular surface squamous neoplasia, cryotherapy alone is not a treatment for OSSN or conjunctival lymphoma.

What is the best treatment for herpes simplex virus (HSV) endotheliitis?

Rationale
Herpetic disciform keratitis is a primary endotheliitis, which presents as corneal stromal and epithelial edema in a round or oval distribution, associated with keratic precipitates underlying the zone of edema.
Currently available topical antiviral medications are not absorbed by the cornea through an intact epithelium, but orally administered acyclovir penetrates an intact cornea and anterior chamber. In this context, anecdotal evidence suggests that oral acyclovir might benefit the deep corneal inflammation of disciform keratitis.
Oral prednisone without acyclovir coverage may make epithelial keratitis more likely if the patient sheds HSV.
Topical trifluridine can be used to treat epithelial disease but cannot be absorbed by the cornea through an intact corneal epithelium.
Topical erythromycin and artificial tears would not address the inflammatory or the infectious basis of the disease.

Correct answer: C. sebaceous gland carcinoma
Rationale
Recurrent unilateral chalazia, especially in an elderly patient, should raise suspicion for occult malignancy. In this case, the description is most suggestive of sebaceous gland carcinoma with several white perilimbal lesions representing extension into the bulbar conjunctiva (which may occur in up to 50% of cases). Ocular surface squamous neoplasia (OSSN) may present similarly, but the more typical appearance is that of a vascularized lesion centered on the corneal limbus. In this case, the history of a primary location originating from the eyelid (with multiple chalazion procedures) favors a sebaceous gland origin. Basal cell carcinoma is typically a malignancy of the eyelid and rarely affects the bulbar conjunctiva. Sarcoidosis may cause conjunctival granulomatosis, but the typical appearance is that of small yellowish/tan nodules, usually in the lower fornix. Sarcoidosis would not be expected to cause the palpebral changes (eyelash loss, hypervascularity) in this case.

What is the classic slit-lamp feature of a neurotrophic corneal ulcer?

Rationale
The classic features of a neurotrophic corneal ulcer include a rounded or ovalized lesion with thickened, rolled edges and minimal stromal infiltration. Over time, these lesions may develop stromal fibrosis or necrosis, but a dense infiltrate is more suggestive of an infectious process. The ulcers are typically central or inferior in location (corresponding to areas of maximal exposure) and not typically superior. A single confluent epithelial defect is more commonly seen than multiple discrete epithelial defects.

Q2534

Twelve hours after an endothelial keratoplasty procedure, a patient complains of severe pain, nausea, and vomiting. What is the most likely cause of this problem?
Correct answer: D. pupillary block
Rationale
All of the choices are potential postoperative complications following endothelial keratoplasty. In the given scenario—early postoperative period with symptoms indicative of elevated intraocular pressure (IOP)—the most likely etiology is pupillary block. Pupillary block following endothelial keratoplasty occurs when the air bubble occludes the pupil and induces secondary angle closure. The typical presentation is that of a flat or very shallow anterior chamber with total or near-total peripheral anterior synechiae. The IOP is typically markedly elevated, and the air bubble may be difficult to discern behind the iris.
Graft dislocation is typically painless and presents with decreased vision and a visibly detached or decentered donor corneal graft, which is usually in the inferior angle.
Endophthalmitis may present with pain, inflammation, and decreased vision, but it would not typically present in the first 24 hours after the surgery with symptoms suggestive of high IOP.
Graft rejection may present, often insidiously, with pain, photophobia, and decreased vision, but it typically does not develop until months or years after the surgery. Again, symptoms of elevated IOP would not typically be present.

Q2535

For the treatment of bullous keratopathy, penetrating keratoplasty may be preferred over endothelial keratoplasty in what situation?
Correct answer: A. presence of significant central stromal scarring
Rationale
For most cases of endothelial failure, endothelial keratoplasty--Descemet stripping endothelial keratoplasty (DSEK), Descemet stripping automated endothelial keratoplasty (DSAEK), or Descemet membrane endothelial keratoplasty (DMEK)--is preferred over penetrating keratoplasty. Compared to penetrating keratoplasty, endothelial keratoplasty provides faster visual rehabilitation, lower risk for intraoperative suprachoroidal hemorrhage (due to smaller incision size), and more predictable refractive outcomes.
However, endothelial keratoplasty does not remove central stromal scarring, and penetrating keratoplasty may be necessary to provide optimal visual quality in this situation.
The presence of a posterior chamber intraocular lens or a known history of Fuchs endothelial dystrophy would not affect the decision to perform penetrating keratoplasty in this situation.
A previous suprachoroidal hemorrhage in the fellow eye would favor endothelial keratoplasty for the reasons listed above.

What optical phenomenon is used with Placido disk-based topography?

Placido disk-based topography uses the reflection of a target-shaped image projected onto the patient's cornea. The reflected image has aberrations corresponding to the altered curvature, from which the software calculates keratometric measurements. Chromatic dispersion occurs when white light is unequally refracted into its polychromatic components. This can be bothersome to some patients with high corrections in spectacles. Interferometry can be employed in visual potential assessment by measuring the patient's ability to discriminate between closely spaced lines. Refraction refers to the angle of light as it passes between different media.

In children with untreated congenital syphilis, the onset of interstitial keratitis is usually between 6 and 12 years of age. Corneal haze, edema, and high astigmatism are not often found in this condition. What is a common side effect of doxycycline?

Rationale
Oral doxycycline in doses of 40 mg to 200 mg per day is generally well tolerated for external disease, mostly meibomian gland dysfunction. Adverse effects of oral tetracyclines include photosensitization, gastrointestinal upset, and, in rare instances, azotemia. Long-term use may lead to oral or vaginal candidiasis in susceptible patients. The use of tetracyclines is contraindicated during pregnancy, in women who are breastfeeding, and in patients with a known hypersensitivity to these agents. These antibiotics should be avoided in children younger than 8 years because they cause permanent discoloration of teeth and bones in this population.
Photophobia, blurred vision and onychomycosis would be very uncommon from doxycycline.

Q2543

The fibrovascular ridges seen in the photo are crucial for replenishment of what mature cell type?
Correct answer: D. corneal epithelial cells
Rationale
The fibrovascular ridges shown in the photo are the palisades of Vogt, which house corneal epithelial stem cells at the limbus. These cells will proliferate and replenish the corneal epithelium with centripetal migration from the periphery to the center of the cornea. Damage to the palisades may result in limbal stem cell deficiency, poor corneal wound healing, and conjunctivalization of the cornea.

Q2544
External Disease & Cornea
An adult patient who suffered a severe unilateral alkali injury to his right eye developed progressive pannus, conjunctival epithelialization of the cornea, and a central persistent epithelial defect, despite appropriate treatment. What is the most appropriate surgical option for visual improvement?
Correct answer: C. conjunctival limbal autograft
Rationale
The clinical scenario describes a unilateral limbal stem cell deficiency after an alkali injury. Since the limbal stem cells of the other eye were not affected, a conjunctival limbal autograft can be performed. In this procedure, healthy limbal stem cells are harvested from the unaffected eye and transplanted to the affected eye of the same patient.
If there is loss of limbal stem cells bilaterally, a patient may receive stem cells from an eye bank donor cornea via a keratolimbal allograft (KLAL). A KLAL has a higher risk of rejection than a conjunctival limbal autograft and requires systemic immunosuppression. A penetrating keratoplasty requires healthy stem cells to maintain a clear graft. A superficial keratectomy could be performed to clear the pannus and conjunctival epithelium but requires healthy limbal stem cells to maintain a clear cornea. Likewise, a penetrating keratoplasty requires healthy limbal stem cells to maintain a clear graft.

Q2545
External Disease & Cornea
A patient who has had a corneal transplant complains of decreased vision. Corneal topography can identify what issue in a previously transplanted cornea?
Correct answer: D. irregular astigmatism
Rationale
Corneal topography is a structural, not a functional test. It will identify irregular astigmatism, including ectasias. Specular microscopy can be used to quantify loss of endothelial cells. Tomography is required to examine the posterior corneal curvature. Corneal topography may detect regions of corneal edema change, but it is not capable of detecting corneal transplant rejection or endothelial cell viability.

Q2546

The outcomes of what surgery could theoretically be improved by sophisticated measurements of corneal hysteresis?
Correct answer: C. laser in situ keratomileusis (LASIK)
Rationale
Corneal hysteresis is the difference between the pressure at which the cornea bends inward with air-jet applanation and the pressure at which it bends outward again. It gauges elasticity of the cornea. Theoretically, accurate measurement of this biomechanical property would identify corneas at risk for ectasia during laser refractive surgery such as LASIK or photorefractive keratectomy (PRK).

Q2547
External Disease & Cornea
What is the most common complication of a conjunctival flap?
Correct answer: D. retraction of the flap
Rationale
The most common complication of conjunctival flaps is retraction of the flap, which occurs in approximately 10% of cases. To lower the risk of retraction, the surgeon should take care to minimize tension on any conjunctival flap when it is placed.
Hemorrhage beneath the flap and formation of epithelial inclusion cysts are other possible complications of a conjunctival flap but are less common than retraction. Ptosis may occur after a conjunctival flap but may or may not be related to the flap itself.

Q2548
External Disease & Cornea
A young adult presents with a chronic red right eye. His previous treatments for dry eye have not worked. He has a small fleshy pink lesion near the limbus. He has had night sweats and lost weight over the past year. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: B. conjunctival lymphoma
Rationale
This patient has systemic symptoms of weight loss and a pink mass that are typical for conjunctival lymphoma. Usually described as a "salmon patch," a conjunctival lymphoma lesion can be seen near the limbus or in the fornix region. Chronic redness is possible. HIV disease can be a risk factor. The other answer choices (squamous cell carcinoma of conjunctiva, sarcoidosis, and amyloidosis) are in the differential but are not correct. The night sweats and weight loss are helpful in identifying this patient as a potential lymphoma patient.
Other ocular surface squamous lesions are in the differential as well. Treatment depends on whether systemic disease is present. Night sweats are a common symptom of lymphoma, but not of the other conditions. Squamous cell carcinoma presents with a white or yellowish pink lesion near the limbus with possibly leukoplakia. This rarely metastasizes. Amyloidosis of conjunctiva usually presents with a waxy yellowish localized lesion.

Q2549
External Disease & Cornea
Peripheral ulcerative keratitis can be associated with what gastrointestinal disease?
Correct answer: B. Crohn disease
Rationale
Peripheral ulcerative keratitis (PUK) is associated with many autoimmune conditions, and can cause keratolysis, or melting of the corneal stroma, typically peripherally. It can be found in such diseases as rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly called Wegener granulomatosis), relapsing polychondritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and inflammatory bowel disease (both Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis). Irritable bowel syndrome, peptic ulcer disease, and celiac sprue are not associated with PUK.

Q2550

A 65-year-old patient is complaining of constant foreign body sensation, tearing, and discomfort that has not been relieved by topical medication. Given the patient's appearance shown, what in-office procedure can be performed to treat this condition?
Correct answer: C. conjunctival cautery
Rationale
The patient is symptomatic from conjunctivochalasis. This is a process where aging and chronic inflammation lead to poor adherence of the bulbar conjunctiva to the underlying tissue. If medical treatments such as lubricants, anti-inflammatory agents, antihistamines, or nocturnal patching are not effective in controlling symptoms, surgical treatments can be performed, including conjunctival cauterization, conjunctival fixation, resection, or amniotic grafting. Conjunctival cauterization has the advantage of being able to be performed in the office.
Silver nitrate is a treatment administered at birth to prevent neonatal conjunctivitis, and it can also be used to treat superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis. Bandage contact lenses are used in a variety of clinical scenarios to protect the ocular surface and promote healing. Punctal plugs can be used to treat aqueous tear deficiency dry eye.

A 42-year-old woman has noted decreased vision in her right eye. The slit-lamp examination is abnormal, as shown. What histological findings would be expected on lesion biopsy?
Correct answer: C. localized replacement of Bowman layer by hyaline and fibrillar material
Rationale
The figure depicts Salzmann nodules. These nodules are noninflammatory corneal degenerations and may be seen in the setting of ocular inflammation or may be idiopathic. Histopathologic examination reveals localized replacement of Bowman layer by hyaline and fibrillar material. The other findings are not present in Salzmann nodular degeneration. Symptomatic nodules in this condition are usually treated by superficial keratectomy.

Correct answer: B. B‑cell mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma
Rationale
Most conjunctival lymphomas are B-cell mucosal associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphomas. T-cell lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, and plasmacytoma are less common. Conjunctival lymphoma presents as a salmon-colored mobile conjunctival mass and appears identical to lymphoid hyperplasia. Patients with conjunctival lymphoma should be referred to an oncologist to exclude systemic disease.

Q2553
External Disease & Cornea
What is the typical conjunctival finding in atopic keratoconjunctivitis (AKC)?
Correct answer: B. small and medium-sized papillae
Rationale
AKC is characterized by the presence of chronic inflammation, small or medium-sized papillae, and milky conjunctival edema with possible subepithelial fibrosis. Corneal neovascularization, punctate staining, and/or corneal epithelial defects are commonly seen.
Giant papillary reactions are associated with vernal keratoconjunctivitis rather than atopic disease. Follicles can occur with several infections, including viral and chlamydial infections, and can also occur with medications. However, they are not associated with atopic disease.

Q2554
External Disease & Cornea
What underlying disorder should be suspected in a patient with prior bariatric surgery and bilateral corneal ulceration (as depicted in this image)?
Correct answer: B. vitamin A deficiency
Rationale
Several etiologies can lead to corneal melts or ulceration, including infection, trauma, connective-tissue disorder, or systemic ischemic vasculitis (rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, rosacea, atopic disease, Wegener granulomatosis), xerosis (Sjögren syndrome, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, mucous membrane pemphigoid, vitamin A deficiency), and exposure (cranial nerve [CN] VII palsy, thyroid ophthalmopathy, ectropion, lagophthalmos).
Specifically in this scenario, patients with a history of bariatric surgery are at risk for malabsorption of vitamins (including vitamin A). Vitamin A deficiency ophthalmic findings normally include conjunctival xerosis (with or without Bitôt spots) and corneal xerosis prior to corneal ulceration.

Q2555
External Disease & Cornea
A newborn baby is noted to have bilateral, central corneal opacities. Ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) shows iris and lenticular adhesions to the cornea. What is the most likely diagnosis?
Correct answer: D. Peters anomaly
Rationale
The stem describes Peters anomaly, which is characterized by the presence of a central or paracentral corneal opacity at birth. This is due to the localized absence of the corneal endothelium. Peters anomaly type I is characterized by iridocorneal adhesions, and Peters anomaly type II is characterized by corneolenticular adhesions. Glaucoma is present in 50% of patients with the condition.
Congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy (CHED) is characterized by thickening of Descemet membrane, with sparse, atrophic corneal endothelial cells. Posterior embryotoxon involves a thickened and anteriorly displaced Schwalbe line. Sclerocornea is a nonprogressive, noninflammatory scleralization of the cornea. Sclerocornea, CHED, and posterior embryotoxon can all manifest as a cloudy cornea but do not have iris or lenticular adhesion to the cornea.

Q2556
External Disease & Cornea
Lattice corneal dystrophy is characterized by the deposition of what material in the corneal stroma?
Correct answer: D. amyloid
Rationale
Lattice corneal dystrophy is a bilateral autosomal dominant condition, with the deposition of amyloid within the central corneal stroma. It is a form of primary localized amyloidosis. The amyloid forms typical branching linear opacities and is deposited by the epithelial and stromal cells, most heavily in the anterior stroma. Pathologically, the amyloid is visible in hematoxylin and eosin stains as eosinophilic fusiform deposits, which stain positive with Congo red and show metachromasia with crystal violet. Amyloid exhibits dichroism and "apple-green" birefringence with polarized light. Lattice dystrophy may recur in corneal grafts. The TGFB1 (formerly BIGH3) gene has been shown to undergo multiple mutations, which can variably lead to Reis-Bückler, Avellino, granular, or lattice dystrophy.
There are 4 subtypes of lattice corneal dystrophy. Type I is the classic variant, with visual or corneal epithelial abrasions by the end of the first decade. It is linked to 5q31, with type A amyloid. Type II (Meretoja syndrome) shows symptoms by the end of the second decade and is associated with mask-like facial features, blepharochalasis, cranial and peripheral nerve palsies, and dry, lax skin. A mutation at 9q34 in the gelsolin gene has been identified. The familial form has been described in Scandinavian families. In Type III, deposits are type AP amyloid, with a later onset, possibly autosomal recessive inheritance, and deeper, larger deposits of amyloid. In Type IV, deposits are larger, deeper, and more nodular, occurring only in later life with mild visual disturbance.

Q2557

A 56-year-old woman presents with a red, painless lesion on the nasal aspect of the right eye, shown in the photograph. What topical medical treatment would be appropriate for this lesion?
Correct answer: A. interferon-alfa 2b
Rationale
The image depicts a conjunctival squamous papilloma, which is caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Treatment may include systemic cimetidine, topical interferon alfa-2b, or surgical excision using no-touch technique, followed by cryotherapy and one of the medical treatment options.
Prednisolone acetate can be for topical treatment of ocular inflammation; however, it is not the preferred treatment for conjunctival squamous papilloma. Cyclosporine A 0.05% may be used to treat moderate aqueous tear deficiency. Topical mitomycin C may be used to treat ocular surface squamous neoplasia.

Q2558
External Disease & Cornea
What antifungal agent is indicated as first-line treatment of superficial keratitis caused by Fusarium species?
Correct answer: B. natamycin
Rationale
Natamycin is generally considered first-line therapy for most cases of fungal keratitis due to infection with filamentous fungi (eg, Fusarium species). Amphotericin B is preferred for treatment of yeast keratitis (eg, Candida). Voriconazole is efficacious against a variety of fungal infections, but it was shown to be inferior to natamycin in a prospective, randomized clinical trial. Fluconazole has largely been replaced by newer azoles (voriconazole, posaconazole) because of their improved ocular penetration with systemic administration. Of note, ocular penetration through intact corneal epithelium is poor for many antifungal agents, including natamycin; for deep lesions, serial epithelial debridement might be indicated to enhance tissue penetration.

Q2559
External Disease & Cornea
A 55-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of burning and irritation in both eyes. Her eyelids and conjunctivae are abnormal as shown (figure). What test might be helpful in assessing risk factors for this condition?
Correct answer: B. thyroid function tests
Rationale
The photograph demonstrates inflammation of the superior bulbar conjunctiva. This presentation, along with the patient's symptoms, suggests superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis (SLK). SLK is thought to be caused by superior bulbar conjunctival laxity with secondary inflammation from mechanical trauma. SLK has been associated with thyroid dysfunction and, therefore, thyroid function tests should be obtained.
Other conditions associated with superior conjunctival inflammation include floppy eyelid syndrome, giant papillary conjunctivitis, and trachoma. Floppy eyelid syndrome has been associated with sleep apnea, and sleep studies are reasonable in patients with the appropriate history. Floppy eyelid syndrome can be differentiated from SLK by eyelids that can be everted with minimal effort (a finding not shown here). Although systemic allergy testing may be performed in patients with allergic keratoconjunctivitis, this condition is not typically localized to the superior conjunctivae. A chest x-ray is used in evaluation for sarcoidosis or tuberculosis, which are not generally associated with SLK.

Q2560
External Disease & Cornea
A 30-year-old woman presents to the clinic for evaluation of ocular redness and mild irritation that began suddenly several days ago (Figure 1). After instillation of tropicamide and phenylephrine to dilate her pupils, the redness subsides. What is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient?
Correct answer: A. topical artificial tears
Rationale
Episcleritis is a transient condition that typically has a sudden onset. Unlike scleritis, which affects the deeper tissues, episcleritis is usually painless, is self-limited, and is not usually associated with systemic disease.
Most patients simply need reassurance that their condition is not sight threatening and can be treated with lubricants alone. Episcleritis generally clears without treatment, but topical or oral nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may be prescribed for patients bothered by the pain. Topical corticosteroid use should be kept to a minimum in this benign, self-limited condition. In cases that do not respond to lubricants and NSAIDs, a course of topical corticosteroids may be necessary and beneficial.

Q2561 · flashcard
External Disease & Cornea
What findings on computerized corneal topography are typical of keratoconus? Picture 1: Picture 2: Picture 3: Picture 4:
Answer
Picture 2

Computerized corneal topography in keratoconus typically displays high keratometry values, inferior or eccentric steepening, and inferior-superior dioptric asymmetry. Keratometry findings include high keratometry values (steeper in the periphery, especially on upgaze) and irregular mires (inability to superimpose central keratometric rings). Pachymetry will show thinning of the cornea as corneal thickness is measured from the center to the inferior position of the cornea. This is most consistent with Picture 2.
Picture 1 represents the classic "crab claw" deformity seen in pellucid marginal degeneration.
Picture 3 is an axial topography and is consistent with regular astigmatism.
Picture 4 shows a decentered myopic laser vision ablation.

Q2562
External Disease & Cornea
What medication is the most common cause of the corneal findings seen in this photo?
Correct answer: B. amiodarone
Rationale
The findings in the photo are cornea verticillata. The most common cause of cornea verticillata is amiodarone. Other common causes include chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine, indomethacin, phenothiazines, netarsudil, and tamoxifen. Cornea verticillata deposits take on a whorl-like appearance, typically bilateral and involving the inferior cornea. The deposits are usually visually insignificant and often go away with discontinuation of the offending medication. The differential diagnosis for cornea verticillata should include Fabry disease, a disease of abnormal metabolism of sphingolipids. Fabry disease (X-linked recessive inheritance) is caused by a deficiency of alpha-galactosidase A and leads to an excessive accumulation of ceramide trihexoside in the kidneys and cardiovascular system.

Q2563
External Disease & Cornea
By what route is cytomegalovirus (CMV) typically transmitted?
Correct answer: A. sexual contact
Rationale
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is a DNA virus from the herpes family that causes subclinical infections in children and a nonspecific febrile illness in adults. The virus becomes latent in the CD34+ myeloid progenitor cells, which can then be activated and allow for shedding of the virus. CMV manifests in the eye most commonly as a sectoral, necrotizing retinitis in immunocompromised patients. It can present in the anterior chamber and cornea as fine stellate keratic precipitates, epithelial and stromal keratitis, and endotheliitis. The risk of contracting CMV through casual contact is very small. The virus is passed through body fluids such as saliva or breast milk or through sexual contact.
Adenoviruses, which can cause follicular conjunctivitis, pharyngoconjunctival fever, and epidemic keratoconjunctivitis (EKC), are transmitted by close contact with ocular or respiratory secretions or contaminated fomites. Varicella-zoster virus (VZV), which can present as a dermatomal vesicular dermatitis, follicular conjunctivitis, keratitis, or acute retinal necrosis, can be spread by direct contact with VZV skin lesions or respiratory secretions via airborne droplets. The fecal-oral route of disease transmission is seen in toxoplasmosis and toxocariasis.

Q2564
External Disease & Cornea
A 45-year-old man presents with decreased vision in the right eye from an old ocular injury. On examination, there is scarring in the mid-posterior stroma of his cornea, located in the visual axis, severely limiting vision. The patient is interested in improving his eyesight. What anterior segment procedure can best treat his pathology?
Correct answer: A. deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty
Rationale
Deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty is a surgical procedure in which corneal tissue is excised down to the Descemet membrane, with replacement through transplanted corneal donor tissue. This procedure can be used in treatment of keratoconus, corneal dystrophies, and deep stromal corneal scars. It confers some advantage over penetrating keratoplasty by leaving the Descemet membrane and endothelium intact, preventing the risk of endothelial rejection. Additionally, because full-thickness corneal incisions are not needed, there is less risk of expulsive hemorrhage, retinal detachment, or cystoid macular edema.
Phototherapeutic keratectomy and superficial keratectomy can be utilized for more superficial pathology in the subepithelial layer, Bowman layer, or anterior stroma. Endothelial keratoplasty would confer little benefit in this patient.

Q2565
External Disease & Cornea
A 21-year-old myopic medical student complains of poor vision. She has been wearing glasses since age 6 but is no longer happy with the quality of her vision in glasses. Her refraction is -5.00 +3.00 × 70 20/30 OD and -4.00 +1.25 × 60 20/20 OS. Corneal topography of her right eye is abnormal as shown. What management is recommended for her?
Correct answer: B. contact lens fitting
Rationale
The topography depicts irregular astigmatism with inferior steepening, a classic finding in keratoconus. Risk factors for keratoconus include eye rubbing, allergic conjunctivitis, and certain systemic diseases (eg, Down syndrome). Since the patient is unhappy with her vision in spectacles, the best management option would be to fit hard contact lenses. Observation would not be appropriate, due to the visual complaints; penetrating keratoplasty would be premature without first maximizing nonsurgical approaches. Due to the instability of the cornea, refractive surgery is contraindicated, as there is high risk for progressive steepening and worsening astigmatism after the procedure.
Corneal crosslinking is used in patients with progressive disease. The risk of progression is greater in adolescents, who may benefit the most from this treatment. The greatest efficacy is achieved in mild to moderate cases.

An 11-year-old girl presents with a unilateral granulomatous conjunctivitis accompanied by a tender submandibular lymphadenopathy and low-grade fever. What is the most likely etiology?
Correct answer: A. Bartonella henselae
Rationale
Bartonella henselae

The presentation is that of Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome: unilateral granulomatous conjunctivitis with regional lymphadenopathy. The lymphadenopathy may occur concurrently with conjunctivitis or 1 to 2 weeks following. The primary causative agent is Bartonella henselae, which may be transmitted by a cat-scratch injury, and serology can be used in confirming the diagnosis. While no definitive standard is established for antibiotic treatment, azithromycin, doxycycline, and erythromycin are common choices.
Chlamydia trachomatis, Borrelia burgdorferi, and adenovirus are causes of follicular conjunctivitis.

For what corneal disorder is deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty an appropriate procedure?
Correct answer: B. granular corneal dystrophy
Rationale
Deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty (DALK) is appropriate in cases where the corneal abnormality is limited to the stroma, with normal Descemet membrane and endothelium. As such, granular dystrophy is the most appropriate choice. Lesions in granular corneal dystrophy involve the superficial stroma and mid-stroma.

Q2568
External Disease & Cornea
A 12-year-old boy from the Dominican Republic is referred to an ophthalmologist for evaluation. His primary care doctor noted significant darkening of his bilateral medial and lateral recti muscle insertions as well as the adjacent sclera. Furthermore, there is a similar darkening of his earlobes and nose. What urine abnormality is this patient most likely to have?
Correct answer: D. urine that turns dark when exposed to air
Rationale
This patient has examination findings consistent with ochronosis. Ochronosis is seen in alkaptonuria, a disease of tyrosine and phenylalanine metabolism deficiency, which leads to the accumulation of alkapton, a brownish/blackish material, in body tissues. Homogentisic acid accumulates in the body. Common tissues affected include the medial and lateral recti and cartilaginous tissues such as earlobes, the nose, heart valves, and tendons. This condition is seen most frequently in patients from the Dominican Republic and from Slovakia. The urine in these patients will turn dark after exposure to air. These patients frequently complain of arthropathy, which high-dose ascorbic acid can help alleviate.

Q2569
External Disease & Cornea
In a patient with a traumatic hyphema, what factor can increase the risk of developing the finding shown in the figure?
Correct answer: B. high intraocular pressure
Rationale
The combination of elevated intraocular pressure, corneal endothelial damage, and blood in the anterior chamber can result in corneal blood staining. Red blood cells within the anterior chamber release hemoglobin; the hemoglobin penetrates the posterior corneal stroma, where it is absorbed by keratocytes. Hemoglobin is broken down into hemosiderin within the keratocytes, which can result in keratocyte death. It can be difficult to detect when blood is in apposition to the endothelium on slit-lamp examination, but with close observation, early blood staining is seen by yellow granular changes and reduced fibrillar definition in the posterior corneal stroma. Blood staining can lead to a reduction in corneal transparency that can be permanent. Histologically, red blood cells and their breakdown products can be seen within the corneal stroma. Corneal blood staining often slowly clears, starting in the periphery.

Q2570

A 35-year-old woman presents with a 1-year history of decreased vision in both eyes. A slit-lamp photograph of her right eye is shown. What histochemical stain would best highlight the deposits seen in her cornea?
Correct answer: B. Masson trichrome
Rationale
The slit-lamp image demonstrates discrete deposits in the central cornea with clear intervening stroma. This finding is characteristic for granular corneal dystrophy. Masson trichrome stain is used to demonstrate the hyaline material in the stroma of patients with granular corneal dystrophy. Congo red stain is used to demonstrate the amyloid material in the stroma of patients with lattice dystrophy. Alcian blue stain is used to demonstrate the mucopolysaccharide deposits in the stroma of patients with macular dystrophy. Oil red O stain is used to demonstrate the cholesterol deposits in the stroma of patients with Schnyder crystalline corneal dystrophy.

Q2571

A 19-year-old man is referred for evaluation of ectopia lentis. The patient has a tall, thin appearance with kyphoscoliosis and abnormally long and slender fingers. The patient reports that he has not been to a doctor since he was a young child and has no known systemic abnormalities. Aside from treatment of the ectopia lentis, the patient must be referred for workup of what potentially fatal systemic association?
Correct answer: A. aortic aneurysm
Rationale
Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the FBN1 gene, which encodes fibrillin. It is associated with disorders of the eye, skeletal system, and heart. Ectopia lentis is an eye finding that is classically associated with Marfan syndrome. A cardiac evaluation is necessary to look for aortic dilation or aneurysms that can cause premature mortality in Marfan patients.

Q2572

For a patient with Thygeson superficial punctate keratitis, what is the recommended initial management?
Correct answer: A. artificial tears
Rationale
Thygeson superficial punctate keratitis is characterized by multiple, slightly elevated corneal epithelial lesions with negative staining. This can be accompanied by symptoms of foreign-body sensation, photophobia, tearing, and reduced vision. These lesions usually regress rapidly with the use of mild corticosteroids but can recur after tapering. Supportive therapy with artificial tears is often adequate in mild initial cases. Topical steroids can hasten the lesions' resolution, but use of these drugs should be minimized because the lesions often recur after the steroids are tapered. Topical cyclosporine or tacrolimus ophthalmic preparations may also be effective in causing regression of the lesions.

Q2573

What is the most likely diagnosis for a patient with bilateral crusting of the eyelashes, eyelid margin telangiectasias, papillary conjunctivitis, and peripheral corneal infiltrates?
Correct answer: B. staphylococcal blepharoconjunctivitis
Rationale
The description is classic for staphylococcal blepharoconjunctivitis. Herpes simplex blepharoconjunctivitis is characterized by a follicular conjunctival reaction, vesicular eyelid skin, or ulcerated eyelid margin lesions, and often preauricular lymphadenopathy. It is almost always unilateral, except in patients with underlying immunodeficiency or atopic disease. Vernal keratoconjunctivitis can present with bilateral papillary conjunctivitis (it is typically severe enough to be labeled "giant" papillary conjunctivitis). However, crusting of the eyelashes and eyelid margin telangiectasia are not typical features. Floppy eyelid syndrome can also cause a velvety upper lid papillary reaction, but marginal corneal infiltrates are not typical.

Q2574

Superior limbal keratoconjunctivitis (SLK) is characterized by what pattern of fluorescein staining?
Correct answer: D. superior corneal staining
Rationale
Different disease states can produce various punctate staining patterns. Superior limbal corneal staining may be seen with SLK, upper eyelid foreign body, trichiasis, or localized superior limbal stem cell deficiency.
SLK is a chronic, recurrent condition characterized by ocular irritation and injection superiorly. Ocular findings include fine papillary reaction on the superior tarsal conjunctiva, injection and thickening of the superior bulbar conjunctiva, hypertrophy of the superior limbus, superior filamentary keratitis, or fine punctate fluorescein, lissamine green, or rose bengal staining of the superior bulbar conjunctiva above the limbus with involvement of the superior cornea just below the limbus.
Corneal staining at 3 o'clock and 9 o'clock is typical of contact lens wear. Interpalpebral staining is typical of dry eye disease, exposure, and neurotrophic keratopathy. Diffuse punctate staining is typical of viral conjunctivitis, trauma, or toxicity.

Q2575
External Disease & Cornea
A 24-year-old female presents with a foreign body sensation and irritation of her right eye. On examination, the ophthalmologist notes trichiasis of the right lower lid with 2 aberrant eyelashes. The patient wants to have the lashes removed for the greatest duration possible without causing any collateral damage to the lid. What treatment would meet this criterion?
Correct answer: A. radiofrequency ablation
Rationale
Electrolysis with a radiofrequency probe is useful for removing a few eyelashes at a time and is most effective at preventing recurrence without causing collateral damage. Eyelashes removed by cutting grow back quickly, and lashes removed by epilation can recur in as few as 3 weeks. Cryotherapy can also be used to treat trichiasis, but can cause eyelid margin thinning, loss of adjacent normal lashes, and depigmentation.

Q2576
External Disease & Cornea
During treatment and recovery from a corneal abrasion, a patient develops a chalky white plaque covering the extent of the abrasion and obscuring the visual axis. What is the most likely medication being used?
Correct answer: D. ciprofloxacin
Rationale
Use of topical fluoroquinolones, especially ciprofloxacin, can result in chalky white deposits that adhere to corneal epithelial defects. A major factor in drug deposition is pH-dependent solubility of the drug. Also, patients with dry eye using eyedrops more frequently and for a prolonged period are prone to drug precipitation. Corneal deposits are more common in the interpalpebral region because of ultraviolet radiation–induced corneal damage and because of the maximum accumulation of topical ophthalmic medications in this part of the eye. These cases can be managed conservatively, avoiding debridement; deposits resolve after discontinuation of the medication.
