Q2577
External Disease & Cornea
What is the most common adverse reaction caused by topical trifluridine drops for the treatment of herpes simplex virus (HSV) keratitis?
Correct answer: B. epithelial toxicity
Rationale
Epithelial toxicity is a common adverse reaction caused by the frequent administration of topical trifluridine for the treatment of herpes simplex keratitis. It should be suspected in patients with nonhealing epithelial defects or worsening epitheliopathy. When epithelial toxicity is found, the medication should be discontinued or replaced with oral antiviral prophylaxis (eg, acyclovir, valacyclovir).
Increased iris pigmentation can be caused by administration of topical prostaglandin analogues.
Induced myopia can be seen in patients taking oral topiramate.
Follicular conjunctivitis, not papillary conjunctivitis, appears as a toxic reaction in some patients receiving topical trifluridine.

Q2578
External Disease & Cornea
A 34-year-old man has a hyphema after being struck in the right eye with a tennis ball. Primary therapy should include what intervention?
Correct answer: B. topical steroids
Rationale
Topical steroid therapy is frequently employed in the traumatic hyphema patient. Topical corticosteroids are beneficial in controlling anterior chamber inflammation and preventing synechiae formation, and they may play a role in preventing rebleeding. Topical cycloplegics are also recommended, not miotics such as pilocarpine. Patients should adopt an elevated position, not supine. Nonaspirin analgesics should be used for pain relief to reduce the risk of rebleeding.

Q2579
External Disease & Cornea
What process precedes Salzmann nodular degeneration?
Correct answer: B. hyaline deposition
Rationale
Salzmann nodular degeneration represents postinflammatory deposition of hyaline and fibrillar material, which replaces the Bowman layer. Oftentimes, patients have a history of corneal trauma, trachoma, corneal surgery, recurrent corneal erosions, or contact lens wear, but other patients present with nodules without any of these risk factors. Calcium deposition is seen in band keratopathy. Genetic dystrophies would result from mutations in various genes such as the TGFB1 gene in lattice corneal dystrophy. Lipid deposition can be seen with corneal neovascularization, which can occur following various types of keratitis; however, the Salzmann nodules do not contain lipid.

Q2580
External Disease & Cornea
What pterygium excision technique is associated with the complication seen in Figure 1?
Correct answer: A. beta irradiation
Rationale
The complication illustrated in Figure 1 is bacterial scleritis. Bacterial and fungal infections of the sclera are very rare. Most cases result from the extension of microbial keratitis involving the peripheral cornea. Trauma and contaminated foreign bodies (including scleral buckles) are possible risk factors. Bacterial scleritis has also occurred in sclera damaged by previous pterygium surgery, especially when beta irradiation or mitomycin has been used.

Q2581
External Disease & Cornea
A 35-year-old man has had recurrent episodes of pain and redness in both eyes. Given the slit-lamp appearance of his right eye (see photo), what other ocular or extraocular manifestations may develop from the known genetic mutation?
Correct answer: A. facial nerve palsy
Rationale
The figure demonstrates refractile lines (lattice lines) in the central cornea. This finding is highly characteristic of lattice corneal dystrophy. The patient's episode of pain and redness in both eyes is suggestive of recurrent erosion syndrome, a common complication in patients with lattice dystrophy. There are several types of lattice dystrophy (types I through IV). Type II lattice dystrophy (Meretoja syndrome) is associated with a mutation in the gelsolin gene and can have other manifestations of systemic amyloidosis, including facial nerve palsy, polyneuropathies and cutis laxa. Optic nerve atrophy, uveitis, and hearing loss are not characteristics of amyloid associated with lattice corneal dystrophy.

Q2582
External Disease & Cornea
A 50-year-old man born in rural Pakistan presents with 10 years of decreased vision and chronic foreign body sensation. Ocular findings are demonstrated in the figure. What is the most likely etiology of his vision loss?
Correct answer: B. bacterial infection
Rationale
Taking into account the patient’s age, clinical features, and country of origin, the most likely diagnosis is trachoma. Trachoma is caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis (serotypes A–C) and is the leading cause of preventable blindness worldwide. Although major efforts have been undertaken to decrease the incidence of trachoma, it remains endemic in the Middle East, Africa, and parts of Asia. The distinctive features are conjunctival and corneal scarring (predominantly superiorly, although severe cases can be diffuse), bandlike or stellate tarsal scarring (also typically superiorly), trichiasis, and aqueous tear deficiency. Entropion and tear duct obstruction are also common. The ocular manifestations of autoimmune disease (eg, Sjögren syndrome, mucous membrane pemphigoid) can be similar, but the superior predilection, place of birth, and relatively young age favor the diagnosis of trachoma. Cicatrizing changes from severe viral conjunctivitis (adenoviral, HSV, etc.) are possible, but still less likely. Toxic injuries (eg, from alkaline substances) tend to affect the inferior ocular surface in excess of the superior surface.

Q2583
External Disease & Cornea
What  preoperative test is most helpful when considering peripheral corneal relaxing incisions for the treatment of astigmatism at the time of cataract surgery?
Correct answer: A. corneal topography
Rationale
Limbal relaxing incisions (LRI) can correct the astigmatism contributed by the cornea. A preoperative topography reveals how much astigmatism there is and whether it is regular. Irregular astigmatism cannot be corrected as well by LRIs.

Manifest refraction includes both lenticular and corneal astigmatism and would not be useful on LRIs performed during cataract surgery as the natural lens is removed. 
Specular microscopy is used to evaluate the endothelium and contributes less to the evaluation of astigmatism.

Hartmann-Shack aberrometry is a wavefront analyzer that describes the optical aberrations of the eye for use in wavefront-guided laser refractive surgery.
